turns.text: Never initialize the SD memory card on the FX5-PLC495 without first backing up the recipe folder to the engineering PC. Initialization wipes all the FTP staging files.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So flip the switch OFF, retry once, and only then chase 41E4H. I'll set the deletion setting to 'Not delete' while I'm in there.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Retry first, and let me know if 41E4H shows up.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need your input on MR-JE-AX167 on Line 11, machining cell B. Operator keeps hearing a grinding noise from the HG servo motor during Z-axis rapid traverse, about three times a shift since Monday. No alarm, drive runs fine otherwise, and it only happens when the axis moves.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Any vibration or just noise? And the noise stops when the machine is idle, right?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, quiet when it's sitting still. Records say the motor's from 2019, around 21,000 running hours. I was thinking maybe encoder's going bad, should we just swap the whole motor out?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on, don't jump to the encoder. On this cell, bearing noise on MR-JE-AX167 usually first shows up between 18,000 and 22,000 motor running hours. You're right in that window.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so how do I confirm it before pulling anything apart?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you remove the load, jog MR-JE-AX167 at 50 mm/min and listen with a stethoscope right at the motor flange. That'll tell you if it's the bearing or the machine.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if the bearing is the problem, can we just repair it here on the line?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, if the bearing is suspect, tag the motor and send it to the Binh Duong workshop for replacement, not local repair.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. What about checking the shaft by hand? Someone said we could spin it while it's still hooked up.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't do that. Always disconnect the motor power cable and wait 15 minutes before rotating the shaft by hand to release the brake safely.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And what if I spin it and hear nothing?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then the motor's fine and you go maintain the machine itself. But if it makes noise when you turn it by hand, bearing's worn and the motor gets replaced.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: One more thing, someone suggested tweaking the servo amplifier gain parameters to kill the noise. Worth trying?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the gain to hide a noise. Check the bearing first, that's the real issue here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? MR-JE-AX841 on Line 8, cell F keeps tripping AL. 33. Three times already during the 14:00 to 16:00 shift.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: AL. 33 again? That's the regen overload, right? What did the drive recorder show?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, I pulled the capture. Bus voltage spiked to 390 VDC during deceleration of the dispensing head, and the regenerative load ratio hit 88% right before it tripped.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, that matches. Listen, on Line 8 AL. 33 usually means the regenerative resistor mounting screws have loosened after 8 to 10 months of thermal cycling.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Huh. So not the amplifier itself? One of the other guys said just swap the MR-JE out because the output stage is probably fried.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't do that yet. Before you replace any amplifier, check the regenerative resistor terminal screws with a torque wrench set to 1.2 N·m.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. And if they're already tight?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then set parameter PA02 to 1 to enable the built-in regenerative resistor and retest for one shift. See if it holds.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Oh, by the way, did the spare nozzle kit show up yet? The one for cell D.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet, delivery's supposed to be Thursday. Anyway, one more thing on this one — the dispensing head inertia on cell F went up when the new 2.5 kg nozzle was installed back in March 2024. That's part of why this axis is loading the regen resistor so hard.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That makes sense. Should I just bump the deceleration time constant in the PLC to smooth it out?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. That just hides the alarm. Check the resistor first like I said.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll grab the torque wrench after lunch. Are you on second shift tomorrow?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I'm on second shift all week. Let me know what the screws read.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we've got a problem on MR-JE-AX671 in Palletizing cell E. Alarm 35.1 tripped three times this morning, always within two seconds of starting the new palletizing recipe. The display alternates between 35 and 1. It only happens during the fast traverse segment.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 35.1 is command frequency error — input pulse frequency too high. Before you even think about swapping the amplifier or touching Pr. PA13, first verify the PLC pulse output frequency against the drive rating. That new recipe jumped the axis from 1200 to 1800 mm/s, which is beyond the original 1200 design, so the commanded frequency could simply be out of range.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if the frequency is within the drive rating, do I just widen the filter in PA13? That's cause two in the manual, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on. If the commanded frequency is within the drive rating but the filter is marginal, reduce the recipe acceleration ramp by 15 percent before changing any drive parameter. And remember the 2022 palletizing upgrade left the PLC pulse train filter at the default 1.5 ms — nobody ever retuned it after the higher-speed recipe came in. So it's sitting right at the edge.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Do we know if the drive itself is actually failing? Should we have a spare MR-JE on standby?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't jump to replacing the drive. The manual lists command pulse frequency and the PA13 filter setting as causes, not a dead amplifier. But before any of that, check the PLC-to-drive pulse cable shield grounding at the cabinet entry first. Last time on Line 5 we had a loose shield that caused intermittent 35.1 alarms during fast moves — looked exactly like this.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so the order is: verify PLC pulse frequency versus drive rating, check the shield grounding, then if the frequency is fine and the filter's marginal, back off the accel ramp 15 percent before touching PA13. And only correct the PA13 filter if the command pulse frequency is genuinely out of the filter range.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. And don't just set PA13 to the widest filter right away — the manual's cause four says check the operation pattern and confirm the controller command isn't exceeding permissible speed first. Run it and call me if 35.1 comes back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with the FX5-PLC772 on Line 12, Packaging cell D. The HMI showed a communication alarm on the serial link at 14:20 today, and I read SD8500 as 7010H.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 7010H on channel 1, okay. When does it actually happen — steady, or only during certain movements?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It's intermittent, two or three times a shift. Always while the carton indexer is running at 45 packs per minute. We replaced the RS-485 cable to the barcode scanner last week, but no PLC parameter changes recently.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On this FX5-PLC772 at Line 12, 7010H almost always comes from the scanner side. Its 24V supply dips when the carton indexer starts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So you think it's the scanner power, not the PLC module? I was about to swap the communication module.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before touching the PLC, put a meter on the scanner supply at terminal TB2 and watch it during a cycle. If it drops below 21.5V, the error is electrical, not protocol.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if it does dip below that, what's the fix? Do we change the baud rate to 38400? Someone suggested that.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the baud rate. 7010H is parity, overrun, or framing — the manual says check wiring and communication settings, not blind parameter changes.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The site workaround is to add a 1000 microfarad capacitor across the scanner 24V terminals, then re-torque the shield clamp to 0.5 newton-metres.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, cap across 24V and re-torque the shield clamp. Did we see this before on this cell?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, back in March 2023 we had a similar 7010H on this cell. That one was fixed by re-terminating the shield at the scanner end, not by replacing the PLC.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So check TB2 voltage during a cycle first, then cap and shield clamp if it dips. I'll measure now and report back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on FX5-PLC437. Around 09:14 the SCADA HMI on Line 7 lost comms to the PLC for 45 seconds right in the middle of dispensing cycle 1123.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 45 seconds, huh. What's the event log showing for that window?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: MC protocol error code 7143H, ASCII '7143'. It's logged three times in the last 8 hours, and every single time it's within the first 10 seconds after a recipe change.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Recipe change only, that's the tell. Before you send the new recipe, clear the SCADA driver's frame buffer. Stale frames sitting in there will trigger that first-detected error every time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. But also, line 7 shows 12 rejected units after each timeout — the dispense head keeps moving without updated position data.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, and whatever you do, don't power-cycle FX5-PLC437 during one of these timeouts. The dispensing head can lose its absolute position and then you're stuck doing a 20-minute homing routine.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Good to know. One of the guys was saying we should just swap the Ethernet module right away. Should we?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, no. 7143H is a transient communication fault, not a hardware failure. First thing I'd check is the Ethernet cable shield grounding at the panel — a loose drain wire caused 7143H timeouts twice back in 2023.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Shield grounding, got it. Anything else on the driver side? Ambient temp at the panel is 41°C, but nothing's been changed in 30 days.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then set the MC protocol receive timeout to 3000 ms in the SCADA driver for Dispensing cell A. There's a 2.5-second network burst from the welding robot nearby — that timeout lets you ride straight through it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So shield grounding first, then the timeout setting, and clear the buffer before recipe changes. What about just ignoring it since it clears on its own after 45 seconds?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't ignore it. The manual says when multiple errors hit at once, only the first-detected code gets reported — so those repeated 7143H events line up exactly with your rejected units on Line 7.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll start with the shield grounding at the panel and go from there.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember the order — grounding, then the 3000 ms timeout, then buffer clear on recipe change. Don't touch the power.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need a hand. FX5-PLC794 at Packaging cell E, Line 9 — it couldn't upload the daily production log this morning at 09:15. SP.FTPPUT came back with completion status 0002H in (s1)+1.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 0002H? Yeah, on this line that usually means the external FTP server was unreachable. First thing I do is ping 192.168.10.25 from the PLC's Ethernet diagnostics.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. I was about to swap the Ethernet module, honestly.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold off on that. The manual says check the completion status first and act on the error code before you start replacing hardware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Did anything change on the network lately? They rerouted the cable through a new patch panel on the 10th.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's probably it. The patch panel port for FX5-PLC794 was miswired during that 2024-06-10 reroute, so you get intermittent link loss. Reseating the RJ45 at port 14 brings it back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Port 14, got it. Also, should I just change the FTP server IP? Maybe it drifted.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch that. Check the IP address entered at login and log in again — the manual's clear on that. And 192.168.10.25 hasn't changed in six months.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. By the way, did you see the spare-parts delivery came in? New sensors for Line 9.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, saw the boxes by the crib. We'll sort them after lunch. Before you call IT about this, always verify the FTP server service is running on 192.168.10.25 — check port 21 with a laptop.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Port 21 with the laptop, okay. And if the server really is down?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then temporarily store the log file on the PLC's SD card and retry the SP.FTPPUT once the server's back up.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. The filler on Line 7 was acting up again too, by the way.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That thing's always something. Don't worry about it now, focus on the packaging cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: You on second shift tomorrow or the early one?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Early. Swapped with Somchai so I can leave by four.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Nice. Okay, I'll go ping 192.168.10.25 from the diagnostics and check port 14.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Reseat that RJ45 first, then redo the transfer. If it still fails after that, ping and check port 21 before you escalate.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Grab lunch after?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, give me twenty minutes. Let me know how the SP.FTPPUT retry goes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Sure thing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we got alarm 54.1 on MR-JE-AX717 at 14:30 shift start. I can see an 8 Hz vibration on the motor, and Configurator2 shows continuous oscillation on the torque ripple monitor.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 54.1 means it detected oscillation. Did you already touch any gain parameters?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, not yet. I measured the equipment resonance at 172 Hz, but the machine resonance suppression filter is still at 145 Hz. Machine ran fine for 11 months, but we introduced a new product size last week and now the axis moves at 2800 mm/s.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch any gain parameter on this cell, first reduce the speed override to 80% for one cycle.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Just 80% for one cycle? Then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Back in 2022, this same MR-JE-AX717 had a similar 54.1 after a product change. The fix was raising the machine resonance suppression filter to 172 Hz. So set the filter to your measured 172 Hz, then re-run auto tuning with a 2 mm positioning step.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, filter to 172 Hz, then auto tuning with 2 mm step. Should I also check the encoder? The manual lists encoder malfunction as a possible cause for alarm 54.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't jump to replacing the motor or encoder yet. If the 172 Hz filter does not stop the 8 Hz oscillation within two cycles, then suspect mechanical looseness in the coupling rather than the encoder.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And what about turning off auto tuning and manually increasing the gain to stiffen the axis? Someone suggested that.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that without first measuring the resonance frequency. You already measured it at 172 Hz, so use that. Set the machine resonance suppression filter to 172 Hz, then re-run auto tuning with a 2 mm positioning step.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll reduce speed override to 80% for one cycle first, then set the filter to 172 Hz and re-run auto tuning with a 2 mm step.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And remember, if the 8 Hz oscillation doesn't stop within two cycles after that, check the coupling for mechanical looseness. Don't waste time swapping the encoder.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with a fault on FX5-PLC253, Line 7 Dispensing cell C. The operator said the inverter on the dispensing nozzle drive stopped responding to speed commands at 14:20.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, what are the error flags showing on the PLC?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: SM8510 is ON on channel CH1 and SD8510 has error code 7010H. It happened twice this week, both times within 10 minutes after the cabinet door was opened for filter cleaning. No program or inverter parameter changes in the last 3 months.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, 7010H is a parity, overrun or framing error. Before you even think about replacing any board, go verify the CH1 shield drain is landed on the cabinet PE bar, not on the inverter 0V terminal.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And if the shield is fine, what next?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check the inverter comm cable connector J3 first. That one loosens after about 6 months of cell vibration and causes intermittent framing errors.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I just swap the CH1 communication board while I'm in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. 7010H is usually caused by cabling, grounding or supply voltage before any board failure. And don't just reset SM8510 and ignore the code, because SD8510 tells you whether it's a framing or parity issue or an inverter communication error.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. Anything else I should check on the supply side?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Historically, 80% of 7010H faults on Line 7 trace to the 24 VDC supply sagging below 21.5 V when the dispensing heater cycles. So watch that supply while the heater kicks in.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if it comes back again during the same shift?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If 7010H recurs within one shift, temporarily set inverter parameter Pr.37 to 1 ms and log the change in the Line 7 comm logbook.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. Shield drain to PE bar, J3 connector, 24 VDC sag, then Pr.37 to 1 ms if it repeats, and log it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. Work through it and let me know what you find.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on Inspection cell C, Line 6. The external HMI can't talk to FX5-PLC746 and it's throwing error code 0x0C every 15 minutes. I tried the loopback test from the HMI but got no response.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, PLC in RUN mode right now?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, still in RUN. Same test worked on the identical FX5 on Line 5 yesterday, so I figured the CPU here is shot. Should I just swap the FX5-PLC746 CPU out?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the CPU — the loopback test only confirms whether the connection is correct, so the fault could just be the cable or the connector. Replacing the CPU is a waste and won't fix a physical layer problem.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, so what do I check first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you run any loopback test, always look at the link LED on the FX5 CPU Ethernet port. If that LED is off, reseat the cable before you do anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Link LED… okay, let me look. Also, could I run the loopback from the SCADA station over the network instead? Might be easier than climbing into the cell.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that — the loopback test is restricted to the directly connected FX5CPU, it can't be used on a remote station over the network. You have to be plugged in locally.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, local only. The link LED is actually off on the CPU port. Cable was just replaced after a forklift tore up the old one.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There you go — reseat that cable first. And remember back in 2022 we had a loopback failure here at Binh Duong that turned out to be a loose shield on the RJ45 connector, not a faulty CPU. Check the shield crimp while you're at it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, the RJ45 feels a little loose in the port. I'll push it in and check the shield. Should I also run Clear Error again? I already did subcommand 0000 twice and the 0x0C keeps coming back.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Clear Error won't help here. That command doesn't reset communication errors caused by physical layer issues — it only clears internal error flags. So the 0x0C will keep showing until the physical link is good.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, cable is reseated and the link LED is on now. So I can run the loopback test right away?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. On this cell the loopback test has to be run with the PLC in STOP mode — if you leave it in RUN, you get intermittent timeouts from scan interference and you'll chase a ghost.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Stop mode, got it. Anything else before I switch it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Just confirm the link LED stays solid after you reseated it, like I said about checking the port first. Then flip to STOP and run the loopback.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: LED is solid. Switching to STOP now… okay, running the loopback test from the HMI.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: What's it say?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It passed. Communication's normal now, no more 0x0C.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Put it back in RUN and watch the HMI for a bit. And next time don't reach for the CPU swap — check the link LED and the RJ45 shield first, like we did here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Thanks, that saved us a CPU.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, you got a minute? The i4L-R358 at Dong Nai Line 10, cell D - the emergency stop button did nothing on Tuesday at 14:15. Robot just kept going.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Did nothing at all? What about fault codes, anything on the pendant?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No code. It runs fine otherwise. I reseated the XSYSTEM cable and it still won't stop. Two door interlocks and a light curtain are on that cable.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, listen. At Dong Nai Line 10, the door interlock switch on the cell D rear gate has historically been the first failed device in this emergency stop circuit. So don't start swapping buttons yet.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right. So how do I find which one is holding it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Use the XFP jumper plug, part 10052-000. Put it on the XSYSTEM cable, one device at a time, to isolate which safety device is holding the circuit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: One at a time. And I just leave it in and see if the E-stop works?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you jumper anything, verify the robot is in a safe state and no personnel are inside cell D. Then jumper one device.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And if the E-stop comes back when I jumper the rear gate interlock?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On the i4L-R358, if the XFP jumper restores the emergency stop function, the fault is in the bypassed device, not the robot. So that rear gate interlock is your culprit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. Hey, did the spare parts order come in? We're low on those door switches.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. Should be here after lunch. And don't leave that XFP jumper installed permanently to keep production running - it bypasses a safety device instead of isolating the faulty one for repair.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll pull it once I confirm the rear gate switch. Thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Morning, we've got a problem at Plant Hanoi Line 2. The i4L-R390 in Palletizing cell E won't power ON — no LEDs, no fault display at all when the operator flips the control power.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Night shift swapped out the 24 VDC control power supply on Sunday and re-terminated the wires at the Primary Interface Panel. I put a meter on the supply output and it reads 23.9 VDC, but the robot still won't come up.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Cell was running fine Friday afternoon before that supply replacement, so something in the re-termination went wrong. Junior, you're thinking it's the controller board?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, honestly with good voltage at the supply and still nothing lighting up, I figured we just pull the robot controller board and swap it. That's usually the next step when there's no display.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go pulling the controller board yet — the manual says check control power wiring polarity and voltage and the 24 VDC connector fastening first. A dead board is the last thing to suspect, not the first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, but the meter already shows 23.9 VDC at the supply. Isn't that good enough to rule the power side out?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On the i4L-R390 a 23.9 VDC reading at the supply can still fail if the connector at the Primary Interface Panel is only half-latched after wire re-termination. The meter reads fine at the source but the robot never sees it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: So at Palletizing cell E, always reseat the 24 VDC Control Power connector with an audible click before you chase any internal faults. Go do that and tell me what you hear.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Junior, while you're in there — could we just jumper past that connector to force power on and see if it boots?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't bypass the 24 VDC Control Power connector to force power on. That skips the polarity and fastening checks we need, and you risk blowing internals.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And check control power polarity at the Primary Interface Panel before you go looking at ground connections. Like I said about the manual — polarity and voltage first, fastening first.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Reason I'm pushy on polarity: Hanoi Line 2 had a 2022 incident where reversed control power polarity blew the internal 24 VDC input fuse on the Primary Interface Panel. Took us half a day to find that fuse.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll reseat the connector till I hear the click, then check polarity at the panel before touching anything else.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. If it still won't power ON after that, call me and we'll meter the fuse at the Primary Interface Panel — but reseat and polarity first, every time on this cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with FX5-PLC183 on Line 1, Pick-and-place cell E. It stopped communicating at 14:20 today. The HMI showed 2DA6 then 2DAB. The log shows someone changed the IP to 192.168.10.55 and port to 5001. Cable's untouched and the switch link LED is green.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch anything, check the last edited parameter. On this cell, 90% of 2DA6 events follow a download of a changed IP address.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the IP change is the likely cause? Should I just fix the IP and port?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on. Before changing any parameters, note the current IP and port on the panel label. That keeps us from overwriting the validated line network settings.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. The label says IP 192.168.10.53 and port 5000. The log shows 192.168.10.55 and 5001 were set.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That 5001 looks wrong. In March 2024, a similar 2DAB event was caused by an old port number 5000 left in the PLC project after a laptop swap.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the port should be 5000, not 5001. What about the IP? 192.168.10.55 seems close to the label.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The line uses a fixed IP range 192.168.10.51 to 192.168.10.60. Any address outside that range is rejected by the line switch. 192.168.10.55 is inside, but it's not the validated address.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I should set it back to 192.168.10.53 and port 5000?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Restore both to the panel label values. Then download and check the HMI clears.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I replace the Ethernet cable or power-cycle the PLC first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. 2DA6 points to a parameter error, not a physical link fault. And don't power-cycle without saving the project; that won't clear a parameter mismatch and may lose recent edits.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll restore the IP and port from the label, save, download, and verify.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we got a problem on Line 4, Assembly cell C. This morning at 06:30 start-up, the FX5-PLC441 showed error code 7646H on the comm diagnostic screen. The inverter kept running with no alarm, but the IVMC instruction wouldn't write the new speed parameter. It happened twice this week, both times within 10 minutes after a recipe change. No hardware swaps lately, just routine cleaning three days ago. I'm thinking maybe we should just replace the inverter—7646H sounds like a hardware fault to me.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the inverter—that code isn't a hardware fault. 7646H means both send data 1 and send data 2 have mode errors, so the inverter rejects both but doesn't alarm stop. Before any IVMC write, you need to verify the inverter is in computer link operation mode by checking parameter Pr.79 equals 2 on the keypad. On this line, a recipe change often leaves the inverter in local mode, so always reset it to remote mode via the keypad after a recipe update.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, that makes sense. Another guy suggested power-cycling the PLC to clear the error, but I wasn't sure.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't power-cycle the PLC—that won't correct the inverter mode setting, and the error will just come back on the next IVMC instruction. If 7646H appears, first re-send only send data 1 with send data 2 disabled, then re-send both after confirming mode correction. Also, the site standard for this cell is to set inverter parameter Pr.340 to 10 to allow computer link mode without a separate mode switch.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So I should check Pr.79 first, then try the send data sequence. By the way, did you hear about the spare-parts delivery for the other line? They said it's coming Thursday.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I heard. But back to this—like I said about checking Pr.79 equals 2, that's the first thing. And remember, after a recipe update, always reset to remote mode via the keypad. That should keep 7646H from coming back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll go verify Pr.79 and then try re-sending send data 1 only. Thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand. FX5-PLC244 at Line 4, Inspection cell C — tried to change the IP address this morning and it just won't take. HMI shows error 1921H, and the module diagnostics says IP address storage area clear error code. I wrote the new settings into Un\G50 to Un\G55, then toggled both the Write request and Clear request bits to force it, and it failed twice in a row.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Did you check the Ethernet module? If it's throwing errors like that, maybe the module itself is going bad. We've got a spare in the cabinet — could just swap it out and see.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the Ethernet module. Error 1921H means the request sequence is wrong, not a hardware failure. First thing — verify that the Write request Un\G56 and Clear request Un\G58 are not both ON in the same PLC scan.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So they shouldn't be on at the same time? I think I toggled them pretty much together. What's the right way to sequence it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, this FX5 IP change function needs a 100 ms delay between setting the Write request and any Clear request — that's what keeps them from activating simultaneously. And like I said about checking Un\G56 and Un\G58, don't just reset the PLC to clear the error without checking those bits first, or it'll just come back.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Speaking of which, did the spare-parts delivery come in for the line 4 proximity sensors? I need to sign for it before lunch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Back in 2023 we had a similar simultaneous write/clear request on Line 4 and it caused a communication lockup that needed a full power cycle of the PLC. So after you correct the request sequence, always cycle power to the FX5 to make sure the new IP address is stored in non-volatile memory.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it — check the bits aren't both on, wait 100 ms between Write and Clear, then power cycle. I'll redo it that way and let you know.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we got Alarm 52.6 on MR-JE-AX778 twice this week at Pick-and-place cell C — once at 14:32, once at 09:17. Both times right after the operator pushed the arm by hand to clear a jam while the servo was off. It shows 52.6 on the amp and the controller log caught it. No push, no alarm.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, on Line 3 that 52.6 after manual pushing is usually a worn brake in the HG motor, not the amplifier. Don't go swapping the amp yet.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So how do I confirm it's really the brake and not something else? Should I just replace the amp to be safe?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, before replacing any part, measure the motor shaft position at servo-off with a dial gauge to confirm external movement. That's the first check for 52.6 — you need to see the shaft actually moved while the servo was off.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, and if the dial gauge shows movement, then what? Is the brake the usual suspect on this cell?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The HG motor on cell C has a known brake wear issue after 8,000 hours, so check brake torque first. If the brake is weak, that's your root cause.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And until we can swap the brake, can we do anything to stop the nuisance alarms? The line keeps tripping.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the brake is weak, temporarily reduce the servo-off time by setting parameter No. PC05 to 50 ms to avoid nuisance 52.6 alarms. But don't just raise the alarm level to ignore it — that masks the root cause and can lead to uncontrolled movement.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, MR-JE-AX779 tripped again on Line 8, pick-and-place cell A. Alarm 20.1 on the servo display, third time this morning.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Third time? What's the interval?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: About 45 minutes each time, after continuous running. Motor cables are tight, and I only see 20.1, no 1E or 1F.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Lunch is at 11:30 today, by the way. They're doing the canteen menu change, so don't be late.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So should I just swap the encoder? 20.1 is a receive data error, right? Maybe the encoder's gone bad.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on, don't pull the motor yet. On this cell, 20.1 usually shows up when the encoder cable shield isn't grounded at the amplifier end. Check and re-terminate that shield first, before you even think about replacing the encoder.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Also, the spare-parts delivery for Line 5 got pushed to tomorrow afternoon, so don't count on that box today.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. But why now? It was fine before the cell modification.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Because that new cable tray they put in on the 10th runs parallel to the VFD motor cables for 2.5 meters. That's inducing noise, and that's what's triggering 20.1 intermittently.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Can we just reset it and keep running for now? We're behind on the pick-and-place quota.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, manual says 20.1 stop method is EDB, so you stop. And with that routing, the noise will just come back.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Line 3 is also acting up, so keep an eye on both cells while you're at it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: For a temporary workaround, route the encoder cable through a separate conduit away from the VFD cables, and add a ferrite core near the amplifier connector.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And remember 2023, same 20.1 on Line 8 — we solved it by replacing the encoder cable with a shielded twisted-pair type rated for 600 V. Keep that in mind if the shield fix doesn't hold.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, at 14:20 the palletizing cell D HMI popped 'MC protocol NAK error code 1C' on the FX5-PLC458, three times in ten minutes, right after the robot asked for a pallet position. Power-cycling the HMI clears it but it's back within 15 minutes.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Three times already? And it's only Line 10 cell D, or other cells too?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Just cell D. I was thinking we swap the FX5-PLC458 CPU module right away, that's the fastest way to rule out hardware.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the CPU — 1C is a transmission sequence problem, not a hardware failure. On this cell it usually means the HMI's send timing is 20 ms faster than the PLC scan, so add a 30 ms delay in the HMI request.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And don't just reset the HMI to clear it. For this error class the manual says initialize the entire transmission sequence, not only the HMI.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: We had the same 1C thing back in 2022, right? Took us half a shift.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly — in 2022 that 1C on Line 10 was a loose shield on the RS-485 cable near the robot, not the PLC at all. So while you're in there, check that shield.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. How many times should I let it trip before I do the full sequence init?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Always initialize the transmission sequence after three consecutive 1C errors, otherwise the PLC just keeps the error flag until the next power cycle.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: By the way, the spare-parts delivery for Line 11 got pushed to Thursday, so don't count on that conveyor motor today.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Noted. Also, are we still doing lunch at 11:30 or is it after the shift handover?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: After handover, like always. Back to the cell — the site standard here is HMI retry count 3 and timeout 500 ms, that's how we avoid NAK storms.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll set retry 3 and timeout 500 ms, check the RS-485 shield by the robot, and add the 30 ms delay in the HMI request.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And like I said about the sequence init — three consecutive 1C errors and you reinitialize the whole transmission sequence, no shortcuts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand with FX5-PLC815 on Line 2, Inspection cell D. The HMI keeps showing intermittent communication failures, roughly every 2 to 3 hours, and it's always around shift changes.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: What error code is the PLC actually returning?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It gives 05H hex. I only see it when the inspection camera triggers a batch read of 300 bit points from the PLC. If I limit that same read to 200 points, no error at all.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, when 05H only shows up on large bit reads, first thing is to count the requested points. The BR command is limited to 256 points per request.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So 300 points is over the limit. Should we swap out the PLC communication module then? I figured 05H meant a hardware fault.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the module. At this site, the root cause of 05H is usually an oversized single request, not a faulty PLC communication module.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Then why did it start now? The cable was replaced last week after a forklift damaged the old one, but that didn't change the camera program.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The cable isn't your problem. The inspection camera program here was updated 3 months ago to request 300 points, but the PLC communication buffer was never resized to match.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So how do we fix it without rewriting the whole camera sequence?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Split the 300-point read into two BR commands of 150 points each, and add a 20 ms delay between them.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That delay lets the buffer drain so you don't get overflow on the second request.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: A colleague also said to just bump the communication timeout to 5 seconds, because he thinks the PLC is responding too slowly.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That won't help. The timeout isn't the issue, the oversized single request is. Keep it to two 150-point reads with the 20 ms gap and watch the HMI for a shift or two.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood, I'll make that change and keep an eye on it. Thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need your help. The FX5-PLC994 on Line 8, Machining cell C threw a 3F92H Ethernet error at 14:20 yesterday. It happened right after we replaced a VFD on the 11th during scheduled maintenance.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Did you reset the CPU and switch it back to RUN?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, I did, but the error came back within 30 minutes. No other error codes, just 3F92H. The machine was down for 45 minutes.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay. First thing: that new VFD was mounted 15 cm closer to the PLC cabinet than the old one. That extra proximity is radiating more noise into your Ethernet line.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So you think the VFD is causing it? I was about to swap the CPU module because the manual says 3F92H is a memory error.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't swap the CPU yet. Before you even think about replacing PLC hardware, check the grounding on that VFD and route its motor cables at least 30 cm away from any PLC communication cables.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll check the grounding and move the motor cables. What if the error still comes back after that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On this line, we've had two similar incidents. Adding a ferrite core on the Ethernet cable near the PLC cut the 3F92H recurrences by 80 percent. Try that next.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Ferrite core near the PLC, got it. And if it still persists after that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If 3F92H still persists after all that noise mitigation, then swap the Ethernet module with a known-good spare from the warehouse before you escalate to Mitsubishi.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so first grounding and cable routing, then ferrite core, then swap the Ethernet module. I won't touch the CPU yet.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And remember, the VFD being closer to the cabinet is the root cause here. That's why the manual says reduce noise first, not replace hardware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on i4L-R417 — ACE keeps saying 'No controller found' when I scan. It was fine until we swapped that safety interlock yesterday afternoon.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing — did you reset and verify the safety circuit after the interlock replacement? The controller won't allow ACE discovery until that's done.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I don't think so, I just powered it up. Should I swap the Ethernet cable? I used a new one and didn't check the link LEDs.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go swapping cables yet — on i4L-R417 the Ethernet switch port 7 was flaky last month, so use port 3 for ACE connections.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. But honestly, do we even need ACE? Can't I just program it from the teach pendant?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't skip ACE — the software has to be installed on the PC before you can connect to the robot, that's not optional.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And while you're at it, check the controller's Ethernet settings. After a safety circuit reset they can revert to the default IP 192.168.0.1 — check that first before anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll check the IP. Anything else that trips up ACE discovery?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, ACE discovery often fails if the PC firewall is enabled. Disable it temporarily for the initial connection.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so reset the safety circuit, use port 3, check the IP, and turn off the firewall. Let me go through those.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And like I said about the safety circuit — reset it and verify it before you expect the controller to allow ACE discovery. That's the order that matters after an interlock swap.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll verify the safety circuit first, then recheck the port and IP.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Once the safety circuit is verified and you're on port 3 with the firewall off, ACE should find the controller.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, on MR-JE-AX949 at Line 12, Palletizing cell A, the vertical axis coasted about 8 cm after a stop command this morning. Last month it was only about 2 cm. No alarms on the MR-JE display, and it happens mostly after downward moves. I saw it five times already. We did switch to a heavier pallet pattern—28 kg instead of 20 kg.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't just swap the MR-JE amplifier yet—the manual points at increased load exceeding the inertia ratio or brake failure before amplifier replacement. On Line 12, always verify the mechanical brake with the servo motor disconnected and the shaft turned by hand before changing any drive parameters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so should I just bump up the servo gain to stop the coasting? I thought that might make it hold better.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't adjust the servo gain first—the manual says to check the load and brake before that. MR-JE-AX949 has a history of brake wear at about 18 months of service because the palletizing cycle uses frequent vertical stops. So disconnect the motor and turn the shaft by hand to feel if the brake is dragging or slipping.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll check the brake. By the way, did you hear about the spare-parts delivery? The new brake for another line is coming Thursday.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, Thursday. Back to this—remember for this cell, the permissible load-to-motor inertia ratio was locally derated to 80% of the manual value after a 2023 overload incident. So even with the heavier pallet, we're already tighter than standard.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if the brake checks out, what's a quick fix to keep production running while we order parts?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about checking the brake first—once that's done, a quick temporary workaround for excessive coasting on this axis is to lower the positioning command speed and add a short dwell before brake release. That'll buy us time until we replace the brake.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on FX5-PLC696 at Dong Nai, Line 10, machining cell B. Simple CPU communication keeps missing its 100 ms execution interval, like 3 or 4 times a shift. Not constant, just drops out.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Misses the interval, not the whole link? So it comes back on its own?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, it recovers by itself. Timeout is set to 200 ms and the monitoring time is still at the default 10 seconds. I already reseated the cable once.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch any Ethernet parameters on that PLC, pull up the CPU monitor and check the actual scan time. On FX5-PLC696 the scan went up after the last logic edit, that's where I'd start.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Scan was 8 ms before. Now it's showing 22 ms.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. Site history on this PLC says enabling the built-in Ethernet diagnostic function added about 12 ms to the scan. If you don't need it during production, disable it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That was added last month for the network health logging. I can turn it off for now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Do that. And while the scan is still heavy, raise the simple CPU communication execution interval to 250 ms and the communication timeout to 500 ms as a workaround until the scan comes down.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 250 and 500, got it. Should I swap the switch port too? Intermittent stuff is usually cabling, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't chase the cable. The root cause here is almost always the combination of a long scan time and a short execution interval, not a bad Ethernet cable or switch port.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Someone else said just set the interval to 10 ms to make it faster.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That makes it worse. You can't run simple CPU communication faster than the scan allows. And if another Ethernet function is running at the same time, it interferes with the timing too. Last time this happened on Line 10 it was exactly that.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. The 3E frame SLMP device on that network also responds slow when it's loaded.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Expected. So set the interval and timeout with margin like I said, 250 and 500, and don't leave the diagnostic function on in production.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: By the way, are you on days next week? They're changing the shift schedule again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Back on days Tuesday. Did you eat yet? I skipped lunch.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, I'll grab something after this. Oh, the spare parts order for cell C came in, the encoder's on the shelf.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good, we needed that. Anyway, once you disable the diagnostic function, watch the scan for a shift and see if the interval misses stop.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. And if it still misses after that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then we look at the logic edit itself. But nine times out of ten it's scan time plus a tight interval, keep that in mind.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. Changing the settings now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Let me know what the scan reads after. And check the other machines on Line 10 too while you're in the cabinet.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with MR-JE-AX501 on Line 3, inspection cell E. The drive keeps throwing alarm 8E.5, USB communication data number error, every time the PLC sends a position command block. It started after the PLC program update last Tuesday and happens on about one in five blocks.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing, don't replace the servo amplifier just because it says 8E. That's not automatically a hardware fault. On this cell, data-number errors usually come from a mismatch between the PLC's block counter and the drive's expected command index.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: But I already swapped the USB cable yesterday and the alarm still comes back. Should I re-terminate the cable first? Communication alarms are usually wiring, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't chase the cable yet. Before you touch any hardware, always compare the PLC's command block counter with the drive's parameter No. 0000. That tells you whether the numbers match up.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so I check parameter zero zero zero zero against the PLC counter. What should I look for exactly?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The PLC program for cell E was last changed on 2024-06-10, and in that change the block counter was incremented by 2 instead of 1. So the drive is expecting index one, but the PLC is sending index three, then five, and so on.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That would explain why it's only some blocks. But why does it only show up when we're running fast indexing?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the data-number error appears only during high-speed indexing, temporarily reduce the PLC's command send rate to 10 ms to confirm the source. That slows the counter mismatch down enough that you can see it clearly.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. By the way, did you see the shift schedule for next week? They moved me to line 2 for two days.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw that. We can talk about it after we sort this out. Like I said about the counter, check parameter No. 0000 first, then fix the PLC block counter step from 2 back to 1.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. And the spare USB cable delivery? They said it's coming Thursday.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Thursday, fine. But you won't need it for this one. Just remember, data-number errors on this cell come from the PLC counter and the drive's expected command index not matching, not from the cable.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll check parameter 0000 and the PLC counter, and if it only happens during high-speed indexing I'll drop the send rate to 10 ms to confirm.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And once you confirm it, correct the transmission data in the PLC program so the block counter increments by 1. That's the fix.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need your help with something on Line 7. After the two-hour power outage this morning, I powered up the MR-JE-AX825 on Palletizing cell C and the robot's absolute position was off by 12 mm in Z. It's happened three times this week, but only when the arm was left hanging with the 15 kg load.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Wait, was the arm hanging before power-off, or did you lower it first?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It was hanging. And the power came back at 06:15, but the motor got turned by the falling load before I switched the amplifier on. No alarm showed up, we only noticed after the first pick.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's your problem right there. On Line 7, always lower the palletizing arm to a mechanical stop before power-off. If you don't, gravity can spin the motor above 3000 r/min, and that's what causes the absolute position to shift on restoration.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I didn't know that. So it's not the amplifier itself? I was thinking maybe we should just swap out the MR-JE-AX825.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't waste a good amplifier. That 15 kg palletizing load can accelerate the HG motor to over 6000 r/min in 0.15 s if the brake releases during a power failure. The manual even says an external force over 6000 r/min with a 0.2 s acceleration time can cause deviation.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the load is spinning the motor that fast? I thought the brake would hold it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The brake should, but if it's worn or slow, it won't. We had a similar deviation on Line 7 back in 2022. Turned out to be a worn electromagnetic brake on the HG motor, not the amplifier. So before you replace anything, check that brake.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the brake. But what about the encoder cable? I was going to swap that next because it seems like a signal issue.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Cable's probably fine. The deviation happens because the motor turns while the amplifier is off or during power-on. If it spins above 3000 r/min when you switch on, the absolute position gets messed up. That's in the manual too.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So how do we fix it after it's already off? Do we just re-home it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: After any power restoration on cell C, you need to re-zero the absolute encoder using the MR-JE parameter No. PA19 before running production. Don't skip that step.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: PA19. Got it. And then we just run it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, but first make sure the arm is at a mechanical stop when you power down next time. That prevents the whole issue.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll write that in the log. Should I check the brake now or after re-zeroing?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check the brake first. If it's worn, it'll keep happening. Then re-zero with PA19.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. I'll inspect the brake and lower the arm next time. Thanks for the help.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No problem. Remember, that 15 kg load can spin it fast. Keep the arm down and you won't see this again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need to report something that just happened. I was adjusting the gripper on i4L-R771 in cell E when the arm moved on me. I had pressed the emergency stop on the pendant before going in, and it was in manual mode with motor power ON.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Wait, you went in with only the pendant e-stop? That's not enough. The e-stop on the teach pendant does not remove motor power if the controller's internal safety relay is stuck. You have to verify with a meter.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I didn't know that. I thought the e-stop killed everything. The manual says lockout/tagout is required before any maintenance, but I figured the e-stop was enough for a quick gripper tweak.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, you always lock out. Before entering any i4L cell, I always perform a lockout/tagout on the controller disconnect and then verify zero energy at the motor terminals. Every time, no shortcuts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll do that from now on. But how did it move in manual mode? I thought it couldn't move unless a program was running.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Manual mode doesn't mean safe. Motor power can stay on, and if the brake releases, the arm can drop or move. You can't assume it's dead just because no program is running.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That makes sense. I also noticed the gate was open and someone had put a jumper wire in the interlock. I didn't think much of it at the time.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That jumper on cell E has caused two near-misses in the past year. You need to remove it and replace the gate switch immediately. Don't wait.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll pull it right now. Should I also check the brake release? I'm not sure how that fits in.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, and here's a big one: the robot's brake release button on the controller can be pressed accidentally when the pendant is placed on the cell ledge. Keep the pendant in its holster.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if the pendant was sitting on the ledge, it could have hit the brake release and let the arm move even with the e-stop pressed?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. The e-stop might not have cut motor power if that relay was stuck, and the brake release could have let it move. That's why you verify with a meter and lock out.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I see. So the sequence should be: lockout/tagout on the controller disconnect, then meter check at the motor terminals before I touch anything.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's right. And after you lock out, still verify zero energy at the motor terminals. Don't trust the e-stop or the panel lights alone.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And the interlock jumper — I'll remove it and get a new gate switch ordered today.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. That jumper has been a repeat problem. Two near-misses this year is two too many. Replace the switch so the interlock actually works.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll also keep the pendant in its holster from now on so nothing bumps the brake release.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And remember, on i4L-R771 the pendant e-stop doesn't guarantee motor power is off if that internal safety relay is stuck. Always check with a meter.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Thanks. I'm glad you caught this before something worse happened. I'll write it up and make sure the lockout kit is used every time.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. No maintenance on any i4L cell without lockout/tagout on the controller disconnect and a zero-energy check at the motor terminals. That's the rule.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I tried to mount the cable tie mounts on the i4L-R709 with double-sided tape instead of drilling, but the tape failed after about two hours and a mount fell inside the outer link cover. The cables are rubbing now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that — tape won't hold up to robot motion. The manual requires drilling 0.25 inch holes, and you have to remove the outer link cover first. Section 3-4-4 covers that removal procedure.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I thought removing the cover was unnecessary and drilling might damage the robot, so I skipped it. What should I have done?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On the i4L-R709, always drill the 0.25 inch holes at the marked dimples on the outer link; the cover is thick enough there and the dimples keep the bit from slipping.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if I mess up the drilling?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We keep a spare outer link cover in the crib because drilling mistakes happen, so check the cover for cracks before you reinstall it. After drilling, deburr the holes and put a small amount of silicone sealant on them to keep metal chips out of the joint.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll pull the cover and do it properly.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Like I said about tape, the last time it was used on this robot the mounts fell into the joint and caused a Joint 3 encoder error that took 4 hours to fix.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I just finished putting the 350 mm bellows kit on i4L-R232 over in Palletizing cell C, and now it keeps hitting soft overtravel limits on the way down.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's expected. The bellows eat into the stroke — 53 mm on a 350 mm quill, both retracted and extended.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So should I bump up the z-axis speed to make up for the lost travel?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that — the stroke loss is mechanical, speed changes won't recover any of it. You need to fix the software limits instead.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Then maybe I should just pull the bellows back off to get full stroke again?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't remove them. The bellows are there for environmental protection. You just adjust the limits in software.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so what exactly do I change?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On this cell, we reduce the z-axis positive limit by exactly 53 mm in the ACE configuration after fitting a 350 mm bellows kit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Just the ACE side, or is there something in the robot config too?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Both. A 350 mm bellows kit on this robot requires updating the z-axis stroke parameter in the robot's configuration file before any test run.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Anything else before I run it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Always re-teach the palletizing approach points after bellows installation. The old points assume full stroke and will cause crashes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. Has this happened here before?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Last year, a similar overtravel on i4L-R232 was caused by forgetting to adjust the software limit after bellows were added. Like I said about the ACE limit — do that first, then re-teach the points.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on MR-JE-AX932 on Line 8. The servo motor won't rotate when I give the start command, but there's no alarm or warning on the amplifier. Operator says it was fine yesterday, then after a tool change today it just won't move. I'm thinking maybe the servo amplifier is dead, should I swap it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on, don't swap anything yet. On Line 8, first check for mechanical binding by manually turning the ball screw. If it moves freely, then we go check parameters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll try turning the ball screw by hand. But what if it's stiff? And why mechanical? The manual says torque limit or interference can cause this, but no alarm makes me think the motor itself is faulty.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We had a similar incident in 2022 on Line 8, and it was a piece of swarf jamming the coupling, not electrical settings. No alarm doesn't mean the motor is bad. Also, before you troubleshoot the motor, make sure the safety gate is closed, because the brake release signal on this machine is interlocked with the gate.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, gate closed. I checked the ball screw and it turns freely. So now I check parameters? I saw PA11 is set to zero in the current configuration.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, when PA11 is zero, temporarily set it to 100% to test motor movement. But revert it immediately after diagnosis, don't leave it like that.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll set PA11 to 100% just for the test then put it back. So if it moves with that, the torque limit was the issue? And if it still doesn't move, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If it still doesn't move, go back to mechanical interference, like that swarf jam we had. But first always check binding by hand, then parameters. And remember to revert PA11 right after.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with FX5-PLC597 at Plant Hai Phong, Line 6, Inspection cell F. This morning at 06:42 the Ethernet diagnostics showed error code 2DA9H after the weekend power-down, and the vision camera and barcode scanner can't communicate, so production is stopped.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, before you touch any cabling, open GX Works3 and compare the active Ethernet parameter file date with the CPU's last write date. That tells us if the parameter memory got out of sync.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I restarted the PLC twice already and 2DA9H came back both times. One restart also briefly showed 2DABH. Should I just swap the Ethernet module?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the module. 2DA9H and 2DABH point to a parameter setting issue, not hardware failure, and rebooting won't clear it until the external device configuration parameters are checked and corrected. Back in 2022 we had a weekend power glitch corrupt the parameter memory on this same PLC, producing 2DA9H while all the cables and switches tested good.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the parameter file is probably corrupted. What's the first thing I should do to fix it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you rewrite anything, save a current GX Works3 project copy to the line's engineering laptop here at Plant Hai Phong. Always do that first so we have something to fall back on.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll save the project copy now. And what about that 2DABH that flashed up?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: When 2DABH shows up together with 2DA9H, first re-enter the own node port number 5001 for the inspection cell scanner before you change any external device IPs. That port setting is usually what's throwing the extra error.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got a problem with FX5-PLC758 over in Machining cell D, Line 1. After I reconfigured the network yesterday at 14:30, the Ethernet module is showing error 3073H. The PLC is still running, but SCADA comms are intermittent, maybe 5% packet loss.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: All I did was change the gateway from 192.168.1.1 to 192.168.1.254 to match the new router. Subnet mask is still 255.255.255.0, and there are no other error codes.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Maybe we should just swap out the Ethernet module? If it's throwing an error, could be the card going bad.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the Ethernet module — that error is a configuration parameter problem, not a hardware failure. 3073H means the IPv4 gateway address is outside the allowed range for this cell.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The valid gateway range here is 192.168.1.1 to 192.168.1.100. You set it to 192.168.1.254, which is outside that range, and that's what's causing the 3073H.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So should I just ignore the error and keep running? SCADA is mostly working.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, ignoring it isn't a valid solution — you'll keep getting intermittent communication loss. And before you change any network parameter, always check the gateway address against the site's IP allocation sheet first.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We had this exact thing back in 2024 — a contractor set the gateway to 10.0.0.1 and got the same 3073H. Reverting it to 192.168.1.1 fixed it right away.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so what if the router really needs a different gateway? How do I change it safely?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the gateway must be changed, use the engineering tool to update it while the PLC is in STOP mode. That avoids partial writes to the module.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: And we're sure the module itself is fine?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about the configuration parameter, the module is fine. Put the gateway back to 192.168.1.1 and the error will clear.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll revert it to 192.168.1.1 and verify against the allocation sheet before touching anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we had a close call on i4L-R819 at Dong Nai, Line 9, cell C. After I taught some new positions in Manual for 45 minutes, I switched to Automatic and the robot shot off at full speed with the override still at 100%.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's a classic. The speed override in Automatic mode defaults to 100% on i4L-R819, so you always reduce it to 25% for the first cycle after teaching.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I thought switching modes would reset it to something safe, but it just stayed at 100. And I didn't realize how fast it would move.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Nope, it keeps the previous setting. And the root cause is often that the program pointer was left at a step near the end of the cycle, so it jumps straight into fast motion. Before you ever switch to Automatic after teaching, do a dry run in Manual mode at 10% speed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So the key switch position and the override both carry over. Anything else we should be doing on Line 9 specifically?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We had a past incident on Line 9 when an operator switched to Automatic without clearing the cell, so now we use a two-person check. One person confirms the cell is clear while the other stays on the pendant.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Right, and that two-person check is not optional. If anyone's still inside that fence, the E-stop is the only thing that saves you.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll run the manual dry run at 10%, set the override to 25%, and make sure the pointer is at the start before we do the two-person check.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with FX5-PLC620 on Line 11, Packaging cell E. Since the network cabinet rework Monday at 08:15, the PLC can't finish FTP client file transfers to the line historian server. The PLC shows a communication error and the FTP client just retries every 30 seconds with no luck.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: OK, don't replace the Ethernet module yet. First, is the FTP client set to PASV or PORT?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I haven't checked that yet. The laptop on the office VLAN logs in fine with the same user name and password, but from the PLC subnet it won't go through. The cabinet rework changed the managed switch config and added a new firewall rule Friday afternoon.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I just re-enter the FTP user name and password on the PLC a few times? The office laptop login worked, so maybe the PLC just needs the credentials refreshed.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't keep re-entering the FTP user name and password on the PLC. If the office laptop works but the PLC does not, suspect a subnet-specific firewall rule or proxy setting rather than the PLC FTP client.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So what should I check first on the PLC side?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On Line 11, the historian FTP server uses passive mode, so after any firewall change the PLC must be set to PASV. That's the first thing to verify.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if PASV is already set? The firewall rule was added Friday afternoon, so maybe something else got blocked.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then check the PLC subnet can reach the FTP server control port 21 and the passive data port range 50000-50100 before you change any PLC code. Do that reachability test first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll test port 21 and the 50000-50100 range. Anything else from the cabinet rework I should look at?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, like I said about subnet-specific rules, also check the IP filter settings — the external device IP must not be denied. The last three FTP failures on Packaging cell E were caused by the PLC IP being left in the firewall deny list after cabinet rework.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the PLC IP might still be in the deny list from Monday's rework. I'll verify that and confirm PASV mode.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. Confirm PASV, confirm port 21 and 50000-50100 are reachable, and get the PLC IP out of the firewall deny list. Also, if there's any proxy involved, check that with the network administrator.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we've got a problem on Line 9. The SCADA system keeps getting fragmented SLMP responses from FX5-PLC639, and the HMI throws a 1.2-second timeout alarm. It started after we added that vision system to the same switch last week.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Fragmented responses, huh? First thing I'd check is the SCADA TCP receive buffer size. If it's set to 4096 bytes, bump it up to 8192 to match typical FX5 frame sizes. That often clears up fragmentation.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I also noticed the PLC scan time went from 8 ms to 12 ms, and GX Works3 is usually left connected for monitoring. I already tried increasing the SCADA polling rate from 500 ms to 200 ms, but the timeout still happens about twice an hour.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't bother with faster polling. GX Works3 connected for monitoring adds about 0.5 ms per scan. Disconnect it when you're not actively programming to avoid scan time creep.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Before we go too deep, just a reminder: the shift schedule for next week is posted. I need everyone to check their days off by Friday.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Also, on Line 9, that vision system was added without updating the switch QoS settings. You need to enable DSCP priority 46 for SLMP traffic to reduce latency.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I replace the FX5-ENET module? The errors seem hardware-related to me.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold off on swapping hardware. Last time this happened, the root cause was a duplicate IP address on the vision system. Check the ARP table for conflicts before touching the PLC.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the ARP table and the QoS settings. Also, did you hear about the spare-parts delivery? The new proximity sensors are supposed to arrive Thursday.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And while you're at it, double-check that receive buffer setting. 8192 bytes, not 4096. That's the first thing to fix.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Let's grab lunch after this. The canteen has that noodle soup today.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Sounds good. Just remember, disconnect GX Works3 when you're done monitoring. That 0.5 ms per scan adds up fast.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need your help with MR-JE-AX416 on Line 5, Dispensing cell A. It's tripping AL.20 about three times every eight-hour shift, and it's always in the first twenty minutes after the cell powers up.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: What's the alarm detail showing on the drive? And what happens after you power cycle it?

turns.speaker: junior_01
