turns.text: It shows 20.1. After a power cycle the axis runs fine for one to four hours, then it trips again. The encoder cable was replaced six weeks ago with a spare from stores, and the fault started about four days ago after we re-routed that cable around the new dispenser heater duct.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And does it alarm when the cabinet door is open and the heater duct is off?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, nothing. Runs clean with the door open and the duct off. So the guys are saying we should just swap the HG servo motor, since AL.20 is the encoder communication error and the encoder's inside the motor.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't pull the motor yet. On Line 5, AL.20 trips within twenty minutes of power-up usually mean the encoder cable shield is floating at the connector, not a dead encoder.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, but the cable's only six weeks old. Can we skip the ground-plate check since it's basically new?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't skip it. Before replacing any MR-JE amplifier, I swap the encoder cable with the known-good spare stored in cabinet B2 and run it thirty minutes. That tells us fast whether it's the cable or not.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And if the known-good cable runs clean for thirty minutes, what's next?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then check the external conductor of the encoder cable is connected to the connector ground plate, and fix it if it isn't. But honestly, I think your heat is the real problem here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The heater duct? How hot are we talking at the connector?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That duct added last month raised local ambient at the encoder connector to about 62 C, and we historically see 55 C on this cell. That's above what it's used to.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So we should re-route the cable away from the duct? Anything else I need to watch when we move it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, and since 2023 the cable ties on this axis must be re-torqued to 0.4 Nm after any re-route, so you don't pinch the shield drain wire. Do that and re-run it, and I bet the AL.20 stops.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need to flag something on i4L-R533. The High Power push-button on that SCARA is mounted inside the robot's workspace — about 40 cm inside the fence, right near the dispensing nozzle.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Inside the fence? That's not right. The manual is clear — High Power push-buttons have to be installed outside the robot's workspace. Full stop.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I know, but the operators like it there because they can reset fast during the dispensing cycles. Problem is they have to reach through the fence to hit it, and last run one guy's sleeve caught on it. Just a tear, no injury, but still.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: I know exactly how that happened. On Line 11, that push-button was originally outside the fence, but a contractor moved it inside. He didn't follow the manual when he did it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So what do we do? I was thinking maybe we just add a guard around the inside button so nobody brushes against it. Wouldn't that make it safe enough?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, a guard doesn't fix it. The button still sits inside the workspace, and the rule is it belongs outside, period. What we do on i4L-R533 is install a second High Power push-button outside the fence and disconnect the one inside.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Disconnect the inside one completely? One of the other techs said we don't even need to bother, because the push-button is low voltage so it's exempt from the outside-workspace rule.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's wrong. Low voltage has nothing to do with it — it's about keeping the button out of the robot's reach envelope. So we mount the new one outside and disconnect the inside one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. And wiring-wise, how does the outside button hook up? Do we run a fresh cable?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The Front Panel connects directly to the XFP connector on the XSYSTEM cable using the supplied 3 m extension cable. That's your hookup path.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Anything I should watch for on that XFP connector while I'm in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Always check that the XFP connector on the XSYSTEM cable isn't being used for any device other than the Front Panel. If something else is tapped into it, sort that out first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. So new button outside, disconnect the inside one, and verify the XFP is only feeding the Front Panel. I'll set that up.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And remember this cell runs 24/7 with that button hit about 50 times a shift, so put it somewhere the operators can reach without going through the fence.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need help — MR-JE-AX230 at Machining cell E tripped with AL.21 during rapid traverse, around 3000 rpm. It happened twice in 15 minutes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The 7-segment is showing AL. 21.2, and it only clears after I power cycle the cabinet. Encoder cable was replaced two weeks ago after the cable-track failure, about 120 hours run since.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before anyone grabs a motor, did you check the encoder cable shield is bonded to the connector ground plate? On this cell that's the first thing I look at.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, I was thinking of swapping the servo motor since the manual lists encoder malfunction for 21.2. Supervisor said maybe just bump the loop gain up too.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't turn up gain yet — check for oscillation first. And don't order a motor until the shield is verified. We had a similar AL.21.2 back in 2022 and it was a loose shield clamp inside the cable track, not the encoder at all.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Also, lunch is pushed to 12:30 today, the canteen's doing maintenance. And the spare-parts delivery for Line 4 is coming after 2.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Another thing to notice — that new welding robot installed last week on Line 4 shares the same 24 V DC supply. It can inject noise straight into the encoder circuit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So how do I prove it's noise and not the motor? I don't want to order a motor for nothing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Temporarily route a spare encoder cable outside the track and run it. That tests noise immunity before you order a new motor. If it runs clean outside the track, it's noise coupling, not the encoder.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll pull the spare cable and check the shield bonding at the connector plate first. Ambient near the cabinet is 42 C, by the way, not sure if that matters.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Fine, keep me posted. And remind the night shift about the line 3 changeover, they keep forgetting.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Heat's a side note. Focus on the shield and the 24 V shared with that welder. Once you've got the spare cable outside the track, run repeatability and see if AL.21 comes back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it — shield bonding, spare cable outside the track, then decide on the motor. Thanks, I'll report back after the test run.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? MR-JE-AX195 over at Inspection cell B keeps tripping with AL. 33, but only on the high-speed indexing move, and only after the line's been running like twenty minutes. Never on the first cycle after a cold start.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Third or fourth cycle in, right? Yeah, I've seen that before. On this line AL. 33 usually comes from the regenerative resistor bank, not the servo amplifier. First thing, check the resistor terminal screws for looseness.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Really? I was about to just swap the amplifier, since it's throwing an alarm code and all.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't bother yet. That resistor on cell B was replaced back in 2022 after a similar AL. 33, and the replacement unit has a 5% lower ohmic value than the original. So it's already a bit off-spec.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so pull the cover and torque the terminals. Anything else I should grab while I'm up there? The spare-parts guy said our contactor order's coming Thursday, by the way.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you replace any hardware, capture a drive recorder trace triggered by AL. 33. Compare the bus voltage dip against that 285 V threshold we saw in past good cycles.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I already triggered one manually after the last trip. The window shows bus voltage dropping from 310 to 285, and regenerative load ratio peaks at 82% right before the alarm. So that matches?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Matches what we'd expect, yeah. So check the resistor first, and if the resistor checks out, then temporarily reduce the inspection cell acceleration time constant from 120 ms to 160 ms and see if AL. 33 disappears.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And lunch is at eleven-thirty today, right? They moved it because of the shift handover.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, eleven-thirty. Anyway, dry-cycle with the camera off didn't trip it, which also points away from the amplifier and toward the regen side under real load.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. I'll torque the terminals and log the trace, then try the 160 ms if it's still clean.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And don't forget the press on Line 2 is still waiting on that hydraulic top-up, so swing by there after.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on FX5-PLC471 at inspection cell E. At 09:15 the Ethernet port LINK LED flickered off for about 3 seconds, HMI showed 'No communication', and it rejected 5 parts. It happened again at 09:32 and 09:58, each time recovering on its own after 2 to 4 seconds.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay. Before you even think about swapping hardware, tell me what the event history shows.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It's got 3 Ethernet errors, code 0x0201, all since 08:00, all before any power cycle. No parameter or program changes in the last 72 hours and the PLC's been running 21 days straight. I was thinking we just replace the Ethernet module since the history is full of comm errors.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go swapping the PLC or the module yet — that error code alone doesn't mean the module's bad. If the link drops for less than 5 seconds and recovers, the FX5 Ethernet module is usually fine; focus on cable and switch first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So what do I check first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On Line 8, the Ethernet switch port for cell E has a known bad RJ45 clip. Reseat that connector and tape it before you even consider replacing the PLC.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll go reseat it. Oh — did you hear the spare-parts delivery got pushed to Thursday?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw that. Doesn't matter for this, we've got the cable and clips in the cabinet. Also, check the Event History CSV timestamp against the HMI alarm log to confirm the first dropout, not just the latest one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Why the first one and not the latest?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Because the earliest timestamp tells you when it actually started, and that's what you line up with the HMI log. The latest error just tells you it's still happening.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And if I do end up swapping the module, anything special?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah — Plant Dong Nai uses a 100 ms keep-alive on the inspection cell E Ethernet connection. Verify that local parameter after any module swap, otherwise you'll get dropouts that look like the original fault.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. And are we still doing the shift handover at 14:00, or is it moved because of lunch?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Same as usual, 14:00. And like I said about the module being fine — if it drops under 5 seconds and recovers, don't touch the PLC, just work the cable and the switch port. Start with that bad RJ45 clip.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? I need to talk about the i4L-R934. During that near-miss last week, the operator couldn't reach the front panel E-stop within two seconds. It's mounted behind the safety fence now, and the panel was relocated last month to shorten cable runs, but the XSYSTEM cable is stretched tight. No one pressed the stop — the light curtain caught it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Two seconds is way too long. How far is the panel from where the operator normally stands?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Pretty far. It's inside the fence, so they have to go around. And we have a lot of temp workers on that cell who don't know the layout.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's a red flag. I always verify that the front panel is reachable within one second from the normal operator position before I sign off any cell modification. One second, not two. That's how it should be.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: One second? That's tight. So what do we do? I was thinking maybe we swap the XSYSTEM cable for a longer custom one so the panel can stay inside the workspace.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. Last time this happened on Line 9, the front panel extension cable was routed through a cable chain that added 1.2 meters of length, so we couldn't place the panel at the ideal outside-workspace location. That's why it ended up inside.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the cable chain ate up the extra length. Another guy said the light curtain alone satisfies the E-stop requirement, so the panel location isn't critical. Is that true?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, that's wrong. The manual says the front panel must be installed outside the robot's workspace for easy access during emergency stops. The light curtain is a backup, not a replacement.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so we need it outside. But the XSYSTEM cable is only 1.8 meters and the extension is 3 meters. How do we make that work without strain?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There's a workaround we used on the i4L-R934. Mount the front panel on a swing arm outside the fence, using the full 3 meter extension cable and a 1.8 meter XSYSTEM cable without strain. That gives you the reach and keeps it accessible.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: A swing arm. That makes sense. So the operator can just swing it out and hit the E-stop within one second.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And remember, before you sign off, always check that one-second reach from the normal operator position. That's the rule I never skip.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll draft the change and measure the reach from the usual spot. Thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on i4L-R786 in Palletizing cell F, Line 12. I turned the key switch left to go into Manual mode, but the robot won't jog at all.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, what's the pendant showing you right now?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It says High Power OFF, and the status LED is amber. No alarm code though. I pressed the servo enable button and tried jogging axis 1 and axis 2, nothing moves.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't swap out the pendant cable yet. The manual says Manual mode caps speed at 250 mm per sec and limits torque for safe access, so a dead cable isn't the first suspect here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So you think it's the mode entry not fully taking? I was wondering if maybe I need to manually re-enable High Power after switching over.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't try to force High Power back on manually — rotating the key switch to the left automatically disables High Power, and you re-enable it from the pendant, that's normal.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, so what should I check first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On the i4L-R786 specifically, after you switch to Manual mode, wait 3 seconds for the servo enable relay to click before you try jogging.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Three seconds, got it. And if the amber LED is still on after that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then check the pendant's deadman switch — make sure it's fully released, then re-press it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Oh, by the way, did you hear about the shift swap for Thursday? They moved the palletizing crew to nights.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah I saw that on the board. We'll deal with it later, let's get this robot moving first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Fair enough. So deadman switch reset — should I try that now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Try it, but also a really common root cause is that the Front Panel key switch was rotated left but not fully seated. Wiggle it a bit to make sure it clicks into the detent.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, wiggling it now... it did feel a little loose actually.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good, and one more thing for Plant Bac Ninh — always remove the key after entering Manual mode, so nobody can change the mode on you while you're working inside the cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. I'll pull it out. Did the spare parts order for Line 12 come in yet, by the way?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet, still waiting on the gripper pads. Should be here Friday.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. Okay, key is out, I waited the three seconds, I heard the relay click, and I reset the deadman switch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Now try jogging axis 1 slowly.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It's moving! Axis 1 is jogging now. Thanks, that key switch detent was the issue.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Nice. Remember what I said about the relay click — don't skip that 3-second wait next time, even if it looks ready.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. I'm grabbing lunch after this, want anything?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Just a coffee, thanks. And keep the key in your pocket, not in the panel.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm getting an intermittent AL.52 on MR-JE-AX856 during X-axis rapid traverse at 3000 mm/min. The alarm trips about 2 seconds after acceleration starts, and the droop pulse count hits 4500 while the alarm level is set to 4000. The servo amp was replaced two weeks ago for a different alarm and the power cable was re-terminated then.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright, first thing — no, don't just swap the amplifier again. Even though it was replaced recently, that's not where I'd start. On Line 6, the X-axis power cable connector at the motor end often loosens due to vibration; check that first before any other step.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the motor-end connector. But if it's tight, should I bump up the alarm level in Pr. PC24 to mask it? I've seen people do that.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the alarm level yet — that's just hiding the problem. The manual says set it correctly only after other checks fail. And there's more: back in 2022 we had a similar AL.52 on this same MR-JE-AX856, and it turned out to be a partially broken encoder cable near the drag chain, not the power cable.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: While you're at it, remember the spare-parts delivery for Line 6 is coming Thursday, so if you need a new cable, log it today. Also, lunch is at 12:30, so try to wrap up before then.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So I'll check the power connector and the encoder cable near the drag chain. Should I also look at the torque limit? I heard it was reduced to 80% recently.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that torque limit being at 80% is a red flag. When the torque limit is set below 90%, temporarily raise it to 100% and run a test cycle to see if AL.52 disappears. That'll tell you if it's torque-related.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll try that. But if it still trips, what else? The manual mentions servo-on timing if the motor is rotating when servo-on is enabled.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, and that's often the root cause here: the PLC enables servo-on 50 ms after the axis command starts, causing the motor to rotate before servo-on. Check the timing sequence in the PLC — that 50 ms delay is the culprit in many cases.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Also, don't forget the shift handover meeting is at 3 PM today. And the other machines on Line 6 are running fine, so focus on this one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So my plan: check motor-end power connector, inspect encoder cable near drag chain, test with torque limit at 100%, and verify servo-on timing. Anything else?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. Like I said about the connector — it's the most common cause on Line 6 due to vibration. And remember the 2022 case: encoder cable near the drag chain. Don't skip those before touching the amplifier or alarm level.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Thanks, I'll start with the connector and go from there. I'll log any parts needed before the Thursday delivery.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. If you find the encoder cable is partially broken, replace it. And if the torque limit test clears the alarm, we'll need to review why it was set to 80% in the first place. Keep me posted.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand. FX5-PLC992 over at Line 7, cell D palletizing — CH1 keeps throwing 7309H every time the cycle restarts after a three-minute idle.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 7309H, that's the master timing out waiting on a slave. Which station?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Always station 4, the palletizing conveyor VFD. Saw it about forty times between six and two today.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Forty? Did you log the timestamps? I need that for the shift report before I hand over.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, got them on my tablet. Timeout's set to 100 ms right now, 19200 baud, 8 data bits, even parity, one stop.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch any PLC parameters — at Hai Phong Line 7, that palletizing VFD on station 4 drops its RS-485 bias when the DC link falls below 480 volts. Go check the drive DC bus first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: DC bus, okay. Should I grab the meter now or after lunch? I haven't eaten since five.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Go eat, we've got twenty minutes before the next pallet run anyway. Spare parts truck is late too, so nothing's moving.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. Anything else before I head out? Was anyone messing with station 4 wiring recently?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No wiring or drive swap I know of. But on this cell I always raise the MODBUS timeout from 100 ms to 300 ms first, because that conveyor VFD scans its inputs every 180 milliseconds.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 300 ms. Won't that just slow the cycle down?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, the scan is 180, so 100 ms was always too tight. 300 gives margin without hurting throughput.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Speaking of tight — the HMI project got downloaded to that same FX5 last Friday. Could that be it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's exactly what I was going to ask. Last March a downloaded HMI project re-enabled CH1 port sharing with the Ethernet socket — that gives you 7311H and masks the real station 4 timeout.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I should check the port sharing setting before I go swapping drives? Because my first instinct was to just replace the VFD.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't swap anything yet. Before you change any slave drive, verify continuity and shield grounding of the daisy-chain at station 4 — with the line stopped and locked out.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Locked out, got it. Should I bump the timeout to 1000 ms instead and just leave it? That'd hide the fault for sure.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. 1000 ms just hides it and you'll still get drops when the DC link sags. Do the checks in order — DC bus, then port sharing, then daisy-chain.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Also, maintenance wants the Line 9 wrapper looked at after this. Belt's been slipping since Tuesday.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: One thing at a time. Get station 4 sorted first, then we'll look at Line 9.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so DC bus first, then check if the HMI project turned port sharing back on, then continuity and shield on the daisy-chain at station 4. And raise timeout to 300 ms.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. Report back what the DC bus reads before you change anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on Line 11, Assembly cell E. The MR-JE-AX485 servo amp threw alarm 37 with detail 37.3 during a point table move, right after the operator edited point table No. 5.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, 37.3 is a point table setting error. What did they change, and when exactly did the alarm hit?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: At 14:20 they changed the target position from 120.0 mm to 135.0 mm in MR Configurator2. The alarm came the instant the start signal was given and the motor didn't move at all.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Only 37.3 is showing, no other alarms. I was thinking maybe we just swap the servo amplifier since the manual says a malfunction can cause it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the amplifier yet — the manual check order says verify the point table setting first, and only then suspect a servo amplifier malfunction. On this cell, point table 5 is for the clamp approach and its position must not exceed 130.0 mm because of the mechanical hard stop.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Ah, so 135.0 is over the hard stop limit. That explains the 37.3. Should I just set it back to something under 130.0 and restart?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Correct the value first, but here's the thing — the last three 37.3 alarms on this machine were caused by editing point tables while the servo was enabled, which corrupts the table in RAM. Was the servo enabled when they made the edit?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'm not sure, I'll check. If it was enabled, what do I do about the corrupted RAM table?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: You fix the setting value, then always cycle power to the servo amplifier after correcting a point table setting. Otherwise the old value may persist in volatile memory and you'll chase your tail.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, power cycle after the fix. And if it still throws 37.3 even after I correct it and cycle power?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the corrected point table still triggers 37.3, first re-initialize the point table area before you suspect the amplifier hardware. Don't jump to swapping the amp.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Earlier I was also just going to look at parameter No. 37 and ignore the detail number. That would've been wrong, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that — ignoring the point table error number and only checking parameter No. 37 would miss the specific point table entry that's out of range. The 37.3 detail is what tells you it's the point table, so check the table entry itself.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the error number pointed me right at point table 5. Let me go correct it to under 130.0 mm now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, and remember what I said about editing while enabled — that's why you're seeing this again. Make sure the servo is disabled before you touch the table this time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll disable the servo, set point table 5 back under 130.0 mm, then cycle power to the amp.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And like I said about re-initializing, if 37.3 comes back after the power cycle, re-initialize the point table area before you even think about the amplifier being bad.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. I'll let you know what the display shows after the power cycle.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: One more thing — after you re-initialize, re-enter the correct point table 5 value, because the re-init wipes the table area. Then power cycle again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, re-enter the value after re-init and cycle power again. Should I check the error number on the display or in MR Configurator2?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Either works — the point table error number shows on the servo amplifier display or in MR Configurator2. Just confirm it's clear before you hand it back to production.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. So to recap: value under 130.0 mm, servo disabled during the edit, power cycle after, and re-init the table area if it persists.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. And don't forget the last three 37.3s here were all from editing while enabled — so make sure the operator knows not to do that.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll tell them. Thanks, I'll go fix it now.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? i4L-R258 in Inspection cell C was moved over the weekend, about 15 cm closer to the conveyor. During manual jog at 20% the arm grazes a cable tray bracket by the left guard.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: It's touching? How bad?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No alarm. At full extension there's maybe a 2 mm gap. Cell got re-energized this morning, hasn't run a full cycle yet.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, don't power it up for a run. On Line 8, any robot moved within 30 cm of a cable tray needs a slow-speed sweep of all joint limits before power-up. And that bracket at cell C was field-modified back in 2019, it sits 12 mm lower than the original drawing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: One of the guys said just reset the servo and run a full-speed automatic cycle to see if the graze repeats. And another wanted to loosen the bracket and push it aside by hand while it's powered.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, absolutely not. First post-move test runs in manual mode at 10% speed, with a second person standing at the E-stop. You don't push anything by hand on a live robot.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. By the way, did the spare parts for Line 9 come in yet? And are you on second shift Thursday?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Parts came this morning, and yeah I'm on second shift. Lunch first though, then we do the sweep together.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, something's off at inspection cell D. Since 09:15 this morning SCADA just stopped getting data from FX5-PLC672 — the Ethernet LED is blinking fine, so the link is up, but every 30 seconds we get C059, SLMP communication timeout.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: C059 again? What's the SCADA talking on, UDP or TCP?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: UDP, port 5000. And they just updated it so it polls two HMIs and one MES client at the same time.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. We had this exact same thing on line 12 back in 2024 — the SCADA and the HMIs were all sharing UDP port 5000, and switching the SCADA over to TCP port 5001 cleared the timeouts right up.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Before you two dive in, is this going to hold up the afternoon shift? I need to know if I should call in the spare operator.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Give us twenty minutes. But while I'm here — don't just swap the Ethernet module. With the LED flashing like that, it's not hardware, it's the comm settings. Check those first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I was going to try bumping the UDP retry count up. Would that help?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, that's the trap with UDP — if you send a new request before the first response comes back, the new request just gets thrown away. Retrying on the same port won't get you anywhere.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Right. I'll be in the break room if you need me — Thao brought in spring rolls, so don't take too long.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so TCP it is. Anything else I should check before I touch the config?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check the SCADA's monitor timer value. The default 3 seconds is too short for the network here at cell D — we've got about 5 ms of jitter, and that eats into the timeout.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Monitor timer, got it. And how many connections can we actually run on this PLC?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The Ethernet module on the FX5-PLC672 handles up to 32 simultaneous SLMP connections, but our SCADA config is capped at 8. If you keep polling all three devices at the old rate, you'll just overload it — drop the polling frequency.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Also, spare-parts delivery is delayed again. The conveyor belt motor for line 12 won't be here till Thursday, so don't plan any downtime around that.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Noted. One more thing — we've been seeing intermittent packet loss on cell D for weeks now. Could that be the PLC itself?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Usually not. Nine times out of ten that intermittent UDP loss at cell D is a misconfigured subnet mask on the SCADA server, not the PLC. Check the server's network config before you go pulling cards.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, subnet mask on the server, monitor timer, TCP port 5001, lower polling rate. That's a lot to write down.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Write it on the whiteboard, not your hand. Last time your hand got washed and we re-diagnosed the whole thing from scratch.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Lunch is at noon, by the way. If you're still in the panel then, I'm eating your spring rolls.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Fair enough. I'll start with the SCADA server settings, then switch it to TCP and drop the poll rate.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And if it clears, log it — same fix as 2024, so the next guy doesn't spend two hours on the Ethernet module.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: I'll let the MES team know it might be flaky for the next half hour. They've been complaining about the dashboard anyway.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, heading over to the server room now. Thanks, that saved me a lot of guessing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need your help. FX5-PLC801 over at Plant Dong Nai, Line 8, Machining cell F tripped at 14:32 with error 1861H on the Ethernet comm module.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 1861H, okay. That's a packet size error, right? What's it doing, is it just once or repeating?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It repeats every 10 to 15 minutes, but only when the line is running at high throughput. During idle it's fine, no faults.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: So it follows the line speed, not the clock. Any changes on the network recently? New device, someone touching the PLC program?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No PLC program changes, and the existing BACnet device settings are untouched. But a new BACnet gateway was installed on the same subnet two days ago to log energy data from the machining cell.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. Which model is that gateway? Some of the older ones on Line 8 fragment large responses badly.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I think it's an older revision, the vendor manual is still in the box. Should I pull it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, and check the max APDU size on it. The vendor recommends 480 bytes for that model, otherwise it fragments large responses poorly and you get oversized packets coming back at the PLC.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Someone suggested just replacing the Ethernet module on the FX5-PLC801 right away, but I didn't think that was right.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't do that. The manual says 1861H comes from the destination sending a packet bigger than allowed, so it's a comms destination issue, not a hardware failure on our side. Don't swap the module.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That's what I figured. Another guy said to raise the PLC's max packet size setting instead.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch our transmit limit. The manual's action for 1861H is to check the destination device and find out why the packet size increased. Raise our limit and you just hide the problem.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. So what's the first move before I go touching anything on the PLC?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch the PLC at all, isolate that BACnet gateway from the network and check whether the 1861H alarm clears. That rules the gateway in or out as the source first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. If I pull it and the alarm clears, then it's definitely the gateway.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And here's a quick workaround if you need to keep the line running while you fix the settings. Temporarily disable the energy-logging gateway and restart the Ethernet module, then production comes back until the gateway config is corrected.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Nice, I can do that on the next break. By the way, did you see the shift schedule change for next week?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, they moved us to the early slot on Wednesday. Fine by me, I hate the late one. Anyway.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Same. Oh, and the spare-parts delivery for the other line got pushed to Friday, the guy at the warehouse told me.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Figures, they always do that when we don't need it. Let's get back to this though. One more thing on 1861H.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Go ahead.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Last time this happened on this cell, it wasn't a gateway at all. It was a misconfigured trend-log block that appended 200 bytes of metadata to every packet.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So even without the new gateway it could have been something on the log side?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly, so check both. But the timing here points at the gateway first, isolate it and confirm the alarm clears. Then set the APDU to 480 bytes and check the trend-log block too.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll isolate the gateway, verify the alarm clears, then fix the APDU size and check the trend-log block config.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Perfect. And if you need the line back fast, disable the gateway and restart the module first, then do the config properly. Let me know what you find.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? The i4L-R319 on Line 3 in Dispensing cell F threw an encoder backup battery alarm this morning. It was powered down all weekend, and now the controller's showing the alarm code.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I figured that one was coming. What's the voltage on the pack?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I measured 2.9 V. It's been in service about 3 years and 2 months. Can we just keep running until the planned stop in two weeks? The robot's still moving fine.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. At Binh Duong Line 3, anything below 3.0 V after a weekend power-down means you replace it before you restart production. And grab the matched pair from the Line 3 spares cabinet, not a single cell — we keep a matched set there because mismatched cells gave us a false alarm back in 2022.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Do I need to power the controller down for that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Power off, and put the robot in a safe position first — the covers aren't interlocked, so kill and disconnect before you pull them, otherwise you risk losing zero-point calibration. If line management absolutely needs product moving, run i4L-R319 at reduced speed and book the battery swap within 48 hours, no longer.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. Oh — did the new nozzles for the dispenser come in yet? We're almost out.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: They're on the truck, should be here after lunch. I'll help you with the batteries right after the shift change.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with i4L-R179 in Dispensing cell E. I swapped the dispensing gripper last Thursday for the heavier model, and now it keeps tripping collision detection about once every 40 cycles at the same approach point. I only updated the tool weight in the teach pendant, and production restarted that afternoon.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing — did you do a full risk assessment? Any end-effector change over 0.5 kg on Line 4 needs a re-teach of the payload and a collision-sensitivity check at 30% speed. Updating the teach pendant alone doesn't cover the safety side.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, I didn't file one. Could we just disable collision detection until we're sure the new gripper is fine in production?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't disable collision detection — that's the wrong move. We had this exact issue on i4L-R179 back in 2022: a gripper swap caused a false collision stop because the tool center point was left at the old value. And the teach pendant payload update alone doesn't satisfy the post-change safety requirement.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So what should I check before signing this off?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you sign off a gripper change, verify the safety-rated speed limit still triggers within 200 mm of the guard opening. That's the check that actually proves the safety features still work after the swap.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That makes sense. Is there anything I can do right now so we're not stopping every 40 cycles while the risk assessment is pending?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about the sensitivity check, do that at 30% speed first. A quick workaround for the nuisance collision stops is to reduce the approach speed by 15% while the new risk assessment is pending — but that's temporary, not a sign-off.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, you got a minute? i4L-R118 is making this loud single clack on every cycle when joint 3 comes into the hardstop.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Just joint 3, one clack, same spot every cycle? Any alarm on the pendant?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No alarm, but the operator says there's maybe 0.3 mm of position drift right at the hardstop approach. And I looked at the clamp collar — the socket-head screw is backed out about 1.5 mm with a shiny wear mark.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's the joint 3 hardstop clamp collar screw. On this machine it loosens after about 200 e-stop events, because the hardstop takes the full deceleration load.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That tracks. Line speed went up 15% three days ago and we've had four e-stops this week. Should I just crank it down hard?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't overtorque it. Torque that joint 3 clamp collar screw to 4.5 N-m, then mark it with a paint line so we can see if it moves again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, 4.5 N-m. Somebody on the floor said 17 because it's a hardstop fastener.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That'll wreck the collar. Stick to 4.5. And before you touch the hardstop, lock out and tag out all power sources and wait 2 minutes for the residual voltage to decay.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Also, is it easier to lift the robot by the quill or flyover to get in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Never lift by the quill or flyover — only the base and inner link. And listen, if that screw loosens again within one week, inspect the joint 3 hardstop face for fretting and replace the clamp collar.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. By the way, did the spare clamp collars come in with the last delivery?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet, still on the truck. Should be here Thursday. You grabbing lunch after this?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, once I get the LOTO done and the two minutes run out. I'll torque it and paint-mark it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Log the e-stop count too, so we know when it's coming up on 200 again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on Line 9. The SCADA driver on packaging cell E is throwing SLMP error C056H every cycle reading D-registers from FX5-PLC907. Started at 06:42 this morning.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: C056H, huh. What changed right before it started?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Only thing I did was bump the recipe batch from 120 words starting at D500 to 200 words starting at D500 in the driver config. Same read worked fine before that. No cable, switch, or power changes on Line 9 in the last 24 hours.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's your problem. On the FX5-PLC907, keep your SLMP word-read batches at or below 120 words starting at D500 — the device range ends near D799.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Always check the starting address plus point count against the FX5 device map before you go touching the Ethernet cable or switch. D500 plus 200 words runs way past D799.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So it's not the Ethernet module? I was about to grab a spare from the crib.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the module — C056H is an address-range error, not a hardware failure. And don't bother restarting the CPU either, that won't fix it. The request address or point count has to be corrected first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Did we ever see this before? Feels familiar.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Back in 2023, Line 9 had a similar C056H after a recipe edit. The fix was reducing the batch size, not replacing the PLC.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And log the corrected batch size in the Line 9 communication log so the next recipe change doesn't repeat the C056H.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. By the way, are you on the early shift next week? They're shuffling the schedule again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Haven't seen it yet. Oh, and the spare-parts delivery for cell C got pushed to Thursday, just so you know.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll drop the batch back to 120 starting at D500 and write it in the log.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Perfect. Grab lunch after, the noodle place by gate 3 is finally open again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need a hand — i4L-R449 on Line 2, Palletizing cell A just locked out with error -924 mid-cycle.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Operator says the front panel High Power lamp was flickering amber for about 10 seconds before it faulted. Now the enable button does nothing and the lamp's dark.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay. When you get -924, first thing is verify the High Power lamp itself — try an enable request and watch for that flashing amber state within 2 seconds.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If it never flashes, the lamp's done. On this cell the front panel lamp assembly tends to fail after 12–18 months from the vibration off the palletizing conveyor. We keep a spare lamp module in the line cabinet.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Can I just clear the error from the pendant and hit enable again? Or swap the whole front panel?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No — if the lamp is dark and -924 is active, don't bypass the interlock. Replace the lamp module before you even try to enable High Power.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And you don't need the whole panel, just the lamp module. It's faster and cheaper — only the module typically fails.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: How long we looking at? Line 2's already behind on the morning count.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Last time this happened on cell A, swapped the module, then cycled control power at the robot controller to clear the -924. Re-enabled High Power and confirmed the lamp went solid amber.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Cabinet spare's still there from last month, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Should be — and while you're in there, grab the spare-parts delivery slip, they dropped off the conveyor sensor kit too.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: After this, take your lunch — we're shifting the schedule so second shift covers the changeover.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, replacing the module now and cycling power after.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I swapped the pendant cable on the i4L-R331 at cell F this morning, and now High Power won't enable at all. The pendant was taken off for cleaning, it's on the bench, but the cable's still plugged into the controller. No display, no serial comms, enable switch and E-stop both dead.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright, first thing — did you put the jumper plug in? The manual says High Power only enables when either the pendant or its jumper plug is connected to satisfy the safety circuits. With the cable installed and no pendant on it, you need that plug.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, I didn't install it. I figured the cable alone was enough since it's plugged into the controller. There's a spare jumper plug in the cabinet though. Should I just swap the whole pendant assembly instead?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the pendant — the manual says the jumper plug or pendant has to be connected to satisfy the safety circuits, so the missing plug is the likely cause here. And whatever you do, don't try jumpering the E-stop pins to bypass it. That's dangerous and the manual warns never to run with all jumpers installed.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On this cell, the pendant adapter cable's retaining clip has to be fully seated — a 2 mm gap at the connector gives you exactly this no-comm, no-High-Power symptom. We keep a labeled 10048-000 jumper plug taped inside the controller door for pendant-off operation. Go grab that one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I see the 10048-000 plug taped in the door. Anything else I should check while I'm in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, like I said about the retaining clip, check it carefully. Back in 2021 we had a similar no-High-Power incident on Line 7, and it turned out to be a bent pin 6 in the pendant adapter cable after a cable swap. So check pin 6 while you're at it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Seating the clip, installing the 10048-000 plug, and checking pin 6. I'll report back once High Power comes up.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on the i4L-R240 in Packaging cell B, Line 6. It keeps tripping with an intermittent pendant E-stop channel 2 mismatch every two or three hours, and it only happens when the cable flexes during a high-reach pick. Power cycle clears it, but it comes back. Channel 1 never faults.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't start by swapping the pendant E-stop button. Channel 1 is healthy and the fault follows cable flex, so it's the channel 2 wiring, not the button. On this line, channel 2 faults that show up only during cable flex are almost always a broken strand at pin 10 inside the backshell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, that makes sense. I did notice the connector backshell feels loose since the cable was replaced 10 days ago. So what's the first thing I should check?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check the backshell strain relief first, then ohm pins 2 and 10 from the controller end while wiggling the cable. A reading above 5 ohms means the break is there. Don't disable channel 2 monitoring in software either — the manual requires both E-stop channels for the safety circuits.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. If it is the break, do we have to replace the whole cable? And by the way, are you still on for lunch after this shift?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Lunch, yeah. For the cable, our preferred workaround before a new one arrives is to reroute the pendant cable over the overhead tray to reduce flex at the connector. And like I said about pin 10, we had a 2022 incident on Line 6 with the same channel 2 symptom, and it was fixed by re-crimping pin 10, not by replacing the pendant.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Perfect, I'll check the backshell and ohm it out. So re-crimping might get us running until the new cable shows up?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Start with the strain relief and the wiggle test, and if pin 10 reads high, re-crimp it and reroute over the overhead tray. That should hold you until the new cable arrives.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? Operator on Line 6 is stuck — i4L-R884 in Assembly cell C. Pressed High Power enable, amber LED just flashes and the robot never enables. Teach pendant shows no error code at all.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Flashing amber, no error. What's the control power LED doing?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Solid green. So it's getting power. I was thinking maybe the enable button itself is bad, or the controller needs a firmware update — something's not registering.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't go replacing the button. If the LED's flashing, the request is being made — the problem's downstream, in the safety circuit. On this cell, flashing amber with no error usually means the safety gate interlock isn't fully latched. Check the door switch for a bent actuator pin.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The cell door was opened and closed during a tool change about 30 minutes ago, right before this started. I'll go look.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that fits. We've got a known issue — the door interlock switch on Assembly cell C needs a 0.5 mm shim to align properly after tool changes. Happened 4 times in the last 6 months.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Four times? Nobody told me that. And meanwhile the operator keeps mashing the enable button.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Tell him to stop. If the door switch is misaligned, the High Power enable request will never complete and the LED just keeps flashing. Repeatedly pressing the button does nothing except wear it out.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So once I shim and adjust the switch — then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: After you adjust the door switch, cycle the control power to reset the safety circuit. Then enable High Power and verify the LED goes solid amber. And hey — did the spare-parts delivery come in for the other line yet?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, still waiting on that. Shift change is at 3, by the way — think we'll have this wrapped before then?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Should take ten minutes if the pin's just bent. Grab the shim kit from the cabinet, I'll meet you at the cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I was doing the six-month safety function check on i4L-R284 over in cell F, and I spotted a thin dark oil film around the joint 3 quill area. No alarm showing, but it's been in service 92 days. Do we need to swap the joint out right away?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Whoa, hold on, don't go ordering a replacement yet. Over here at Bac Ninh Line 12, a dark film on that joint 3 quill almost always means grease separation, not a blown seal. Nine times out of ten you just wipe it and relubricate.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Really? I figured any oil weeping out means the seal's gone. It's only 92 days and 141 km on the clock too, so I wasn't sure.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, 141 km is already past where we like to be. We don't use the manual's 150 km for joint 3 here — cell F runs a high duty cycle, so the site threshold is 120 km. Once you cross that, you relube, film or no film.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So wipe it down and regrease first, before even thinking about the seal.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, but before you put a finger on that quill, lock out and tag out the robot and confirm the High Power indicator is off. No shortcuts on that one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. And if the film comes back after we relube, then we talk seal?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If it keeps coming back, sure. We learned that the hard way — back in 2023, i4L-R284 had its quill seal replaced after running 180 km with no relubrication. Ever since then the team logs travel distance weekly so we never get caught like that again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. By the way, did the spare-parts delivery for Line 12 come in this morning? I need some more grease cartridges.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet, truck's supposed to be here after lunch. Grab what you need from the cabinet in the meantime.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. So just to recap — wipe and relubricate the quill, log the distance, and only chase the seal if the film returns.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. And keep logging that travel distance weekly like we've been doing since the 2023 seal job. If you're ever near 120 km again, just relube — don't wait for 150.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand with FX5-PLC203 down on Line 9, Assembly cell F. It's throwing 7701H about every forty minutes on the 06:00 to 14:00 shift, then it clears itself in three to five seconds and the line just carries on.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay. And it's the master logging it, so it's local station 3 that's not answering in time. What got changed on that panel recently?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: They put a new 24 V supply in the local station panel last Thursday. Oh — and two cycles got scrapped yesterday, so the supervisor's already asking about it.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Yeah, I don't want a third one. Are we still good on the spare-parts delivery for line 9? I'm chasing that this afternoon either way.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Forget the parts for now. On this cell, ninety percent of 7701H events trace back to the local station 3 power supply dropping below 21.5 volts during servo acceleration.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So should I pull the master comm module? The error's logged there, so I figured that's the first thing to swap.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the module yet. Put a min/max meter on the 24 V rail at local station 3 and watch it while the servo axis accelerates — if it dips below 21.5 volts, that confirms the fault.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if it does dip? Someone was saying just reload the GX Works3 project in case it's a parameter thing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Reloading GX Works3 won't help you here. If the rail dips, add a 4700 microfarad capacitor right at the local station 3 terminal block before you replace any communication module.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, capacitor before module. There's also that network cable from the master to station 3 that runs right next to the new servo drive cable for a couple of meters.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That one bit us in March 2023 — same symptom, and we fixed it by moving the network cable 30 centimeters away from the servo drive cable and adding a ferrite core.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Fine, but do the checks first. I'm grabbing lunch at noon, so if you want me on the floor, catch me before that.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll grab the min/max meter and watch it on the next acceleration.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Do the rail check first, then the cable reroute and ferrite if the dip shows up. And check on press 4 while you're over there, it was acting up earlier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with i4L-R470 on Line 7, Assembly cell D. After maintenance replaced a damaged XSYSTEM cable connector last shift, pressing the High Power request button just throws error -924 on the teach pendant.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing: does the front panel HIGH POWER lamp do anything at all when you press the button?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Nothing. No light, no flash. I waited 30 seconds after the request and it stayed dark. Control power is on, all E-stops are released, and the safety gate is closed. Cell's been down 45 minutes now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright. Before you even think about replacing that lamp, check the High Power lamp current with a clamp meter. The acceptable window is 10 to 500 mA.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if it's outside that range, that's why the robot refuses High Power?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. The robot raises -924 and refuses High Power if the indicator current is outside 10 to 500 mA when High Power is requested. On this cell, a loose XSYSTEM shield clamp after cable rework has twice caused -924 by leaking current away from the High Power lamp circuit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: A loose shield clamp? So the rework itself could be the problem.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Very likely. Go check that shield clamp on the XSYSTEM connector they just replaced. Make sure it's tight and making good contact. That's the first thing I'd look at on this cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the clamp. But what if the lamp flashes for just a split second and then -924 comes up? I thought I saw that once before.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the lamp flashes for less than 1 second and then -924 appears, suspect the 10-second High Power safety timeout was changed to 0 in ACE.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So someone might have messed with the timeout parameter? I didn't touch ACE.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Could be left over from the rework shift. Check the ACE parameter for the High Power safety timeout. Default is 10 seconds. If it's 0, the lamp won't flash properly after a request and you'll get -924.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And while I'm checking, should I just replace the front panel lamp? Error -924 mentions lamp failure, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't jump to replacing the lamp. Measure the current first. A wiring issue like that loose shield clamp or the timeout being wrong can cause the same -924. Replace the lamp only if the current is actually out of window and the wiring is good.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That makes sense. What about disabling the High Power safety timeout in ACE so the lamp just stays on? Would that get us running?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. The manual requires the timeout so the indicator can flash after a request. Disabling it or setting it to 0 is not a fix — it'll just mask the real problem.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I won't touch the timeout. So my plan is: check the shield clamp, measure lamp current with a clamp meter, verify the ACE timeout is 10 seconds. Anything else?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Keep High Power disabled and never bypass the lamp to test motion. That lamp is a safety device on this line. Don't try to jumper it or force the robot to move.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll leave High Power off while I check everything. If the clamp is loose, do I just retighten it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, retighten it and make sure the shield is properly seated. Then measure the lamp current again. If it's between 10 and 500 mA and the timeout is correct, request High Power and see if the lamp flashes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if the current is still out of range after fixing the clamp?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then check the lamp circuit wiring more thoroughly. But on this cell, that loose XSYSTEM shield clamp after cable rework has been the culprit twice. I'd bet on that first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll start with the clamp and current measurement. I'll let you know what I find.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember: no bypassing the lamp, and keep High Power disabled during the check. Safety first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need your help with MR-JE-AX619 on Line 9, Dispensing cell A. It tripped with alarm code 10, undervoltage, three times this morning shift.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Undervoltage on that drive. When does it happen, during what part of the cycle?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It's intermittent, mostly when the dispensing head accelerates quickly from a standstill. And I measured the panel voltage at 158 V AC during the alarms.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 158 is already below the 160 threshold. First thing, before you even chase the power supply, check that the power connector at the servo amplifier is fully seated. A loose connector can mimic a voltage drop.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the connector. But no other servo amplifiers on Line 9 are showing this alarm. Why only this one?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That cell has its own dedicated step-down transformer. If the voltage is low only on this cell, check that transformer first, because it occasionally has a faulty tap setting.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And what about the plant supply itself? Could it just be the incoming power?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: It can be. Our incoming power often sags below 160 V AC during peak production hours, around 9 AM to 11 AM, because of a shared compressor load.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That matches the morning shift timing. So we have two possible causes, the transformer tap or the plant sag. What should I do first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Start with the connector, then the transformer tap. Once you confirm the supply is actually low, we can talk about compensating in the drive.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. If the voltage is consistently low only during acceleration, is there something we can change in the servo parameters?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. If the voltage is consistently low only during acceleration, temporarily increase the acceleration time constant in the servo parameters to reduce bus voltage sag.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Temporarily meaning until we fix the supply, right? I don't want to leave it like that.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, it's a temporary measure. The real fix is the supply or the transformer tap. Don't leave the acceleration time constant changed permanently.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. One of the guys said we should just replace the servo amplifier since it's an alarm. That doesn't sound right.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace it yet. The manual says low supply voltage is a common cause, so check the voltage first before condemning the amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I shouldn't assume it's a loose connector either without measuring, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Correct. You have to measure the actual supply voltage. The manual says if it's 160 V AC or less, review the power supply voltage. Don't jump to the connector without that measurement.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. So my sequence is: check the connector seating, then check the transformer tap, then measure the voltage. Does that sound right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. And if the voltage is 160 or less, the action is to review the power supply voltage. That's straight from the manual.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. I'll go check the connector and the transformer tap now, and measure the voltage during peak hours.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. If it's only low on this cell, the transformer tap is the prime suspect. If it's low across the plant, it's the shared compressor load during peak hours.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Thanks. I'll report back what I find.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with MR-JE-AX444 on Line 1, Pick-and-place cell F. It tripped AL. 50 Overload 1 three times during the 06:00-14:00 shift on 12 March. Operator clears it on the keypad and restarts in about 2 minutes, then the axis runs 8-15 minutes before AL. 50 comes back.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright, stop restarting it like that. No, don't keep pressing reset on the keypad to finish the shift — every time you clear it and run again you're cooking the amplifier and the motor. On Line 1, AL. 50 in cell F usually traces to the Y-axis drag chain binding after we bumped it to 55 cycles/min.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So should we just swap the MR-JE servo amplifier? The alarm points at the amplifier, and the heatsink was noticeably hot after the second trip. Ambient at the cell is 38 degrees C.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the amplifier yet. I always check the Y-axis drag chain and cable carrier before touching the servo amplifier or motor. Back in August 2023 we had a similar AL. 50 cluster on cell F, and it ended when the drag chain was re-routed and lubricated, not when the amplifier was replaced.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so check the drag chain first. And what about restarting after we clear it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about clearing the alarm — after clearing AL. 50 on this cell, I wait at least 30 minutes with the cabinet fan on before the first restart. And use MR Configurator2 to check the cause of the alarm occurrence before you run it again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So drag chain and cable carrier first, re-route and lubricate if it's binding, then let it cool 30 minutes with the fan on before restart. Should I call you before we run it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, call me before the first restart. And remember, repeatedly clearing the alarm and restarting can damage the servo amplifier and servo motor — so no more quick resets on this cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on MR-JE-AX889, Inspection cell D on Line 10. Every power-up home return the position is off by about 0.8 mm, same direction, roughly one motor revolution, and no alarm on the amp at all. It only shows up on first shift start-up, but if I re-home mid-shift it's fine and indexing is stable.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing — don't touch the amplifier. The manual puts dog position, PA10, the proximity switch, and noise ahead of anything inside the amp. We replaced that dog switch two weeks ago, right? Go look at the bracket on cell D. There's a witness mark 4 mm from the switch roller — if that mark is covered, the dog turn-off point is sitting too close to the Z-phase, and that's exactly how you get a repeatable offset like this.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll check the mark. But before I start moving things, should I be adjusting PA10 to widen the in-position window? Someone on the other shift said that usually smooths it out.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't widen it — a too-large in-position range is itself a listed cause of home position deviation, so you'd just be hiding it. And before you even think about touching PA10, write its current value on the line log sheet, because cell D's recipe uses a wider in-position window for the heavy gripper and you don't want to lose that. Also, while you're at the cabinet, check the command cable shield bond at the gland — after the 2021 encoder cable re-route on this cell we kept getting home offset from noise, and that bond was the fix.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. And if the dog timing is the problem, is there something quick I can try before we start re-shimming the bracket?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, quick workaround — jog the axis 30 mm past the dog, power-cycle the amp, then re-home. If the offset disappears, it's the dog timing, not the amp and not the encoder. Last time this happened here that trick saved us a whole afternoon.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Perfect, I'll try that first. By the way, are you on second shift tomorrow or is it still the swapped schedule?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Swapped — I'm on second shift all week, so grab me before noon if the re-home still drifts. And log whatever you find on the sheet, the day shift keeps asking about cell D.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand. MR-JE-AX928 over at Plant Hanoi, Line 8, Machining cell D is showing alarm 3E.6 with detail number 3E.6, and the machine can't home. It started right after the night-shift guy changed Pr. PA01 from point table method to program method.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright. First thing, before you touch anything, check the last three shift logs. The night-shift technician often changes Pr. PA01 without recording it in the logbook, so that's your first stop.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll pull those. So is this a hardware problem? Should we swap the servo amplifier?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the amplifier. 3E.6 just means the positioning mode memorized in the amplifier doesn't match the actual mode. The mode got changed, so the point table needs to be reinitialized.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the Pr. PA01 change is the cause. Can I just power-cycle the whole cabinet to clear it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, cycling the whole cabinet won't reinitialize the point table. On this line, a Pr. PA01 change needs a full 24 V control power cycle before the point table initialization is accepted.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, 24 V control power cycle. Then what do I do to reinitialize?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the mode change was intentional, use MR Configurator2 and do the one-click restore from the last known good backup stored on the line PC.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Anything I should check mechanically before I touch Pr. PA01?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Before touching Pr. PA01, verify the mechanical cam for home position is not within 5 mm of the proximity sensor. If it's too close you'll get a false 3E.6 during re-initialization.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if the mode change was a mistake and they didn't mean to switch to program method?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then set it back to the correct setting — back to point table method — and do the same 24 V control power cycle so the initialization is accepted.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good, sounds like we've got a plan. Junior, log everything you find in those last three shift logs and report back before you restore.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Checking the logs first, then control power cycle, then the cam clearance, then the restore from the line PC backup.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem with MR-JE-AX402 on Line 9. Since Monday when we manually adjusted the fixture, we keep getting AL. 9B warning popping up. It's intermittent, three or four times a shift, mostly during clamping. Droop pulses hit 2500 when the warning level is set to 2000.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: AL. 9B means error excessive — droop pulses went over the warning level. That's not necessarily a hard alarm, but it's telling you something moved. Did you check if the shaft got rotated by external force?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I haven't yet. But I was thinking maybe we should just replace the servo motor. I've heard AL. 9B usually means the encoder is going bad.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't just swap the motor — that's the wrong move. On Line 9, a 0.5 mm shim under the fixture base often causes external shaft rotation and AL. 9B after manual adjustment. Check that first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so look for a shim. But what about the manual? It says if the shaft isn't rotated by external force, the encoder might be bad and you should replace the motor if repeatability fails.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, but before you even think about replacing the servo motor, verify shaft repeatability with a dial gauge. Replace only if deviation exceeds 0.02 mm. That's the rule I use.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So dial gauge first. I'll need to borrow one from the tool crib. By the way, did you hear about the shift schedule change next week?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, they're moving us to 12-hour shifts. Not looking forward to it. Anyway, back to the servo — after any fixture shim change, run the axis through 10 slow jogs to seat the coupling before resuming production.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 10 slow jogs. I can do that. But what if the warning still comes back after that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then you check the encoder. But like I said about the shim, that's the most common cause on Line 9. Don't jump to replacing the motor.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll check the shim and run the jogs. Oh, did the spare parts order for the other machine come in yet?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet, still waiting on that delivery. Should be here Thursday. Now, when you check repeatability, make sure the servo is locked. Measure actual position under servo-lock status.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Servo-lock status, got it. I'll use the dial gauge and see if it moves more than 0.02 mm.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And if it's within 0.02 mm, the encoder is probably fine. Then you just need to reseat the coupling with those 10 slow jogs.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. I'll do that now. Hey, what are you getting for lunch? The canteen has pho today.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Probably just a sandwich. Let me know how the jogs go. Remember, after any shim change, always run 10 slow jogs.

turns.speaker: junior_01
