turns.text: Will do. So just to recap: check for a 0.5 mm shim, if present remove it, then dial gauge repeatability, and if deviation is over 0.02 mm replace the motor. Otherwise just jog it 10 times.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. And don't forget — if the shaft isn't rotated by external force and repeatability fails, then you replace the servo motor. But that's the last resort.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll go grab the dial gauge and check the shim now. Thanks for the help.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No problem. Let me know if the warning comes back after the jogs. And hey, did you see the email about the new safety training?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw it. Mandatory next Friday. I'll be there. Alright, I'm heading out to the line.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, something's up with the FX5-PLC915 in cell C. It lost comms with the line controller for 8 seconds today at 14:35, stopped the pick-and-place cycle. No alarm on the HMI at all.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the third time in 24 hours, right? Five to ten seconds each?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, three drops. And here's the weird part, when I hook up GX Works3 directly after the incident there's no active error showing. I already checked the cable, thinking bad termination, but everything looks fine.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't rip anything apart yet. With intermittent Ethernet drops on the FX5-PLC915, the first thing you check is the CC-Link IE Field Network Basic diagnostics log in GX Works3, look for hidden event codes that don't show up as active errors.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Did anything change on the network recently? We had work done on Line 4.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, a new Ethernet switch went in on Line 4 two days ago to expand the network. Could that be it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That switch is a prime suspect. That model had a known firmware bug causing periodic link resets, and a firmware update to v2.1.3 fixed the exact same issue on Line 3.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I just swap out the FX5 Ethernet module? Maybe it's going bad.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace hardware yet. The manual says check parameter errors and network diagnostics first, and download corrected parameters if you find any. Follow that order.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: For a temporary workaround, disable the energy-efficient Ethernet feature on the switch port connected to the FX5-PLC915. That stops the link from cycling while we sort out the firmware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, but even with the firmware, why does it only drop sometimes and not all the time?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Because the root cause is likely a duplicate IP address conflict with the new vision camera on the same subnet. It only manifests when the camera wakes from sleep and grabs the address.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So we've got the switch firmware and the camera IP both to deal with. What's first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Pull the diagnostics log first, then update the switch firmware to v2.1.3, and reassign the camera IP off the PLC's address. That covers it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we got a problem on Line 7, Palletizing cell A — the i4L-R998 just lost all its joint position data after I swapped the batteries. I replaced all three at once because there was no 24 VDC control power available. Now on power-up it throws encoder position error E-101 and won't move to any taught positions.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright, first thing — did you drop any of those new batteries? Because if one hit the floor, don't even think about using it. A dropped battery often reads below 3.0 V and causes immediate data corruption, so check the encoder backup battery voltage first before anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, one of them fell off the bench before I installed it. I figured a little drop wouldn't hurt, so I put it in anyway. Can I just restart the controller to get the joint positions back?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't just restart — that won't restore anything. After data loss you have to do a zero-position calibration, and on the i4L-R998 always use the calibration jig stored in the maintenance cabinet. That dropped battery is exactly why you got E-101; the manual says any battery that's been dropped or shocked must be disposed of because it may leak.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And I used whatever batteries were in the drawer — I think they were generic, not OMRON. Is that a problem?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's a problem — only OMRON-supplied parts should be used. Like I said about checking voltage, using non-OEM can bite you. At this plant we keep a spare set of OMRON 20269-000F batteries in the line supervisor's office so we never have to use non-OEM parts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll grab those. And for next time, how do we avoid losing data when there's no 24 VDC?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: When you replace batteries without 24 VDC, always connect a temporary 24 VDC supply from the adjacent cell to maintain voltage — that keeps the encoder alive. Then do the zero-position calibration with the jig, and we're good.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Boss, inspection cell D indexer stopped again. HMI showed AL. 90.1 right after the operator pressed home return start at 08:42. Machine stopped about 15 mm before the usual home dog, no crash sound. But earlier this week, Monday and Wednesday morning, we had AL. E3 absolute position counter warning twice. Servo-on accepted, jog works fine, only the ZP completion signal never turns on after homing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, before you even think about swapping the servo amplifier, what's the battery voltage on that HG motor encoder? On this cell, when AL. E3 and AL. 90.1 show up together, low battery in the encoder is the first thing I check. Measure it under load, not just open-circuit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I haven't measured it yet. I was thinking maybe the MR-JE-AX777 amplifier is faulty, since 90.1 points to internal positioning. Or maybe just reset 90.1 and ignore the E3, because the axis jogs and the dog might be misaligned.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't ignore E3. If that battery reads below 3.2 V under load, replace it, then clear E3 and re-home before you touch the servo amplifier. Last year we had the same cell with a loose CN2 encoder connector after a cable drag chain replacement — intermittent E3 warnings for three days. So check that connector too while you're there.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And after I clear the E3 and re-home, should I just watch the ZP signal once?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, always perform home position return twice and confirm ZP stays on for at least 10 seconds. That's how you know it's really complete. If it drops out, you still have an issue.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. By the way, did you see the shift schedule for next week? They moved lunch to 11:30.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw. We'll deal with it. But first get that battery checked and the CN2 connector seated properly. Then clear E3, re-home twice, and watch ZP for 10 seconds. If it still fails, then we look at the amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: At 02:14 on Line 4 night shift, MR-JE-AX739 threw an E6.1 forced stop on the drive display and the machining cell F axis just stopped. I checked the EM2/EM1 terminal voltage at the block and it was 0 V DC. Then I found fuse F24-3 open, replaced it, 24 V came back, but E6.1 came back after about 10 minutes. No other alarms anywhere.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, so the manual says E6 is the forced stop signal being off, and if EM2/EM1 is on you check the external 24 V. But on Line 4, fuse F24-3 in panel LP-4 feeds the EM2/EM1 circuit and it's opened twice in 18 months from coolant mist ingress. So this isn't a one-off.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the manual says if the 24 V is there, the amplifier's probably bad and we should swap it. Should I pull MR-JE-AX739 now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, before you replace MR-JE-AX739, check terminal block TB-EM for a loose strand or corrosion. A high-resistance short there mimics an amplifier fault. And always verify EM2/EM1 is de-energized and press the local emergency stop before you probe TB-EM with your multimeter.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: What if F24-3 pops again during this shift? Do we just keep swapping fuses?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If F24-3 opens again within one shift, fit a 1 A slow-blow fuse and apply silicone sealant to the panel cable gland. That's what's been letting the coolant mist in.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll lock out, check TB-EM for corrosion and strands, then decide on the fuse and sealant before touching the amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, at 14:22 Line 6 lost SLMP comms with FX5-PLC138 in pick-and-place cell D. The PLC error history shows C816H, and right before that C815H after exactly 10 failed remote password attempts from the engineering laptop. A junior tech changed the remote password at 14:05 because the old one was too simple. No cables, switch ports, or hardware were touched, and the cell was running fine until the lockout.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That C816H means remote password authentication is locked out. On Line 6 the lockout timer is 60 seconds, so wait a full minute before trying unlock again. Don't keep hammering it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So just wait a minute, then unlock from the laptop? The password was changed at 14:05, so I'm not sure which password to use.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The engineering laptop at cell D keeps two stale password profiles. Always select the 'FX5-PLC138_PROD' profile before unlocking. Don't use the default or the other stale one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, 'FX5-PLC138_PROD'. Should I check anything else before I hit unlock? I don't want to trip C815H again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before unlocking, verify the PLC's remote password setting in GX Works3 and confirm the port is not already unlocked by another tool. If another tool has it open, your unlock will just fail again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right. One of the guys said to just power-cycle the FX5-PLC138 to clear the lockout. Will that work?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, power-cycling won't clear it. C816H clears only after the specified time elapses, so wait that full 60 seconds. And replacing the Ethernet switch or comm module won't fix C816H either—it's a password lockout, not hardware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood, no power cycle and no hardware swap. So after the minute, I select FX5-PLC138_PROD and unlock. Has this happened before on this cell?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, we had a previous lockout at 02:10 on 2024-06-12. That one was caused by a night-shift technician typo, not by a PLC fault. Same fix—wait the timer, pick the right profile, unlock.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. And after unlock, C201H should clear once the port is out of locked status, right? I saw that in the manual.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Correct. C201H means the port is still locked, so the password must be unlocked before any data communication. Once you unlock with the right profile after the full 60 seconds, comms should come back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Wait 60 seconds, check GX Works3 that the port isn't already unlocked, select FX5-PLC138_PROD, then unlock. I'll do that now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the sequence. And remember, the 'FX5-PLC138_PROD' profile is the only one to use on that laptop—the other two are stale. If it locks out again, just wait the full minute and repeat.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I can't get GX Works3 to go online with the FX5-PLC711 at Line 12, Pick-and-place cell D. I tried a direct Ethernet cable from my laptop and it just won't connect.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright, walk me through it. What's your laptop set to right now?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 192.168.0.1 with subnet mask 255.0.0.0. And the PLC Ethernet module is 64.64.255.255. I was thinking I should change the PLC to 192.168.0.10 so it's on the same subnet as my laptop.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the PLC IP. The problem there is your mask. With 255.0.0.0, that 64.64.255.255 address falls in the all-ON host range, so direct connection fails. On Line 12 the engineering laptop has to be set to 192.168.10.77 with mask 255.255.255.0 before you even try a direct connection.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll set that. But I also unplugged the hub cable from P1 to try the direct cable, and the line GOT lost communication.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's expected. For direct connection at cell D you always disconnect the hub cable from P1 first and use only P1. P2 is reserved for the line GOT, so leave that alone.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I can't just leave the hub cable in P1 and also plug in my direct cable?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. Direct connection through the Ethernet module only allows one port to be used. And before you start blaming the CPU, check the P1 link LEDs. That P1 port at cell D was replaced in March 2024 after a lightning surge, so the LEDs are the first thing to look at.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: How long is this going to take? Line 12 is stopped.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Give us a few minutes. If the direct connection still fails after the laptop's set right, power-cycle the laptop Ethernet adapter before you touch any PLC IP settings. Last time this happened, that adapter reset was all it needed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so laptop to 192.168.10.77, mask 255.255.255.0, hub cable off P1, only P1 used, and check the P1 link LEDs.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. And remember the same laptop went online fine through the hub yesterday, so nothing changed on the PLC side overnight. Don't go changing the PLC address.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good. Report back once the laptop is talking to the FX5-PLC711.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with MR-JE-AX266 at Inspection cell E, Line 5. Since the PLC retrofit last Tuesday, the HG motor won't move when the new PLC gives a speed command. No alarm on the amplifier, but the status display shows speed command as zero even when I force the PLC analog output to 5 V.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, don't swap the amplifier yet. Where did you measure that 5 V?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right at the PLC analog output terminals. I didn't check anything at the servo amp side. I was thinking maybe the amplifier is dead since there's no alarm, or maybe I should adjust the electronic gear to match the new PLC scaling.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Stop there. Before you touch any electronic gear parameters, always verify the analog command at the servo amplifier CN1 terminals with a meter. That's the first thing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll meter CN1. But what am I looking for exactly?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On this cell, the new PLC analog output card is current-sinking, so DICOM and OPC must be linked at CN1 to power the open-collector interface. If that link isn't there, the command never gets through.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: DICOM and OPC... those are on the CN1 connector, right? Could the retrofit have missed that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. The retrofit contractor reused the old CN1 cable, and pin 20, DICOM, and pin 3, OPC, are often left unconnected on the new PLC side. Go check those two pins first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if pin 20 and pin 3 are floating on the PLC side, the open-collector interface has no power and the amp sees zero command. That fits what I'm seeing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And once you've confirmed the analog command is actually reaching CN1, then you can look at scaling. But for this axis, the correct electronic gear numerator is 1 and denominator is 1. It was set during original commissioning and should not be changed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, so leave the gear at 1 to 1. I was about to mess with that to match the new PLC. Glad I asked.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, don't. That gear setting hasn't changed in three years and it's correct. The problem is upstream in the wiring, not in the amplifier parameters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll check pin 20 and pin 3 at CN1 now and meter the command there. If they're unconnected, I'll link DICOM and OPC.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Meter the command at CN1 first, then fix the DICOM and OPC link, and confirm the motor moves before you even think about electronic gear. That's the order.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a low battery alarm on the i4L-R652 over in Dispensing cell A. Code E-042. Robot's just sitting there idle and Line 7 is still running.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: E-042, huh. Yeah, that unit's been in service about three years two months since the last set. Don't panic though — that alarm on this unit usually shows up two to three weeks before the batteries actually die, so it's not like it's gonna drop dead this shift.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so can we just swap them now? I was gonna pull all three at once, quick job.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, no — do not pull all three at once, especially with no 24 V control power at the cell. You'll wipe the joint position data. Without 24 volts you go one at a time: leftmost first, then the middle, then the rightmost, and wait thirty seconds between each one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And we don't have 24 V at the cell this shift, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, so one at a time. And listen — use only OMRON part number 20269-000F. Those aftermarket equivalents bit us twice back in 2022, gave us premature alarms both times.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Speaking of which, did the spare-parts delivery come in? I saw a pallet by the dock earlier.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the conveyor belts for Line 5, not our stuff. Our battery order's still pending. Anyway — at this site we normally schedule battery replacement on the i4L-R652 during the annual August shutdown, so we don't hit production. That's the plan.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: August, that's like four months out. Are you sure we can leave it that long? What if it just dies?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said, that alarm's typically two to three weeks ahead of real depletion. It's not urgent — just don't ignore it for weeks on end either, because if it does die suddenly you're looking at a full recalibration. So we track it, and we swap at shutdown.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. Hey, you grabbing lunch after this? The canteen's doing that noodle thing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Maybe. First let me log the alarm and check the other cells — cell B had a weird noise yesterday. You go ahead and note the E-042 in the logbook.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Leftmost, middle, rightmost, thirty seconds, OMRON 20269-000F. And we wait for August.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. And keep 24 volts on it if you ever do get power at the cell — makes it easier. But for now, just log it and leave it running.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we've got a serial communication error on FX5-PLC257 at Packaging cell F. The flag SM8500 is ON and SD8500 shows 7010H. It happened at 14:35 today, right after a tech swapped a communication cable.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, 7010H is parity, overrun, or framing error — manual says check the wiring. But before you go swapping the FX5 CPU, don't. That code points to wiring, not a dead module.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I was about to grab a spare CPU from the crib. So what should I check first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First thing: on FX5-PLC257, intermittent 7010H errors often come from loose shield grounding on the CH1 RS-485 cable. Re-torque the shield clamp to 0.5 N·m and see if it clears.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Also, I noticed SM9090 — the parallel link operation flag — is still ON, so the link is running but with errors. Should I just ignore that and focus on the error flag?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't ignore SM9090. That flag being ON means the link is still active, so the error might be transient. But always verify the parallel link partner station — the FX3 compatible one — is powered and not in STOP before you even think about replacing FX5 hardware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the partner station power and mode. By the way, did you hear about the shift schedule change next week? We're moving to 12-hour rotations.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw the email. We'll deal with that later. Back to this — last year we had a similar 7010H on Line 4, and it turned out to be a faulty termination resistor in the junction box, not the PLC. So check that resistor too.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: A termination resistor? I thought the site uses a non-standard 120 Ω resistor on the CH1 port here.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, we do — 120 Ω on the FX5-PLC257 CH1 port to reduce reflections from the long cable runs. But the junction box one is separate. Like I said about the shield clamp, start with the simple mechanical checks first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll re-torque the shield clamp, then check the junction box resistor, and confirm the partner station is powered and not in STOP.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And if all that checks out, then you can look at the cable the tech replaced earlier. But don't skip the order — shield first, then resistor, then partner station.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Oh, lunch is at 12:30 today, right? The cafeteria has that noodle special.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, 12:30. Let's finish this up before then. Keep me posted on what you find.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got a weird one on FX5-PLC285. At 14:32 today the SLMP read request to the cell SCADA gateway timed out with error C035H. It started right after we rerouted the Ethernet cable around that new conveyor guard at 13:50.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: C035H means the external device didn't respond within the response monitoring timer. So it's a communication timeout, not a CPU crash. What's the frequency?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: About 8 times an hour, always on long read requests but not on short writes. I checked the gateway—it's powered and the link LED is solid.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On FX5-PLC285 the response monitoring timer is set to 3 seconds in the SLMP parameters. But the gateway occasionally needs 4 seconds during SCADA polling. That's one piece of it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So should I just bump the timer to 10 seconds? That would stop the timeouts, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the timer first. That rerouted cable at Line 9 passes within 20 cm of a 7.5 kW conveyor VFD. That has caused intermittent C035H timeouts before.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: What do you want me to check first, then?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First check the cable shield grounding at the PLC cabinet end. Then verify the gateway response time. Only after that should you think about changing any timer values.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, shield grounding first. If that's good, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then measure the gateway response time with a scope or the diagnostics. If it's coming in around 4 seconds on long reads, the 3-second timer is just too tight.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if the shield grounding is bad? I'm still thinking we might just replace the FX5-PLC285 CPU module to be safe.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't replace the CPU. Back in 2019 we had an incident on Line 9 after a similar reroute. It was fixed by replacing the RJ45 plug, not by replacing the PLC.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Really? Just the plug? So the vibration from the conveyor or the reroute loosened the connector?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. The reroute put stress on the plug. So before you change any timer values, check that shield grounding and then the gateway response time. Then inspect the RJ45.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll start with the shield at the cabinet end. If it's loose, I'll fix it and watch the error rate.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember the gateway sometimes needs 4 seconds during SCADA polling, so even with good grounding the 3-second timer in the SLMP parameters might still be tight.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if the grounding and plug are fine, then I can adjust the timer from 3 to 4 seconds?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, but only after the shield grounding and response time checks. And keep in mind that cable is still running within 20 cm of that 7.5 kW VFD—that's the root cause of the intermittent timeouts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should we reroute the cable again, further from the VFD?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If you can, yes. But first fix the shield grounding and the plug. We've seen C035H on Line 9 before from that VFD proximity, so physical separation helps.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. I'll check the shield at the PLC cabinet end, then the gateway response time, then the RJ45 plug. I'll leave the timer alone for now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the right order. And if you do change the timer, go to 4 seconds, not 10. The gateway only occasionally needs 4 seconds during SCADA polling.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll report back after I check the shield and plug.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on FX5-PLC938 over here. After that two-second power dip on Line 3 at 09:14, the Ethernet port stopped answering SCADA pings and the HMI is showing alarm 1920H on the comm diagnostics screen. I changed SD8492 to SD8497 two days ago to move it to a new subnet, so I'm thinking maybe the card's fried.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Whoa, slow down. Don't go ordering an Ethernet module yet. On this cell, before you cycle power on anything, you always verify that SD8492 to SD8497 actually contain valid IP octets, because corrupted values stick around in the battery-backed area.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the values I typed could have gotten scrambled by the dip itself?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And 1920H is a parameter range issue, not a hardware failure — the manual says recheck SD8492 to SD8497. It's not telling you to swap cards.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, but couldn't I just toggle SM8492 and SM8495 together to force a clean reset? That's what I was about to try.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. If 1920H shows up after a power dip, first clear SD8498 by toggling SM8495 alone, then re-enter the IP values with SM8492 — never both together. The manual's clear that simultaneous ON gives you 1921H.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right, I see it here — SM8492 and SM8495 both ON causes 1921H. Good catch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And honestly, the root cause here is usually a race — the line controller's scheduled clear going off at the same time as a manual write from the maintenance laptop on the same subnet. You had a write request from your laptop and a clear from the line controller at the same moment, didn't you?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, that timing lines up. I was pushing the write right when the controller fired its clear.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Back in 2019 we had a lightning strike on Line 3 and it kept throwing 1920H alarms over and over until we cleared the IP storage area and re-entered everything from the panel — not from the laptop. Laptop writes kept getting stomped.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: From the panel, got it. So first SM8495 alone, then the values with SM8492.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. Clear SD8498 with SM8495 on its own, then write with SM8492. One at a time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: By the way, did the spare-parts delivery ever show up? I saw a pallet near the dock this morning.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No idea, I was on the other line all morning. Ask Linh, she handles the receipts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Also, are you on first shift tomorrow or moving to nights?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Nights starting Thursday. Swap with Duc so he can take his kid to the doctor.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And lunch — you eating at the canteen or did you bring something?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Brought rice. The canteen's doing that fish thing again, no thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Fair. Okay, so let me go clear SD8498 first.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yep. And remember what I said — corrupted values persist in the battery-backed area, so verify SD8492 to SD8497 are valid octets before you cycle anything.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Panel only, no laptop this time.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. That's how we finally killed the repeat 1920H after the 2019 lightning strike — cleared the storage area and typed it all in from the panel.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, heading over. Thanks.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Let me know if 1920H comes back. If it does, check whether the line controller's clear is racing your write again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need to flag something on MR-JE-AX809 at Da Nang, Line 12, pick-and-place cell B. About 2 out of 10 power-ups it throws AL. 14.1 on the seven-segment, mostly after the cell's been sitting idle overnight.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Once it actually starts up it runs fine all shift. But it's happened Monday morning three weeks straight now. I already restored factory defaults on the drive last Friday and it still comes back.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on — don't go condemning the amplifier just because it's intermittent. The manual order is parameters first, then power supply noise and shorted connectors, and only then the drive itself.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right, but I was thinking, since it's so random, maybe we just swap the MR-JE-AX809 out now and save the downtime.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that yet. And before you ever reset a drive on this cell again, always record parameter No. PA01, PA05, and PA06 on the drive label first — a previous default restore on this cell wiped out the original gain settings and we had to chase them for two days.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: That fan install two months back — the new 1.5 kW cabinet fan — did that get put on the same circuit?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, actually it did. And now that I think about it, the alarm shows up more often when that fan is running.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There you go. On Line 12, that 24 VDC branch feeding the MR-JE-AX809 also feeds the new cabinet fan, so measure ripple right there with a scope before you touch the drive.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Scope on the 24 VDC at the cabinet? What am I looking for exactly?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Ripple. We had identical AL. 14.1 events on Line 12 back in 2023 and a 1000 microfarad, 35 volt electrolytic capacitor across the 24 VDC input at terminal CN1 took it from weekly to none.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Speaking of which, did the spare-parts delivery come in for the other line? I need those couplings before Thursday.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, still on the truck. Should be here tomorrow morning.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so if the ripple checks out fine, what then? I still don't want to be swapping drives blind.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Simple test. If AL. 14.1 follows the drive when you swap it to another cell, tag MR-JE-AX809 for replacement. If it stays with cell B, then the noise source is local and you keep digging here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. One more thing — could I just change parameter No. PC49 and shut the alarm off? That'd stop the nuisance trips.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch PC49 for that. That parameter is for clearing the alarm history, not for suppressing control process errors — you'd just be hiding the problem.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Alright, let's grab lunch before this turns into a whole afternoon. Who's on the next break rotation?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'm up after I finish logging this one. Give me ten minutes.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about the order — parameters, then noise, then the drive. Don't skip ahead to the swap.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So I'll scope the 24 VDC at CN1 first thing in the morning before the fan even kicks on.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And pull PA01, PA05, PA06 off the label and write them down before you do anything else to that drive.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: While you're at it, the Line 12 changeover got moved to Friday afternoon, so you've got time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Perfect. I'll have the ripple reading and the parameter record ready by then.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on the MR-JE-AX343 in cell D. Every time the operator restarts cam control after a manual jog, we get F6.1 on the servo amp.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: F6.1 again on Line 4? What's the feed current value showing right now?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It's reading -12.5 mm, but the reciprocating cam stroke is programmed 0 to +80. The fault showed up after a mechanical adjustment pushed the follower negative.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's not an amplifier failure. On this cell F6.1 historically follows a manual jog that leaves the feed current value negative. Before you touch any cam data, jog the axis back inside the physical stroke marks painted on the machine guide.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Also, spare-parts delivery for the other line is coming after lunch, so don't pull a new amp off the shelf for this.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. Quick workaround: command a move to 40 mm in manual mode, then start cam control without cycling power. On Line 4 we locally set the cam standard position to 40 mm, the mid-stroke, to avoid F6.1 after any manual intervention.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I shouldn't power-cycle the amplifier first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, power-cycling before moving the axis back into the stroke won't clear F6.1 and just wastes production time. Move it to 40, then start cam control.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on FX5-PLC298 over in Machining cell F, Line 12. SCADA logged error 7E41H three times in ten minutes, all during random reads.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 7E41H? That's a data length error — too many points in the random read. Did you check the point count in the SCADA message log before you start blaming the comms module?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It was asking for 300 points from D5000. And nothing changed on the PLC, only the recipe got downloaded at 08:05.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. The FX5 only allows a max of 192 points per random read command, so anything bigger has to be split into chunks of 192 or less. And the line controller defaults to a block size of 256, which is over the limit — you have to manually set it to 192 in the communication settings.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So it's not the hardware then. Somebody else was saying we should just bump the timeout.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, timeout won't help — it's too many points, not a slow response. We saw this exact thing back in 2022 after a firmware update reset the block size to 256; fix was setting it back to 192 in the controller's communication settings. By the way, did the spare-parts delivery for Line 9 come in yet?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, still waiting on that. Lunch at eleven still?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, eleven. Go change that block size to 192 first, then we eat.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on Line 4. The FX5-ENET/IP module on FX5-PLC520 at Machining cell A is throwing 1901H on the Ethernet diagnostic display after Monday power-up. It came up at 06:12, we did a CPU reset, it talked to SCADA for about twenty minutes, then faulted again at 06:47.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No new EtherNet/IP devices were added, but the cabinet was opened Friday for filter replacement and the module got re-seated. Cabinet temp was logged at 41 degrees when it faulted the second time. Manual says run the hardware test and call Mitsubishi if it persists, so should I just order a replacement module?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold off on ordering anything. On this cell, 1901H after a weekend power cycle has twice been caused by condensation on the FX5-ENET/IP connector, not by a dead module.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before condemning the module, dry the connector with dry instrument air and let the cabinet stabilize for 15 minutes. And don't reseat it while the cabinet is still powered, that risks damaging the bus connector and doesn't fix the condensation anyway.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then run the hardware test twice. A single pass can clear a transient memory check while the fault is still latent, so one pass tells you nothing.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: What do you want logged for this one? We had a run of these last quarter and I don't want to lose the trail.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Record the module serial number and cabinet humidity in the line log whenever 1901H appears. The site had three repeat cases on the same module batch, so we need those numbers to spot it if it's that batch again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Dry the connector, let it stabilize fifteen minutes, hardware test twice, and log the serial and humidity. I'll do that now and call you if 1901H comes back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need you over at FX5-PLC963 on Line 12, Assembly cell D. The RD LED is completely off but the SD LED is solid on — PLC's still sending to the master, but nothing's coming back and the HMI is stuck on values from 14:18.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch anything at the PLC end, go check the master station — is its send LED actually flashing? If the master's silent, the fault is upstream and nothing you do at our end will help.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Master's blinking fine, so it's sending. Nothing was changed in the program or wiring that I know of... though they did run a new cable between the PLC and the switch last week.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Solid SD with RD off on this FX5 usually means the receive pair is reversed. First thing, pop the RJ45 and swap the orange and white-orange wires. And while you're in there, check whether that new cable is stranded — back in March 2024 we had a replacement cable with stranded wire instead of solid core that gave intermittent receive failures about two weeks after install.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Should I also just swap the comm module while I'm at it, in case it's dead?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go there yet. If the LEDs aren't flashing, the manual says check wiring and communication settings first — and on this line a reversed pair or wrong cable type is way more common than a bad module. Resetting the master is a waste of time too.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Anything else on the settings side?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: One more thing — the local receive timeout on the FX5-PLC963 is set to 100 ms. If the master polls slower than that, RD can look off even though valid data is arriving, so keep it in mind before you blame the hardware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck. On FX5-PLC646, the line-side FTP client keeps failing to download the previous shift's data logging CSV from the SD card. Seven out of ten attempts since 08:15 show '530 Login incorrect', then it works if the operator retypes the password manually. The client config was updated yesterday during a Windows patch, and the login name field now has a 14-character auto-generated string.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the SD card — intermittent FTP failures usually aren't card wear. And don't reboot the CPU module or the FTP client either, a power cycle won't clear a login name length mismatch. First, check the CPU module's FTP server login name parameter, not the Ethernet cable or switch port.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so what do we do about that 14-character login name? The manual says the FTP server login name max is 12 one-byte alphanumeric characters, and the default is FXCPU.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about checking the CPU module first, that's still step one if login fails after truncation. But the immediate fix: that 14-character login name exceeds the 12-character limit, so truncate it to the first 12 characters and store that value in the client profile. Also, at Plant Hanoi, the FTP client on Line 1 Inspection cell E has a known bug that appends the domain suffix to the login name after a Windows patch.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Should I just change it now, or do we need to back anything up first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before changing any FTP credentials on FX5-PLC646, always export the current SD card logging files via a direct USB card reader as a backup. That way if something goes sideways you still have the shift data.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll grab the USB reader from the crib. By the way, are you on days next week? They're talking about swapping the shift schedule again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: I think so, but let's not worry about that now. Do the backup first, then truncate the login name to 12 characters in the client profile. If login still fails after truncation, check the CPU module's FTP server login name parameter first, not the Ethernet cable or switch port.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck. At 14:20 on Line 8 I tried to upload a 12 MB recipe file from the FX5-PLC870 to the engineering PC over FTP, and after 90 seconds it just said 'Connection timed out.' Then I tried to log right back in and got '530 Login incorrect' even though I never changed the password.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch anything — check the PLC's connection status LEDs. Is anyone else logged into the FTP server? I bet another technician on a different PC is still connected. The CPU only allows one FTP client at a time, so a second login gets an error and no connection.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, actually I saw another tech logged in from a different PC. So that's why my login failed? Should I just reset the password now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. The password may need a reset if repeated login failures keep happening, but first make sure no other client is connected. And after a timeout, don't hammer it — wait 30 seconds for the TCP/IP stack to fully release the old connection before you retry login.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Speaking of waiting — lunch is at 12:30 today, and the spare-parts delivery for Line 4 is supposedly arriving around 13:00. Just so you two don't disappear mid-fix.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Also, that 12 MB file — anything larger than 8 MB, you should switch the CPU to STOP mode before the FTP write. Writing a big file to the SD card in RUN state can cause a communication error. I've seen it corrupt transfers more than once.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So first confirm no other client is logged in, wait 30 seconds after a timeout, and for files over 8 MB put the CPU in STOP. Should I power cycle the PLC to clear the error faster?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't power cycle — if the SD card is mid-access you could corrupt it. Just follow the steps: check the connection LEDs, wait the 30 seconds, and for big files switch to STOP first. Last time this happened on Line 8, that sequence fixed it without a reboot.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Boss, the FX5-PLC866 on Line 9, cell E keeps dropping its serial link to the barcode scanner. It throws 7F68H about eight to twelve times a shift, and a power cycle clears it for maybe twenty to forty minutes.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: When did it start?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Monday morning. Two days after they put the new VFD on that same panel for the conveyor. Scanner's daisy-chained with a second scanner and the weigh scale on the same two-wire bus.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: One of the guys said the serial port must be fried, wanted to swap the CPU out right away.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't swap the CPU. On this cell, ninety percent of framing errors come back to the scanner's 9600 bps, 8-N-1 setting being changed to 8-E-1 during a firmware update. Check that before you touch anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if the scanner setting is fine?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then look at the VFD. That new drive on panel 9 was wired with its motor cable in the same tray as the RS-485 bus, and it's injecting noise. We had the same 7F68H back in March 2023 and fixed it with a 30 cm separation and a ferrite on the bus.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Someone also said to re-terminate the shield at both ends to improve grounding. Should I do that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. Terminating the shield at both ends makes a ground loop and makes the noise-induced framing errors worse. Leave it single-ended.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Anything else before I start changing parameters?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First check SD1005 for a momentary power failure at the PLC station. A 20 ms brownout on the 24 V rail mimics a framing error, so I always look at that before touching any parameter.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And while we wait on the cable re-route?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Use the site workaround. Drop the bus from 19200 bps to 9600 bps and enable the scanner's 50 ms inter-character timeout until the VFD cable is re-routed.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good. Junior, start with the scanner setting and SD1005, then get me a plan for the cable separation.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand. The FX5-PLC473 on line 12, packaging cell F stopped talking to the line SCADA this morning at 06:42, right after the weekend parameter restore. Diagnostics show event code 3098, and 3095 popped up twice in the hour before.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 3098, that's the IP filter complaining that address 1 is greater than or equal to address 2. Did night shift touch that list?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, they added three target addresses for the new vision camera subnet. And the Ethernet diagnostic LED is flashing, so I was about to swap the comm module.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't waste your time on the module. The manual for 3095 and 3098 points at parameter values, not hardware. On FX5-PLC473 you always enter the lower address first, because the firmware compares address 1 against address 2 before it does any range validation.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if they typed the higher IP first, it trips 3098 even if the range itself is fine?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And here's the thing — back in 2019 on line 12 we had the same 3098, and it turned out someone had copied a filter row from another cell. Not a bad Ethernet module, just a copied row. Check for that pattern.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. What about the 3095s? Could that just be noise from the restore?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, 3095 means the number of target IP addresses in the filter settings is outside the allowed range. Site limit here is at most 8 target IP addresses per filter group on this PLC. That was set locally after the 2021 network audit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So with the three new camera addresses, how many do they have now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If they had six before and added three, that's nine — over the limit. For quick recovery I keep a known-good IP filter CSV for cell F on the maintenance laptop and just restore it instead of retyping addresses. That avoids both the order mistake and the count mistake.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I just delete the whole filter list to clear the alarm and start fresh?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. Deleting the list removes the target-address range check and leaves the cell exposed on the plant network. Restore the known-good CSV, then add the camera addresses in the right order, keeping it under 8 per group.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need a hand. On MR-JE-AX559 in Packaging cell F, the HMI logged warning E1.1 three times between 14:10 and 15:40 during indexing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Motor housing felt hot to touch, and it got worse after we bumped the line from 40 to 55 packs a minute last week. No alarm latched, machine just kept running. Ambient was 38 degrees this afternoon.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't go ordering a new servo amp yet. On this cell, E1.1 after a 15 pack a minute speed increase usually means mechanical drag in the gearbox, not a bad servo amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So what do I check first? I was about to swap the MR-JE-AX559 amplifier because E1 points that way in the book.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check the gearbox oil level and coupling alignment before you touch any MR-JE-AX559 amplifier parameters. That's the order.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: We're pushing 55 packs a minute today, can we just reset and keep running? Machine cleared itself every time.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. Cell F had the same E1.1 pattern back in March 2023, and the fix was replacing a dry gearbox oil seal.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so I'll pull the cover and look at the oil level and the coupling.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And before we decide to derate the cycle, log the warning timestamps and motor surface temperature every 30 minutes for one shift.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Every 30 minutes for a whole shift, got it. Then we look at the data?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then we look at the data. If the gearbox oil is low or the coupling is off, that's our drag, not the amplifier.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll hold off on replacing the amp and keep the line at 55 for now while you log it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: One shift of logs first. If the temps and warnings keep climbing, we derate. If it's the seal like in March 2023, we swap it and recheck alignment.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand. MR-JE-AX572 on Packaging cell E keeps throwing E8.1. Three times this week, all during the 14:00 to 16:00 high-duty run.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: E8.1, cooling fan speed reduction. Does it clear on its own when you stop the line?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, it clears by itself after each stop, but it comes back about 40 minutes after restart. No trip, just the warning. Cabinet's at 41 C and I can smell something hot near the amp.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't order a new amplifier yet. On cell E, E8.1 is almost always the fan intake foam clogged with carton dust, not the fan itself dying.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So should I just pull the fan unit and swap it? We've got spares in the Line 6 cabinet.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. Before you replace the MR-JE-AX572 fan, vacuum that foam filter first, then spin the fan blade by hand and feel it for at least 10 seconds. If it turns smooth, the fan's fine.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. What about the cabinet filter? It was last cleaned 5 months ago.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Clean that too, but I've seen this before. Back in March 2023 we had an E8.1 on Line 6 and what fixed it was rerouting the cabinet exhaust duct 15 cm away from the packaging film roll.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So are we pulling the fan or not? I need to know if we're stopping the line.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold off. We keep spare MR-JE fan units in the Line 6 cabinet, but I only swap them after two consecutive E8.1 warnings within 8 hours. This is spread out over the week, so clean first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if I just ignore it? It's only a warning, not a trip.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't ignore it. The manual says E8 stops by DB, and if it keeps overheating you'll get an unplanned stop right in the middle of the run. Clean it, then let the equipment cool about 30 minutes before you restart.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on FX5-PLC725 over in Line 3, Machining cell B. The HMI keeps throwing C0B2H, buffer full, maybe every 2 to 3 hours during production.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Buffer full, huh. What changed recently? Anything touched on that cell?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: SCADA got updated last week, it's polling the PLC every 100 ms now instead of 500. No cable damage, no switch alarms, same subnet, and the other cells are fine. Cycle just pauses 5 to 10 seconds and resumes on its own.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I just swap the Ethernet cable and the switch to rule out the physical layer?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go swapping cables and switches. This isn't a physical layer problem, it's buffer overflow from the request rate. Before you change any parameters, grab a Wireshark trace on the PLC port for 10 minutes so we can confirm the request rate and the ACK timing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll get the capture. What do you think we'll see?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: My bet is the SCADA server is sending both MELSOFT and SLMP requests to the FX5-PLC725 on the same connection. That overloads the buffer. You need to split those two protocols onto separate connections.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Could we just disable SLMP and run MELSOFT only? Simpler, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. The manual says don't access through one station like that, and we may need both protocols. The fix is to increase the request interval and wait for a response before sending the next one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. By the way, did the spare-parts order for Line 3 come in yet? I saw a box by the crib.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that came in this morning. Anyway, back to this — we had the same buffer-full thing on Line 2 a while back. Increasing the SCADA poll from 100 ms to 300 ms and adding a 50 ms wait after each response fixed it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 300 and a 50 ms wait, noted. Anything else on the PLC side?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: For this cell, set the FX5-PLC725 receive buffer to 4096 bytes and the send buffer to 2048 bytes in the Ethernet parameters. That's our local tuning baseline. And like I said about the Wireshark trace, do that first before you touch anything.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. Trace first, then split the protocols and adjust the buffers. I'll grab lunch after and get on it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand with FX5-PLC836 on Line 5, Inspection cell D. The TCP link to the vision system dropped around 09:12 and I can't get it to reopen.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: What did the OPEN instruction give you?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Error code C0H. I tried reopening on host port 5000 and target port 5000 within about 120 ms of the close, and it just failed. I'm thinking the Ethernet cable's gone bad — I want to swap it out right now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go changing the cable — that's not your problem. After you close a TCP connection, that socket sits in TIME_WAIT on the vision system's stack for about 2 seconds on Line 5, so you need to wait 2.5 seconds before retrying the same port. You fired it off way too early.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if I just drop the retry to 50 ms it'll come back faster?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, that'll make it worse — going faster on the same port is exactly what's failing. Also, never use ports 5549 to 5569 for socket comms on this PLC, the system reserves those for internal diagnostics.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Anything else I should know about this cell specifically?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, we had this exact failure in Inspection cell D back in March 2025 after a power flicker. The fix then was switching the PLC's active-open port to 5010 and updating the vision recipe.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. By the way, did the spare-parts delivery come in for the other line yet?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet, should be here after lunch. Anyway — if you need a quick reconnect, change the host station port on the active-open side to 5011 for this cell instead of reusing 5000, like I said about not hammering the same port.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: OK, so 5011 for cell D and wait the 2.5 seconds. I'll set that up now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And remember the vision system got restarted ten minutes before this for that firmware update, so its stack was fresh — nothing wrong with your program.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood, thanks. I'll go update the recipe and retry on 5011.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got AL.69.3 coming up on the MR-JE-AX344 over at cell E again. It only pops when the carriage runs toward the forward end, never on the way back. The LSP LED on the drive stays off even when I push the limit switch by hand.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright, don't go ordering a new servo amp yet. On Line 9, a 69.3 is almost always the LSP input common wire being loose at terminal CN1-13, not the limit switch itself.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: But it's a command error, right? I figured the drive's internal position tracking is messed up, so I was going to swap the amplifier.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the amp — that's the wrong move. Before you replace any controller, put your meter between CN1-13 and CN1-20 and measure for 24 V DC. If it's missing, check that connector first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. What about the software limits? I could change Pr. PT15 to PT18 and just jog it past the forward end to clear the alarm.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the parameters yet — that just hides it. When the LSP LED is off like that, temporarily jumper CN1-13 to COM and jog slowly. That confirms the switch circuit before you go near any parameters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And you know, there was a new cable routed right next to the limit switch two days ago during the gripper swap. Could that be related?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's exactly the kind of thing that causes it. The last three 69.3 faults we had at cell E were all fixed by reseating the CN1 connector after a cable tie got overtightened.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. By the way, are you on days all week or do you move to nights Friday?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: I'm on days till Friday, then nights next week. Anyway, like I said about checking the connector first — go reseat CN1 before anything else and see if that LSP LED comes back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Also the spare-parts guy said our CN1 connectors won't be in till Thursday, so hopefully I don't need one.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Probably won't. Reseat it, measure that 24 V DC at CN1-13 to CN1-20, and if it's still dead we'll jumper CN1-13 to COM and jog slow to prove the wiring. Report back what you find.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with the MR-JE-AX580 on Line 5. It tripped alarm 8A.1 three times during the 06:00 startup while I was commissioning with my laptop.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 8A.1 on the MR-JE is a communication time-out. When does it trip — only with the laptop plugged into the front USB port?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, only when my laptop is connected. The drive's been running all week without alarm when the laptop is disconnected.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And the USB cable — I heard it was recently routed around the cabinet door hinge. Any sharp bend at the connector?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yes, there's a sharp bend right at the connector. Pressing reset clears it, but it comes back within 2 to 5 minutes if I move the cable.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing: on the MR-JE-AX580, wiggle the USB connector at the drive while watching the alarm. If it trips 8A.1 within 10 seconds, replace the cable before you touch the amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I shouldn't just swap out the drive right away? The manual says 8A.1 could be a communication time-out, but I thought maybe the amplifier is internally faulty.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the amplifier yet. The last three 8A.1 events on Line 5 were caused by a damaged USB cable at the cabinet door hinge, not by the servo amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the hinge is the real culprit. Should I just replace the cable and be done?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Replace the cable, but also keep the laptop USB cable strain-relieved with a 50 mm service loop so the MR-JE front connector is not loaded when the door closes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, a 50 mm service loop. But before I replace anything, is there anything else I should check? The manual mentioned checking if a command was transmitted.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. Before replacing MR-JE-AX580, confirm the laptop terminal software is actively sending commands, because an idle USB session can also trigger 8A.1.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if the terminal software is idle, that could cause the alarm even with a good cable?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. So check that first, then do the wiggle test. If it trips within 10 seconds, replace the cable. Only after that, if it still trips, consider the amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll make sure the terminal is sending commands, then wiggle the connector. If it trips, I'll replace the cable and add the service loop.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the right order. And remember, the last three 8A.1 events on Line 5 were the cable at the hinge — not the drive.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Thanks. I'll let you know if it comes back after the cable swap.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. If it does, then we'll look at the amplifier, but I doubt it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? Something really bad just happened on i4L-R269, cell E. I was doing a teach-pendant job and the robot went from Manual to Auto with the guy still inside the cell.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Wait, the pendant job — was the cell door interlock bypassed again?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, bypassed two days ago for the fixture alignment. And the weird thing is the Front Panel showed AUTO but the pendant still said MANUAL. No alarm at all, and the high power light on the XFP connector was on solid.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the classic back-feed. On i4L-R269 a 24 V signal wired in parallel with the Front Panel mode contact can feed back and force AUTO while the pendant is still sitting in MANUAL.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So it's not the mode selector switch itself being stuck? Someone suggested just swapping the Front Panel selector right away.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't chase that first. Check the XFP Automatic/Manual selection inputs — they have to be dual-channel and not jumpered together. We had exactly this in 2023, a single jumper across pins 3 and 4.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And someone else said just disconnect the high power enable input to force it into Manual as a quick fix. That sounds wrong to me.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's a bad idea, don't do that. Before any teach-pendant work in cell E, pull the cell-door bypass and meter 0 V on both XFP mode-selection channels. Both of them, with a meter, every time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Also, did you hear the spare-parts delivery got pushed to Thursday? The gripper fingers we ordered are stuck at the warehouse.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Figures. By the way, the site log shows the last three mode-select faults on Line 9 all happened right after weekend fixture changes, when contractors added a parallel AUTO button.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So contractors wiring in an extra AUTO button — that's the pattern. Are you on second shift tomorrow or the early one?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Early, I'm covering for Linh. Anyway, grab a meter and we'll check those XFP channels before anyone touches that cell again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Sounds good. Oh, and cell C on Line 9 was throwing a minor position fault earlier, nothing serious, just so you know.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Noted. Let's deal with R269 first — lunch after, I'm buying.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with i4L-R838 in cell F. This morning it threw E-STOP CH1/CH2 MISMATCH three times in about forty minutes, and each time the robot just stopped mid-cycle. The XUSR status LEDs were flickering green to red on channel 2 only, channel 1 stayed green the whole time.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, and the operator panel E-stop button was replaced last week after that mechanical hit, right? First thing, don't let anyone tell you to swap the safety relay — a Category 3 PL-d relay is allowed to have intermittent channel faults, that's exactly what dual-channel checking is for.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Production is breathing down my neck though. Can we just disable the channel 2 status output in the config to stop the alarm and keep running?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that — never disable a safety status output. That's masking a real channel 2 dropout, and the safety relay will still trip you unpredictably. We diagnose it properly.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So where do I start? I checked the button wiring and it looked fine after the replacement.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Put a scope on the dual-channel E-stop status outputs at XUSR. A mismatch shorter than 30 ms is invisible to the controller but still trips the safety relay — that's why you get the alarm with no obvious cause.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if I see a short dropout on channel 2, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then look at the wiring. There's a 0.5 mm² wire on XUSR pin 7 of i4L-R838 that has a 12-year-old crimp — it oxidizes in Bac Ninh humidity and causes channel 2 dropouts every 6 to 8 weeks. That fits your timeline perfectly.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So it's just a bad crimp? Should I order a new cable?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before that, since the operator E-stop button was just replaced, re-torque the XUSR terminal screws to 0.5 N·m. Loose screws on pins 7–8 produced identical CH1/CH2 alarms back in 2022.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll check the torque first. Anything else I should have on hand?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about the cabling, the site keeps a spare 10356-10500 extension cable in the Line 5 cabinet — a damaged cable shield can also cause channel 2 noise, so swap it if the crimp and torque don't clear it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, scope first, then torque the XUSR screws to 0.5 N·m, then the crimp on pin 7, and the spare cable if needed. I'll report back after the scope check.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember the manual says the XUSR gives dual-channel E-stop inputs and status outputs — so a one-channel dropout there is a real fault, not a ghost. We fix it, we don't configure it away.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: We're getting NAK 7F69H parity errors on the FX5-PLC919 inspection cell link on Line 2, about 3 to 5 times every 8-hour shift. They cluster within 10 minutes of the 06:00 and 14:00 shift changes when the camera and barcode reader cabinets power on.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: If the error is logged in the PLC, just swap the FX5-PLC919 CPU module. That's the fastest way to rule out a bad CPU.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the CPU. 7F69H is a line-level parity fault, usually from noise or simultaneous multi-drop transmissions, not a CPU failure. Let's check the supply and the line first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The PLC and the two devices are on RS-485 multi-drop, all at 9600, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, even parity. No cables or connectors changed in 30 days, and the errors stop when the camera cabinet is left powered off.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On this cell, 90% of 7F69H bursts trace to the vision camera cabinet sharing the same 24 VDC supply as the barcode reader. Check that supply first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I should check the 24 VDC feeding both cabinets before anything else?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Then, before touching parity settings, scope the RS-485 A/B pair at the PLC end for ringing above 1.5 V during camera boot.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: What if we just change the PLC parity from even to none? That might stop the errors.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. Changing the PLC parity to none without matching the camera and reader will create the parity mismatch the manual warns about. Keep all three on even parity.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll leave parity alone. What about the noise — has anything been added to the site to stop these shift-change alarms?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Since 2022, we've added a 120 ohm termination resistor at the far end and a ferrite on the camera cable to suppress these shift-change 7F69H alarms.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I verify those are still in place and not damaged?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, check the 120 ohm resistor at the far end and the ferrite on the camera cable. If either is missing or loose, that could explain the bursts.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: And if the noise is from both cabinets powering up at once, how do we interlock them?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: For multi-drop interlock, site practice is to delay camera and reader power-up by 5 seconds after the PLC reaches RUN, using the PLC's Y10 output.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So Y10 drives a relay that holds off the camera and reader for 5 seconds after RUN?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's right. That prevents simultaneous multi-drop transmissions during boot.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll scope the A/B pair first, then check the 24 V supply, the 120 ohm resistor, the ferrite, and the Y10 delay.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And like I said about the 24 VDC supply, start there because it's the most common cause on this cell.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: If we still get errors after all that, what's the next step?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the errors persist, we initialize the entire transmission sequence, because when multiple errors occur simultaneously the smallest-numbered code is reported. But first make sure the parity settings match and the noise countermeasures are in place.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, MR-JE-AX391 on Line 9 is acting up again. Monday morning, 06:05 power-up, Palletizing cell C, and it throws AL.16.3 right away.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It came back on three power cycles in a row, same alarm every time. Then the operator wiggled the CN2 encoder connector by hand and it cleared and ran fine.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Line was down since Saturday 18:00, right? And didn't we have the cabinet door open Friday afternoon for filter cleaning?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, Friday afternoon filter cleaning. No alarm history before this weekend either. That drive ran 14 months without any encoder trouble.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you even think about swapping hardware, push the CN2 connector in and tighten its two screws. On Line 9 palletizers, AL.16.3 after a weekend stop is usually the CN2 shell loosened by Friday filter-cleaning vibration, not a failed encoder.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That connector works loose about twice a year on this cell, so always do that before you start ohming the cable.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I shouldn't just replace the HG servo motor? The alarm names the encoder after all.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. Cable connection and parameter checks come first. Motor is way down the list.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Should we just reload everything from the backup CF card to be safe?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't do that. Reloading from the backup would overwrite the verified Pr. PC22 four-wire setting and can actually create a new AL.16.3.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: While you're in there, check Pr. PC22 for [A]/[C] or Pr. PC04 for [B]. If the two-wire/four-wire setting is wrong, fix it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Anything else on the power side?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Cell C's 24 V supply dips to 20.4 V during the 06:00 palletizer startup. Log it with a Fluke 1730 for one week before you condemn the drive.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Speaking of which, have you all put in your shift swap requests for next month? I need them by Thursday.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll get mine in tonight. Oh, and the crib guy said the spare-parts delivery from Mitsubishi is running late again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's why we keep two spare MR-JE-70A amplifiers and one HG-KR43 motor in the Line 9 crib. Otherwise it's a 10-day Mitsubishi lead time.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Right. And lunch is at 11:30 today, they're doing the canteen thing for the quarterly safety meeting.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So connector first, then the parameter check, then the voltage logging.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Last time this happened on cell B it was just the shell. Ten minutes with a screwdriver and we were running.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good. Also remind the night shift about the Line 7 conveyor guard — different issue, but they keep forgetting.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. I'll start with the CN2 connector this afternoon and log the 24 V after that.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Perfect. And don't touch that motor until we've ruled out the connector and the parameters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need your help with MR-JE-AX144 on Line 2, Dispensing cell E. I keep getting an E1.2 overload warning on the servo amplifier display during the dispensing stroke.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: E1.2, huh? That's the load warning before it goes to a real thermal overload. What's the cycle look like when it pops up?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It happens about every 30 minutes. The axis is moving at 2500 mm/s with a 4 kg payload, and it clears after a 5-minute pause. Ambient near the cabinet is 38°C, and the motor feels hot but no smoke or burning smell.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay. Before you even think about swapping the amplifier, let's check the mechanical side. Did anything change recently?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, we replaced the dispensing nozzle last week. Since then the axis seems to push harder at the end of the stroke.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That fits. On this line, E1.2 usually shows up when the linear guide rail lacks lubrication. We add 2 g of NSK LR3 grease to the dispensing axis block every 400 hours.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I should grease it now? But what if it's the servo itself? Maybe the amplifier is just bad?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't jump to replacing the amplifier. The manual says E1.2 is a load warning, not an electronic fault. Before touching the servo, I always check the mechanical drag by hand: if the axis needs more than 15 N of force to move, the problem is mechanical, not electrical.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll push it by hand. But what else could cause it? Someone suggested just raising the torque limit to 150% to push through.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. That ignores the 85% load threshold and risks a real thermal overload error. We need to find the actual cause, not mask it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So mechanical drag first. Anything else from past experience on this exact machine?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Three years ago, a similar E1.2 on MR-JE-AX144 was caused by a partially clogged cooling fan filter. We now replace that filter every 6 months.

turns.speaker: junior_01
