turns.text: I didn't even think about the cooling fan. The motor is hot, but that could be from the load too.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. Heat builds up if the fan can't pull air through. Check the filter and clean or replace it if it's clogged. While you're at it, check the guide rail lubrication.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Is there any parameter setting we should look at? Sometimes voltage dips cause nuisance warnings.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: For this cell, we set parameter PC05 to 70% instead of the default 100% to avoid nuisance E1 warnings during voltage dips.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So PC05 at 70%. Should I change that now or check the mechanical stuff first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check the mechanical drag and the filter first. If those are fine and you still get E1.2, then verify PC05 is set to 70%.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll grease the block with 2 g of NSK LR3, check the fan filter, and test the drag by hand. Then look at PC05.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. And remember, E1 can escalate to AL. 50 or AL. 51 if you let it keep running overloaded.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll report back after I check the drag and the filter. Thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got a problem with FX5-PLC792 on Line 4, cell C. After the weekend power-down, I powered it up at 06:10 and the Ethernet ERROR LED came on solid right away. POWER is on, SD and RD stay off even though the cable is plugged into the cell switch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Solid ERROR at CPU power-up, no SD/RD activity. Did anyone touch the Ethernet parameters over the weekend, or is the project the same as Friday?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No parameter changes since Friday 17:30, it ran fine then. The PLC still runs local logic, but the SCADA link to cell C is down. I was thinking we should just swap the Ethernet module, the LED is basically screaming at us.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on, don't pull the module yet. First open GX Works3 and check the Ethernet parameter setting. If the IP and subnet match the last archived project, then you can suspect hardware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I can pull up the project. But what if the parameters look fine? Then it's definitely the module, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not so fast. Remember the 2023 lightning storm here at Binh Duong? It damaged the surge path on the FX5-PLC792 Ethernet module. So before you replace anything, always verify the switch port link LED first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll check the switch port link LED. Which project file should I compare against?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: For cell C we keep the archived GX Works3 project on the maintenance laptop under folder 2024-11-18_FX5-PLC792. That way you can restore parameters quickly if something got corrupted.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Found the folder. By the way, did you see the shift schedule for next week? They moved the start time to 6:30.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw that. We'll deal with it later. What about the switch port link LED, is it lit?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, it's dark. So that points to hardware after all?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you call Mitsubishi Electric for repair, reseat the extension cable between the CPU and the Ethernet module, then re-check the ERROR LED. Sometimes it's just a bad contact after a power cycle.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll reseat it now. Also, the manual says if the ERROR LED is flashing it stores an error code, but ours is solid, so I guess that's different.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, solid at power-up means either a parameter setting error you can fix in GX Works3 or a hardware error. Flashing means an error code was stored and you have to read it to find the cause.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I reseated the cable and the ERROR LED is still solid. So now I check the parameters in GX Works3 against the archive?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. If the IP and subnet match the archived project, then it's hardware. And remember to verify that switch port link LED before you replace the module, because of that lightning damage.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll compare the parameters now. Oh, and the spare-parts delivery for Line 2 is supposed to arrive at lunchtime.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: I'll grab lunch after we sort this. Let me know what the parameters show.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The IP and subnet match the 2024-11-18 archive exactly. So it's looking like the module is bad.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then go ahead and contact Mitsubishi Electric for repair. But first double-check that extension cable is fully seated, and confirm the switch port link LED one more time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. So just to recap: check parameters in GX Works3 first, then if they match, suspect hardware, verify the switch port link LED, reseat the extension cable, and then call for repair.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. And keep using that archived project folder 2024-11-18_FX5-PLC792 to restore parameters quickly next time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? FX5-PLC491 over on Line 7 packaging cell keeps throwing CFB0H on the HMI. Three times in the last twenty minutes, every time we send a write command to that MODBUS/TCP weigh scale.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: CFB0H again? First thing, go reseat the RJ45 connector right at the scale. On Line 7 that connector vibrates loose about every six months, and reseating it makes those errors disappear.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll try that. But shouldn't we just swap the PLC Ethernet module? Feels like hardware.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, no, don't start pulling modules. That code is a retransmission timeout, not a dead card. While you're at it, ping the scale from the PLC and check its ARP cache isn't full. A full cache gives you CFB0H even with the cable in perfect shape.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Oh, by the way, did the spare-parts delivery for Line 5 come in? And are we still on the early shift Friday?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Delivery's supposed to be Thursday, and yeah, Friday we're early. Listen, one more thing on this — I keep a spare Ethernet switch pre-configured with the same IP range in the Line 7 cabinet. If CFB0H keeps repeating, we swap it in within five minutes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. Could that new VFD they installed last week be involved? The cable passes right by it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's exactly it. That new VFD on Line 7 caused the same CFB0H faults on another cell last week until we increased the cable separation to 30 cm. So do the connector first, then the ARP check, then the switch, and if it's still flaky, get that cable moved.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand on Line 7, Palletizing cell E. The MR-JE-AX528 servo motor just won't rotate when I give the start command, and there's no alarm or warning on the amplifier or the controller. It started after a junior tech changed some point table parameters.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing on this cell, a common cause of no motor motion without any alarm is point table number 1 getting accidentally overwritten with zero speed. Go check that table before you touch anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll pull up point table 1. But should I also be worried about the amplifier itself? Another guy thinks the servo is faulty and wants to swap it out.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap anything yet. The manual says incorrect point table settings, speed command, speed limit, or electronic gear can all stop the motor from running or make it accelerate wrong, so those parameter checks come first. And before you even check the point tables, verify that the manual pulse generator MR-HDP01 has +5 V to 12 V and 0 V power connected at terminal block X4.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll check the power at X4. Why is that the first step though?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Because back in 2022 we had a similar incident on Line 7 caused by a loose connector on the MR-HDP01 after a cable drag chain replacement. So always confirm that power first before chasing parameters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. And if the point table looks correct but the motor still won't move, what then?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then temporarily set parameter [Pr. PT03] to 1 to bypass the manual pulse generator input for testing. That'll tell you if the pulse generator side is holding it up.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm looking at i4L-R551 on Line 1, Palletizing cell C. It's been running 24/7 for the last 16 days, and the log shows Joint 3 was last greased 11 weeks ago. The planner says the 3-month date is still a week out, so no work order. But we've done about 2.1 million cycles since then. Should I just wait?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, forget the 3-month box. At Line 1's 24/7 rate, i4L-R551 hits the 150 km quill limit in about 14 days. So we ignore the calendar and grease every second Sunday.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so it's already overdue. What grease do I use? I saw some lithium grease in the crib.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Only THK AFF Grease, part number 20950-000, on that Joint 3 quill. We store a dedicated 20950-000 grease gun in the Palletizing cell C cabinet so nobody borrows the Line 3 grease.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. After I grease it, do I need to check anything?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. After greasing i4L-R551, jog Joint 3 through its full stroke twice with the brake release while watching for a dry stripe on the quill.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: What if I miss a dry stripe? How would that show up in production?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: A dry quill on this robot first shows as a 0.3 mm position drift on the pallet corner after about 300 cycles. That's your early warning.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: At shift start the HMI on FX5-PLC756 showed a major 3CF1 at 06:42, and the remote I/O drop on the infeed conveyor went dead for about 12 seconds before the line tripped. That's three mornings straight now, always between 06:40 and 06:50.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Major event code on the PLC — sounds like the CPU itself is failing. Let's just swap the FX5-PLC756 CPU module now and get the line back up.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the CPU yet — on this cell 3CF1 usually traces to the CN1 Ethernet cable connector at the remote drop, not to the PLC CPU. Also, don't just clear the alarm and restart; check the remote drop cabling and the 24 VDC supply first.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Start with the temporary Cat5e patch cord from the March 2024 line rebalance — it's routed right beside the VFD, so reseat and reroute it first. Then check the 24 VDC supply to the remote drop; it sags to 21.4 V when the infeed brake fires.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Night shift said no new downloads, but the cabinet door was left open after Friday's panel cleaning. Should I still be worried about the CPU?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about the CN1 connector, the CPU is almost never the culprit here. Log the alarm timestamp against the brake firing time in the line historian — a 2-second offset confirms electrical noise coupling.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So we reseat and reroute that patch cord, check the 24 V, and pull the historian trend before we touch any module. Got it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, at 10:15 the operator said pick-and-place cell D on Line 1 stopped talking to the host PC. The HMI showed error 7F40H on channel 1 of FX5-PLC972.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 7F40H is a monitoring time out on the serial link. Did it come back on its own?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, comms came back after about 30 seconds, but the error flag is still ON. Nobody changed the program or touched the wiring lately. Should I swap the CPU module?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't replace the CPU yet. First check the host PC's send timeout setting — it's often set to 100 ms, but for this cell it should be 500 ms.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll look at that. Could a loose cable also cause 7F40H?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Back in 2022 we had a loose D-sub connector on the FX5-PLC972 CH1 port that caused intermittent 7F40H errors three times.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Good to know. So how do I get the latched error flag to clear? Can I just reset the HMI screen?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, the HMI won't clear it. Cycle power on the PLC to clear the latched error flags — a STOP-RUN transition may not clear them on this unit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. Anything else I should verify on the PC side before I power-cycle?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check the handshake lines too. The host PC's serial port occasionally drops the RTS signal, so use a port monitor to verify the handshake lines.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So timeout setting, D-sub connector, RTS signal, then power-cycle to clear the latch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. Remember those serial error flags and codes stay latched even after communication is restored, so don't be fooled by the link coming back. Let me know what the port monitor shows.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, something's off with i4L-R304 in cell C. First warm-up cycle this morning at 06:05 showed 0.3 mm drift on the X axis.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It also vibrates audibly at 40% speed going from home to the tool changer. No alarm, but the first three parts after warm-up are out by 0.15 mm.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Cell was idle 48 hours over the weekend, ambient was around 18°C. Normal running temp is 24°C. What do you make of it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Is the drift under 0.4 mm? On i4L-R304, cold-start drift under 0.4 mm usually disappears after 15 minutes of continuous jogging at 30% speed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, 0.3 mm. So I shouldn't be thinking encoder replacement yet?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, no. A 0.3 mm X drift after weekend idle is often caused by grease settling in the ball screw, not by encoder failure. Last time this happened, we jogged it and it came right back.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So just jog it and run? We're behind on parts already.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not full speed, no. Plant Da Nang records show that i4L-R304 needs a 10-minute warm-up program before production on Mondays.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I load a tool for the warm-up?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Run the warm-up program with the tool changer empty to avoid unnecessary wear on the coupling.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. And then jog at 30% for 15 minutes if the drift's still there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. Don't skip the warm-up and go straight to full speed, the first parts will be out of tolerance and the vibration will get worse.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Alright, start the 10-minute program with an empty changer, then jog if needed. Keep me posted.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, i4L-R265 on Line 4 keeps tripping. Alarm 0x0C, overtravel on Z, during lens insertion. Happens two, three times a shift, always going down into fixture F-17.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Funny thing is it never alarms when I jog it slow by hand. But in auto at 80% it shows up. We just did the Z belt tensioner and re-homed it, so I'm thinking maybe the servo motor's going bad?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't touch the servo yet. After belt work on the i4L-R265, before you go near the servo, check the Z-axis upper limit dog — bet it shifted about 0.5 mm.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And on this machine, an overtravel alarm right after belt work is usually a loose encoder coupling, not the motor. Intermittent like that, only in auto? That's the coupling slipping.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So what's the plan? Do we have the part here or are we down waiting on a shipment?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We keep a spare Z-axis encoder coupling in cabinet A-3 here at Dong Nai. But confirm the dog alignment first — only replace the coupling after that checks out.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Anything I need to watch out for while I'm in there checking the dog?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah — block the Z axis with the red safety pin before you reach under the arm. Every time. And don't just run it at full speed to push through the alarm; repeated overtravel will chew up that lens fixture.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand. MR-JE-AX614 on Packaging cell A tripped with alarm 8A.2 three times in twenty minutes this afternoon, around 14:32 on the 12th. Each time it forced-decelerated the servo and I had to reset the alarm. What's going on?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 8A.2 is a Modbus RTU time-out, so before anything else look at the comms link, not the amp. Has anything changed on that cell recently?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: They installed a new VFD on the adjacent conveyor two days ago. And the Modbus cable from the PLC to the amp runs 18 m right alongside the 400 V motor cables.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That 18 m cable to cell A was re-routed back in 2022 after a similar 8A.2 event. It has to stay at least 30 cm away from the 400 V motor cables, so check that routing first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the separation. Anything about the shield I should look at?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. On this line, alarm 8A.2 shows up first when the Modbus RTU shield is grounded only at the PLC end. Don't ground both ends, that causes circulating currents and random time-outs.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, single-ended at the PLC. Should I also look at the servo amplifier or the PLC comms parameters while I'm in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. When 8A.2 and 8E.8 appear together, check the cable shield and routing first before you touch the servo amplifier or the PLC communication parameters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Actually I did see 8E.8 in the alarm history too. But my instinct was to just swap the MR-JE-AX614 amplifier since it keeps tripping.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't do that. The manual lists 8A.2 as a Modbus RTU time-out, which is external to the amplifier, so it's usually cable routing or shielding. Replacing the amp won't fix it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Fair enough. So once the shield and routing are good, do I need to change anything in the PLC?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, for this cell set the Modbus RTU retry count to 3 and the response timeout to 500 ms in the PLC. Use those, not the servo defaults, so it rides through the conveyor VFD switching noise.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Retry 3, timeout 500 ms in the PLC. And if I'm tempted to tweak the amp's internal comms settings first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold off on that. Alarm 8A.2 points to the Modbus RTU link, so verify the shield and routing before you change any parameters. That's the order that works on this line.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on MR-JE-AX592 at Packaging cell D. Operator powered it off over the weekend, and right after the power cycle it threw AL. 37 Parameter error. No alarm history stored, nothing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: AL. 37 after a long power-off? How long was it off, and how old is that amp?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Off more than 24 hours. Twice this week, both times after a long shutdown. I was going to just swap the whole servo amplifier, honestly.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't swap it yet. On the MR-JE-AX592 the parameter memory backup capacitor weakens after about 5 years, and that's what gives you AL. 37 only after long power-offs. Last time this happened, same thing — replaced the amp for nothing. Check the battery voltage on the control board first.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Before you two get deep in it — lunch is at 11:30 today, and the spare-parts truck is late again, so don't count on a new amp today anyway.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good, that settles it. If that battery reads below 2.8 V, replace it and re-enter the parameters. And once you swap the battery, upload the parameters from the master backup in the line PLC within 10 minutes or you'll lose the data.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So never just power cycle it to clear the alarm?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right — never reset AL. 37 by power cycling alone. Always verify the parameter list against the master backup first, then clear it. Those voltage fluctuations the facility team logged probably aren't helping either.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got a problem at the pick-and-place cell D. The FX5-PLC476 master station showed SM9040 ON at 09:15, and SD9061 had 0x0A — data transfer sequence error.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, and what did you do after you saw that?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: There was a brief power dip on the 24V DC supply to the N:N segment. Communication looked normal after that, but the error flag stayed ON.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I cycled power to the PLC to clear it. The line was stopped 12 minutes, but SM9040 was still ON after restart.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, on this cell a power dip often leaves the N:N Network error latched. Cycling power won't do it — you clear it by turning ON SM50 for one scan.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: SM50, one scan. I didn't know that.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch anything else, what's your gut telling you the cause is?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Honestly, I was thinking the communication module might be bad. Should I swap it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. Historical data shows 80% of N:N link errors here trace to a loose shield on the drop cable to station 3, not to the PLC itself.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Station 3, the drop cable shield. So I should go check that first.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And while you're out there, always check the terminating resistor DIP switch on the last station — station 7 — before replacing any communication module.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, station 7 terminator first, then the module.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: One more thing about why this trips so easily — the site uses a 100 ms debounce on the N:N error input to avoid nuisance trips from contactor noise on the same panel.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the contactor noise can make it look like a link error even when it's just a glitch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. That's why we don't just power cycle and assume it's fixed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so first I turn ON SM50 for one scan to clear the latch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, then go look at the shield on the drop cable to station 3.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And check the terminating resistor DIP switch on station 7.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. Last time this happened, it was the station 3 shield — the module was fine.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. I'll clear it with SM50, then check the cable and the terminator before I even think about swapping hardware.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember the manual says serial communication errors stay latched even after communication returns to normal — that's why it didn't clear on its own.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll go do that now and report back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on i4L-R684. Operator on Line 9 Packaging cell B saw a thin film of clear grease around the base of Joint 2 on Saturday at 07:15. No alarm, robot still moving fine, but it's been running 18 hours a day for the last 12 days for the seasonal peak. Night shift wiped a similar smudge from the same spot two days ago and didn't report it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing: don't run it. Manual says any lubricant leak means stop the robot and call OMRON with the specified info. But before you panic — on i4L units here in Hanoi's humid air, a Joint 2 smear is usually just excess assembly grease, not a seal failure, as long as it doesn't drip within 24 hours.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So we wait and watch? What about the fact that night shift already wiped it once and it came back?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We document it properly. We keep a leak-log photo board near Line 9 — any Joint 2 leak gets photographed with a coin beside it for scale before cleanup. That gives us a baseline. And before you even think about calling OMRON, park i4L-R684 in the maintenance corner and leave the brake engaged so the leak position doesn't shift overnight.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. But what if it does turn out to be a real seal failure? Last time someone said just add more grease through the quill fitting and keep running.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, never add grease to a leaking joint — that just masks the problem. And wiping it off and continuing production because no alarm is active is not acceptable either. If it is a seal failure, we need OMRON to replace it. Remember last year i4L-R684 had a Joint 2 leak after 14 months of 18-hour days. OMRON replaced the seal under warranty because we had the LOG.XML and Diagnostic Summary ready.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I'll photograph it with a coin, park it in the maintenance corner with the brake on, and get the LOG.XML and Diagnostic Summary ready in case we need to call OMRON. Should I log the night shift's wipe too?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, log everything. That photo board and those files are exactly what OMRON will ask for. And keep watching it for 24 hours — if it starts dripping, we call them immediately. If it stays a film, it's likely just assembly grease, but we still don't run it until we're sure.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm getting an SLMP error C05BH on the FX5-PLC388 over in Line 5, Inspection cell B. The SCADA HMI was trying to read D100 and it just threw the error at 14:20.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing before you touch anything — check the SCADA tag's data type for D100. Nine out of ten C05BH calls on that cell turn out to be a wrong device type, not a hardware problem.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Data type? Let me look... it says bit access. But it was word access until 13:50 today, someone changed the recipe.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There you go. On the FX5-PLC388, D100 is the line's reject counter and it gets overwritten every 50 ms. Reading it as a bit is what's causing your C05BH.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the error isn't the Ethernet module failing? I saw the comm LED is green and other tags on the same connection update fine.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, that confirms it's not hardware. Don't swap the FX5-ENET/IP module, and don't power-cycle the PLC hoping to clear it — that won't fix a wrong device type.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so what do I do with the tag? The operator wants that counter value, but the recipe now says bit.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the tag has to stay bit, move the counter over to M100 and read that bit instead of D100.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: M100, got it. And should I change it back to word access on D100 for now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Either way works, but after you correct the tag you need to clear the error history in the Ethernet module diagnostics before you retest. Otherwise the old C05BH still shows up and you can't tell if it's fixed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Clear the error history in the Ethernet module diagnostics, okay. Where exactly is that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: It's in the module diagnostics screen — same place you pull the error log. Just clear it, then re-read the tag.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if I change the tag back to word access instead of moving to M100, that fixes the C05BH too?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, because the manual says C05BH happens when the Ethernet module can't read or write the specified device — the remedy is to reconsider the device. A word device read as a bit is exactly that.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I noticed it only errored three times in ten minutes, always when the operator requested the 32-bit counter value from D100.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That lines up with the 50 ms overwrite on D100. The bit read keeps hitting the device while it's being updated, so it fails.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll fix the tag and clear the history. Anything else I should watch for?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Just remember the order — check the tag data type first, then clear the error history, then retest. Don't skip the diagnostics clear or you'll chase a ghost.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Changing the tag now, then clearing the Ethernet module error history.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. If it still errors after that, then we look at the request content — but I doubt it. This one's the device type.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Done — tag's fixed and history cleared. Retesting the read now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Perfect. That should be the end of your C05BH on FX5-PLC388.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on i4L-R719 in Dispensing cell C. Operator requested High Power at 08:12, the Front Panel indicator was flashing, but he took about 15 seconds to actually press the button, and by then the light had stopped and High Power never engaged. Robot had been idle overnight, no config changes on the last shift.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: That's the third time this week on that cell, right? Twice last week too, both times the operator paused to check a part before hitting the button. Junior, what's your read?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Honestly the button felt fine but I'm thinking the switch itself might be going bad, maybe even swap the controller since the LED flashing makes me nervous. Should I pull a replacement button from stores?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the button or the controller yet — the manual says if the High Power button isn't pressed within the timeout, the safety timeout trips and High Power just isn't applied, so the button and controller are probably fine. That flashing LED is normal during the timeout window, it's not a hardware fault. On Line 8 the 10-second default is too short for operators who verify fixtures, so we set it to 20 seconds in ACE for cell C.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good. Also spare-parts delivery for Line 9 got pushed to Friday, so if anyone needs anything from stores, flag it today.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch any timeout settings on i4L-R719, wiggle-test the XFP cable — that connector had a loose pin last year and it caused intermittent flashing. And when the timeout expires the controller logs no alarm at all, so always check the Front Panel LED state first before you assume a hardware fault.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about the timeout settings, once you've verified the XFP is solid, bump cell C to 20 seconds in ACE. Also tell the juniors to press the button within 5 seconds of the request, then release — that avoids the timeout tripping during setup.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, wiggle-test XFP first, then ACE to 20 seconds, and coach the operators to press within 5 seconds. Thanks, that makes way more sense than a bad button.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got a problem with FX5-PLC667 on Line 8, Packaging cell C. My GX Works3 connection kept dropping this morning around 08:15, and it came up with a remote password locked error. Diagnostics showed connection #3 hit an unlock failure count of 5, which matches our upper limit.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: That's the one you changed the built-in Ethernet port password on last Friday after the vendor visit, right? Did you swap the Ethernet module out yet?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I was thinking that, maybe the module's gone bad. But no other module on the network shows unlock failures, just FX5-PLC667.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go replacing the Ethernet module — this is a software password state, not a hardware fault. A locked-out remote password on the FX5-PLC667 is almost always a stale GX Works3 session still retrying with an old password. Also, deleting the remote password parameter would just strip the security function, and we don't need to do that to get back in; you can re-enter the correct password after clearing the lockout.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On this line, the remote password for FX5-PLC667 was set to 'FX5LINE8' by the integrator back in 2021, and it's written down in the panel binder. Before you reset SD10320, always check that connection #3 isn't an active SCADA link from the packaging cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so I confirm it's not SCADA, then clear SD10320. How do I actually get the lockout cleared?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about it being a stale session — to clear the lockout, power-cycle the FX5-PLC667, but only after disconnecting all the Ethernet cables for 30 seconds. Then reconnect and enter FX5LINE8.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good, so no module swap, no wiping the password parameter. Junior, follow that order and let me know when the GX Works3 link is stable again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need your help on Line 1, Machining cell D. The FX5-PLC640 CPU module has the ERR LED blinking red and the Ethernet link to the cell's MES terminal is dead.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: OK, what do the other LEDs say? And did the MES terminal give you anything else?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: POWER is green, RUN is green, ERR blinking red, and the Ethernet port LEDs are completely off. The MES terminal just shows a communication timeout alarm, no error code.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Has this happened more than once today?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Three times since the morning shift started. And nobody replaced any hardware recently, but they did install a new Ethernet switch in the cabinet last Friday during the network upgrade.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That new switch, do you know what speed setting it's on? On the FX5-PLC640 at Machining cell D we need auto-negotiation, not fixed speed. If it was set to 100 Mbps fixed, that alone causes intermittent timeouts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I think the network guys left it on 100 fixed, I can check. Should I just replace the CPU module first since the ERR LED is blinking?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't jump to that. Start with the LEDs like the manual says, then check module mounting and wiring before you touch the CPU.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First thing, reseat the Ethernet cable connector at the CPU port. The vibration from the nearby milling machine loosens it about once a month on this cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And if that doesn't fix it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then put that new switch on auto-negotiation. Before you power cycle the FX5-PLC640, save the current program and device status to the engineering tool. The event history clears on power cycle, so you lose it if you just restart.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Wait, so I shouldn't just restart the MES terminal to clear the timeout?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, that loses the operation and error history. The manual says check the engineering tool event history when module diagnostics don't show the cause.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. By the way, are you on the late shift next week? They moved the schedule around again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah I saw that. I'll be on nights Tuesday through Thursday, so grab me before then if this comes back. Did you eat yet? The canteen closes at one.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, I'll run over after we finish this. Also the spare Ethernet cables for the cabinet should arrive tomorrow, they were delayed.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. One more thing on this cell, we had three similar timeout events back in 2023 and they were all traced to a loose shield ground on the cabinet door, not the PLC or the switch. Check that ground before you blame the hardware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So reseat the connector, fix the switch setting, check the shield ground, and save the program before any restart. That's the order?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. And use the system monitor in the engineering tool to find which module generated the error, then check the event history if it's still unclear.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Thanks, I'll go reseat the cable now and let you know.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Sounds good. And don't forget the milling machine next door keeps shaking that cabinet, so check the connector again if it comes back next month.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. See you at lunch maybe.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: See you. Remember, auto-negotiation on that switch, not fixed 100.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need your help with the MR-JE-AX628 over in cell F. It tripped AL. 8C.1 three times this shift, and it clears on a power cycle, then runs fine for maybe 30 to 90 minutes before it goes again. We also just put a 7.5 kW spindle drive and a welding transformer on that same panel two weeks ago.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you even think about pulling that amplifier, what's the cabinet temperature in F right now? I bet it's climbing since that welder showed up.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, I measured 47 degrees C at 13:00. It used to sit around 38 before the new gear went in. So you're saying heat's the culprit?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Heat's part of it. Cabinet F has to stay below 45 degrees C, so get the spare 120 mm fan in there before you do any more electrical checks. But don't stop there. On Line 7, AL. 8C almost always traces back to the 24 V control bundle running alongside the new welder feeder in cable duct C4.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I shouldn't just swap the servo amplifier? The alarm says internal network module, that's what I figured we'd replace.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap it yet. Re-route or shield the CN4 network cable and re-test for at least four hours before you even consider replacing an MR-JE on Line 7. Back in 2022 we had the same AL. 8C on cell F and it turned out to be a ferrite core on the CN4 cable that fixed it, not a new amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so fan first, then deal with the CN4 routing and the duct C4 bundle. And if it still trips after four hours, then we look at the amplifier.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And don't just shrug it off as a glitch because it clears on power cycle. That intermittent stuff will bite you on a busy day. Sort the cable and the heat first, then re-test.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? MR-JE-AX560 on Line 6 keeps tripping AL.33 overvoltage, like three times a shift now. Always when the dispensing head stops from high speed.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Again? That's the third one this month. Did you check the supply voltage?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, 380 volts AC stable, but the bus peaks at 415 DC right before the alarm. I'm thinking we just swap the amplifier, the built-in resistor is probably shot.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on, don't pull it yet. On this cell, always check the regenerative resistor resistance first. Anything above 50 ohms means the built-in resistor is broken. And before you replace the amp for a built-in resistor fault, measure at the resistor terminals to confirm it's really open.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Oh, by the way, did the spare-parts delivery come in? We're almost out of filters for Line 4.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet, supposed to be Thursday. Anyway, back to this — in 2022 we had the same AL.33 on Line 6 and it turned out to be a loose connector on the built-in resistor, not the resistor itself. So check that connector before you blame the resistor.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. But why now? Nothing changed except we cut the deceleration time constant from 0.5 to 0.2 last week for cycle time.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There you go. If the deceleration time constant is below 0.3 seconds, temporarily set PA02 to 0100 and add an external regenerative option, otherwise you'll keep getting nuisance overvoltage trips from all that regen energy.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need a hand — MR-JE-AX625 on Line 4 palletizing cell C tripped alarm 50.1 at 14:20. It ran 18 minutes straight then faulted, and the HG motor housing read 82°C with the IR gun right after. Ambient's 38°C.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: We bumped to 1,240 cycles today because of the second shift, up from 900 yesterday. No alarm for the first 6 hours, then it repeats every 15–20 minutes of steady running. Junior, what do you want to do first?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I was going to swap the MR-JE-AX625 amplifier, but honestly the repeat timing makes me think it's not the amp. Maybe just reset and run full speed to finish the shift?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't replace the amplifier and don't just reset and run full speed — the repeated 50.1 after 15–20 minutes points to thermal and mechanical loading, not amplifier failure, and running it hot will degrade the motor insulation. On this cell, alarm 50.1 first means check the regenerative resistor airflow before you even touch the motor.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, regen resistor airflow first. What else should I be looking at while it cools?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check the enclosure fan filter on the MR-JE-AX625 too — it was last cleaned on 2024-03-11 and at Dong Nai those clog within 90 days. While you're diagnosing, temporarily drop the palletizing speed override to 70% so the motor can cool.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, 70% override and check the filter. If airflow is fine, then what's actually causing the overload?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The real root cause is usually a dragging brake on the Z-axis HG motor, not the servo amplifier itself. So once airflow is sorted, put your hands on that Z-axis brake.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one at Line 6, Machining cell D. The FX5-PLC227 threw an SLMP CF71H after a three-second timeout on a read from the line controller, around 14:05. Operator retried right away and then it hit C1B3H, channel busy.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's the laptop. The line controller and the maintenance laptop are both on SLMP channel 1 at that cell, so the laptop connection has to be closed before you start production. Somebody was on MELSOFT direct connect earlier, right?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 13:50, yeah, they unplugged it without closing. So that's what's holding the channel? I was about to swap the CPU module, CF71H sounded like a hardware fault to me.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't swap the CPU. When CF71H shows up, wait two seconds and retry once. If it repeats three times, power-cycle the line controller switch, not the PLC. And leave the IP alone, C1B3H just means the channel's busy, so change the channel number or wait for the instruction to finish.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Oh, before I forget, are you on days next week? They moved the shift schedule around again and I can't tell if I'm on B or C.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No idea, check the board by the lunch room. Anyway, if you keep getting repeated CF71H on Line 6, it's usually the unmanaged switch port 4, it negotiates down to 10 Mbps half-duplex after a power dip. And if you ever see C035H with the line controller powered and the link LED off, grab the spare Ethernet cable from cabinet D-12 and swap it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Cabinet D-12, got it. Spare parts delivery is late again too, so good to know that cable's there. I'll close the laptop connection and retry.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Do that, and if port 4 is still linked at 10 half after the dip, bounce that switch port before you chase anything else. Line 4's been flaky too, so keep an eye on it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? MR-JE-AX999 on Line 10, Dispensing cell C keeps dropping out with AL.86.1. Three times in forty minutes this afternoon, and every time I power-cycle it, it comes back.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Three resets already? Careful — don't power-cycle it more than twice in one shift. On this cell the third reset can corrupt the controller's network parameter backup.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Oh. Okay, I'll stop resetting it. So what's your first move? I was about to grab a spare amplifier, AL.86.1 sometimes means the amp itself is failing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold off on the amplifier. Before anything else, pull the controller communication log and check the timestamps — a genuine cable break leaves a gap longer than 500 ms.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right, I can pull that. Anything else that stands out? The connector at the amp was hand-tight when I checked, and the comm setting hasn't been touched.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: When does it fault? First shift startup was clean, right?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, no alarm at startup. Only when the spindle motor ramps up. And the network cable got rerouted last Friday for that new conveyor leg — it now runs alongside the 400 V spindle cable for about 2 m.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. On Line 10, AL.86 faults that only show up during spindle ramp-up have been induced noise from the parallel 400 V cable run nine times out of ten.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Nine out of ten, huh. So I shouldn't re-terminate the cable first? A disconnected cable is the usual culprit for AL.86.1.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not here. You need at least 200 mm separation between the network cable and any 400 V motor cable — or run it in a shielded duct with the shield grounded at both ends.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Say, did you hear the spare-parts truck is late again? We're almost out of the small fuses on aisle two.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Of course it is. Lunch is at eleven-thirty today too, they moved it for the safety meeting. Anyway — fix the routing first, then if it still faults we test a replacement amp.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. And I only replace the servo amplifier if it's not repeatable after replacement testing, confirming the amp's actually bad, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And if you do find the network cable disconnected, turn the servo amplifier off before reconnecting it. Oh — and check ambient temp and noise around the cabinet while you're in there.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on MR-JE-AX185 over at Line 5, Assembly cell D. This morning it threw warning 9B.1 three times in twenty minutes. It only happens during the normal 800 mm/s traverse with the 2.5 kg tool, clears after a power cycle, and won't show up on slow jog. I checked the U/V/W and encoder cables — they're both tight, no recent crash or cable swap.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright, first thing — don't replace the servo amplifier. 9B.1 doesn't mean the output stage is dying. On this cell, a loose shield clamp on the encoder cable at the motor end has caused intermittent 9B.1 twice in the past year. So before you touch any gain parameter, check that encoder cable shield clamp and the connector pins. Connector fretting is the most common site-specific cause here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I was actually thinking of bumping the torque limit to 300% first, since the peak load ratio hit 210% right before the last warning. Is that worth trying?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't increase the torque limit as your first action. The manual lists torque limit as check number four, and 210% peak load doesn't prove torque saturation. Stick with the shield clamp and pins first. If the warning only happens during fast traverse, then reduce the acceleration time constant by 10 ms as a temporary workaround to keep production running while you dig in.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check that clamp and pins. Oh — did you hear the spare parts delivery for Line 3 got pushed to Thursday lunch? Anyway, what about the gain side? The manual mentions PB08 if it's not repeatable.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I heard about the Thursday delivery. On the gain side — like I said about checking the connector first — don't jump to PB08 until you've ruled out the shield clamp and pins. And remember, the position loop gain Pr. PB08 on this machine was tuned down to 28 rad/s during commissioning to avoid resonance with the belt drive. So don't just crank it up without thinking.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. So shield clamp and pins first, then the 10 ms accel workaround if it keeps tripping on fast traverse, and leave PB08 at 28 unless we're sure. I'll go check now.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? MR-JE-AX828 tripped again on overheat, alarm 46.1, twice today — 14:20 and 15:10.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Twice already? Ambient temp near the motor, what'd it read?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 43 degrees both times. And I checked the load ratio, it was 35 percent, well within normal. Motor body was 50 right after the second trip.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Before you two get deep in this — did the spare-parts delivery come in for Line 3? I've been chasing that all morning.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet, they said after lunch. Anyway — when ambient goes over 40 like that, don't touch the motor load first. Check the cooling fan on the cabinet first.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We had this exact false overheat on MR-JE-AX828 about three months back. Turned out the filter on the cabinet's cooling fan was clogged.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So pull the filter and clean it, that's it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Clean it, and if the ambient's actually normal but the alarm still comes back, then you measure the resistance on the encoder thermal sensor. Below 100 ohms means the sensor's faulty.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Speaking of which, you grabbing lunch after this? The canteen's doing that noodle thing again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Maybe after I check the filter. Somebody said we should just swap the motor out, but that seems like overkill.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, don't jump to replacing the motor. The manual puts ambient and overload ahead of the encoder sensor for a reason — check those first.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: And don't just silence it and keep running, either. Overheating cooks the windings and the encoder, then it's a real repair.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll pull the filter now and call you if the alarm comes back.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And Line 7's been making a weird noise, swing by there after if you can.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on Line 4, Palletizing cell B. The MR-JE-AX264 keeps tripping alarm 31, overspeed, on the third cycle. Started right after we bumped the payload from 8 to 12 kilos.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alarm 31 on the vertical axis when it accelerates hard, right? First thing, what's your acceleration time constant set to? On cell B this usually happens after a payload change because somebody left it at 0.1 s instead of our site standard 0.3 s.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'd have to check, but yeah it only happens on the fast vertical accel. Operator says the motor hits high speed for a split second then it faults. Oh, and we did change the electronic gear from 1:1 to 2:1 while tuning the profile.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That gear change matters. Before you even touch Pr. PC08, always verify the electronic gear ratio matches the 4096-pulse encoder and the 10 mm ball screw pitch we use on Line 4. And heads up, that AX264 unit was replaced back in March 2023 after the lightning strike, and its parameters got restored from an old backup that had a lower overspeed detection level.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Huh, so the detection level itself might be wrong. Someone suggested just dropping Pr. PC08 lower to stop the alarm, but that felt off.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't do that, that's masking it. Leave PC08 alone till you've checked the gear ratio and the accel constant. For now we run the temporary workaround we've been using, limit the cell's max speed command to 2500 r/min until the accel profile is retuned. By the way, did the spare parts order for cell A come in? I need those before Friday.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, I'll chase the supplier after lunch. So 2500 r/min cap for now, and I check the gear ratio and the 0.3 s accel constant.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. Last time this happened on cell B it was exactly that, accel constant left at 0.1 s after a payload swap. Fix the constant, verify the gear, then retune. Don't swap the motor, it's almost never the motor.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with the i4L-R547 on Line 8, cell D. It keeps dropping PROFINET with fault 0x0110 about every 12 minutes, but only when the pick cycle goes under 0.45 seconds.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Does it clear on its own?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, comes back in 2 or 3 seconds. Never happens when I jog it slow by hand either.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I checked the settings — IO Connection Cycle Time is 8 ms and the controller data refresh is 4 ms. And a new vision camera went on that same PROFINET segment last week.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the robot controller over this. That fault code looks internal, but with a camera on the segment this is almost always timing and shielding, not the controller itself.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So should I bump the controller data refresh rate up to match the 8 ms IO cycle?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that — that would overload the controller and make the dropouts worse. On the i4L-R547, when a vision camera shares the PROFINET segment, set the IO Connection Cycle Time to at least 12 ms.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, 12 ms minimum. Anything else before I touch the settings?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Before you touch any PROFINET settings, check the XIO connector's 26-pin D-sub shell and make sure it's torqued to 0.4 N·m, so you don't get intermittent shield contact.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Think it could be the connector rather than just the cycle time?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We saw this exact dropout pattern on Line 8 back in 2022. What actually fixed it was re-terminating the XIO connector shield — not replacing the robot controller.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So torque the shell to 0.4 N·m, re-terminate the shield if it looks bad, and set IO cycle to 12 ms. I'll start there.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And like I said about the cycle time, don't chase the fault code into the controller — get the segment timing and the shield right first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, can you come look at i4L-R193 in Assembly cell C? A pallet whacked the fence yesterday and now the base has a 0.3 mm gap at one mounting foot. It's vibrating something awful on high-speed moves and the XSYSTEM cable's rubbing on the fence.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Gap at the foot after an impact? That's never just a loose bolt. A torque check yet?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, one M8 came up at 18 N·m, other three are 28 to 30. Production wants the line back up in 30 minutes and someone said just re-torque the loose one to 30 and run it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that, and don't just swap the one bolt either. After any impact you replace all four M8 mounting bolts rather than re-torquing, because class 10.9 bolts yield once and lose clamp load. Replacing only the loose one leaves the base unevenly clamped and she can still tip over.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: All four, got it. What about the base itself? Anything I should watch for before I pull them?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We had a pallet strike just like this on Line 1 back in 2023 and it cracked the base casting, and we only saw it after removing all the bolts. So before you re-tighten anything, put a 2-ton toe jack under the base and lift it 0.5 mm to unload the bolts, otherwise you'll gall the threads. Then on this i4L-R193 at Da Nang, use a calibrated torque wrench set to 31 N·m and tighten in a diagonal sequence so you don't distort the base.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Toe jack first, then 31 N·m diagonal. And, uh, did you hear if the new spindles for Line 2 came in on the delivery? I'm supposed to grab lunch before the shift meeting.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: They're still on the truck, we'll chase it later. Focus on the jack and the bolts first, then go eat.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we've got a problem on MR-JE-AX250 at Line 6, Assembly cell A. Operator saw AL. 90 on the HMI at 14:20 during startup of a positioning cycle.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alarm history shows AL. 25 happened earlier today at 06:05 after the machine was off overnight. The battery LED is off and the battery was last replaced 26 months ago.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: After clearing AL. 25, the operator jogged the axis and then tried an automatic positioning move without doing a home position return. That's when AL. 90 came up.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing: on this cell we replace the absolute position battery every 24 months no matter what the voltage reads. We had a failure at 27 months once that caused AL. 25 and scrapped a whole batch, so we don't wait.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you swap it, measure the battery voltage under load. If it's below 3.2 volts, replace it and then do a home position return twice to check repeatability within 0.02 mm.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So the battery is due anyway at 26 months, but what about the alarm sequence? The manual says AL. 90 means a positioning move was done without home position setting after an absolute position erase.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And when AL. 25 popped, we should have checked the battery voltage and the battery cable, fixed the issue, and then executed a home position return before any automatic operation.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The operator cleared AL. 25, jogged the axis, and then ran the automatic cycle. That's probably why we got AL. 90, huh?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Clearing the alarm and resuming automatic operation without a home position return is wrong. You must re-establish the absolute position with a home position return after fixing the battery issue.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Should I just replace the battery now, or is there a temporary workaround so we don't lose position again?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: You can temporarily keep the 24 V control power on while swapping the battery, but even then you still have to do a home position return to re-establish the absolute position. It's not a free pass.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: And what about the repeated AL. 25 we've seen on this machine? Is it always the battery?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Usually it's not the battery itself. The root cause of repeated AL. 25 on this machine is a loose battery connector at the amplifier. So check that connector first before you go replacing the amplifier or anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the connector, measure the voltage under load, replace the battery if it's below 3.2 V, and then do two home position returns to verify repeatability within 0.02 mm.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? I'm stuck on the i4L-R241 in Inspection cell E. Operator tried to enable High Power at 14:05 and the Front Panel indicator stayed off, robot won't move.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Did the pendant throw anything?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No specific alarm. But the diagnostic screen shows the safety circuit as 'not ready.' Gate's closed and the light curtain looks clear, so I'm scratching my head.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alright, first thing—the LED on the robot body doesn't tell you anything about High Power status. Don't trust it. Use the Front Panel indicator or whatever's wired to the XFP connector.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, I figured the LED was just cosmetic. Should I bypass the safety circuit real quick just to see if the arm moves?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. Absolutely not. High Power won't come on unless every safety circuit is satisfied, and you don't jumper around that. Ever.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, okay, understood. There was a robot on Line 7 last month with something similar—turned out to be the light curtain needing a reset.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Could be, but on Line 7 the safety relay for the light curtain occasionally sticks after a power dip. Before you go chasing wiring, just tap the relay cover to free it. Nine times out of ten that's it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Tap the cover. Got it. Anything else I should check while I'm in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah—the XFP connector on the R241 is prone to vibration loosening. I check its seating every Monday morning as a habit. Give it a push and see if it clicks in.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Huh, Monday morning. So it's a regular thing?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yep. That cell vibrates more than people think. Anyway—when was the last ACE software update on that cell?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Uh, I think last week? Somebody pushed an update to cell E.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then check the safety timeout function. It gets misconfigured after ACE updates. Verify the 10-second default is still active for cell E.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 10-second default, cell E. Okay. Also, the gate switch reads closed, but could it be lying to me?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Funny you ask—back in 2025 we had a 'not ready' just like this from a faulty gate switch. It showed closed but had high resistance. We swapped it for a sealed type and never saw it again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So that's three things to check. Relay tap, XFP seating, timeout setting, plus the gate switch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's four. But do them in that order, quickest first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: By the way, did you hear the spare-parts delivery got pushed to Thursday? Half our order's stuck at the dock.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw the email. Typical. Are we still on for lunch at eleven-thirty? The canteen's doing that noodle thing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should be fine, unless this robot eats my whole morning. Oh, and Line 4's conveyor's been making that grinding noise again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not my problem today. Focus on cell E. Call me if the relay tap doesn't do it and you're down to wiring.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Heading over now. Thanks.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hey—before you go, remember: tap the relay cover first, then check the XFP seating. Don't start pulling wires until you've done both.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Relay cover tap, then XFP. Got it. Then the 10-second timeout and the gate switch. I'll report back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on FX5-PLC876 at Line 11, Assembly cell F. The HMI threw up alarm 1F00H at 14:20 today during a routine parameter check with GX Works3.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 1F00H, that's a MELSOFT connection comm error. What was connected to it at the time?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Two laptops and the panel PC, all through MELSOFT. Fault cleared after 30 seconds but came back twice more in the same shift.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No recent changes to the PLC program or the Ethernet module parameters. Only thing I can think of is we swapped the Ethernet cable to the PLC a week ago because the connector was bent.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I just replace the FX5-ENET/IP module right away? That cable swap seems suspicious.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the FX5-ENET/IP module yet. The manual and our site history both say 1F00H is almost always about too many or stale MELSOFT connections, not hardware failure.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, then what do you want me to check first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First thing, on Line 11 the panel PC and the engineering laptops tend to leave stale UDP connections open. Power-cycle the panel PC before you do anything else — that clears 1F00H about 80% of the time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Just a power-cycle on the panel PC? Not the PLC?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Just the panel PC. But also check the total number of connections — the manual says for 1F00H you check the total connections and the number of UDP connections.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I was just going to look at the physical cables and skip the UDP count.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. Ignoring the UDP connection count and only checking cables is wrong — the manual explicitly tells you to check UDP connections for 1F00H.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So how many MELSOFT connections are we allowed on this one?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We keep a maximum of three simultaneous MELSOFT connections on FX5-PLC876. A fourth one historically triggers 1F00H within minutes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So with two laptops plus the panel PC, we're right at the edge of three.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. If someone plugs in a fourth, expect 1F00H fast. That's why we cap it at three on this machine.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: What if the alarm only shows up when the panel PC is connected?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then the root cause is usually the panel PC's network driver, not the PLC Ethernet module. That's a known pattern here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if I power-cycle the panel PC and it's still throwing 1F00H with just the laptops, what then?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then count your MELSOFT sessions carefully. Like I said about the three-connection limit, drop anything extra before you start chasing hardware.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And the cable we replaced last week — leave it alone?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Leave it. Like I said about the panel PC and stale UDP connections, that's where 1F00H comes from on this line about 80% of the time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll power-cycle the panel PC now and check the UDP connection count in GX Works3.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. If it comes back after that, check whether it only happens with the panel PC connected — that points at its network driver.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need your help with MR-JE-AX327 on Line 12 in Machining cell C. At 06:12 this morning during shift start, it threw alarm 10.1 and the cell stopped. I measured 185 VAC phase-to-phase at the servo amplifier input terminals, which is below the nominal 200 VAC. This is the second time this week, both during the first start of the morning shift. No other servo amplifiers on Line 12 are showing undervoltage alarms.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alarm 10.1 means undervoltage, usually a voltage drop on the supply side. Don't jump to replacing the servo amplifier yet. On Line 12, the first thing to check is the main transformer tap setting — it was left on the 220V tap after last year's plant voltage upgrade. That's likely why you're seeing 185 VAC instead of 200.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll check the tap. But why does it only happen at shift start and not later in the day?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the alarm appears only at shift start, inspect contactor K12 for pitted contacts before you even think about replacing the servo amplifier. Morning start-up draws a big inrush, and pitted contacts will cause a voltage sag right then. Also, measure the 24V control power supply ripple with an oscilloscope — a ripple above 200 mV has preceded alarm 10.1 on this cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so check K12 and scope the 24V ripple. What else should I look at after an undervoltage alarm on this unit?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: After any undervoltage alarm on MR-JE-AX327, always verify the regenerative resistor wiring is tight. A loose connection there can cause repeated nuisance trips. So once you've sorted the tap, K12, and the ripple, put a wrench on those regen resistor terminals.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. One of the other guys said we should just replace the MR-JE servo amplifier because alarm 10.1 means the internal power circuit has failed. Is that right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, that's a waste of time and money. Alarm 10.1 is an undervoltage condition caused by a voltage drop in the power supply — it's not telling you the internal power circuit failed. You can reset it via alarm reset or power cycling, but that doesn't fix the root cause.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Another operator said just reset the alarm and keep production running since it clears on its own after a few minutes. Should we do that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. Resetting without checking the incoming power just lets it come back. You need to fix the supply issue — start with the transformer tap, then K12, then the 24V ripple, and finally the regen resistor wiring.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll go check the transformer tap first and let you know what I find. Thanks for the clear order of checks.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Remember, if the tap was left on 220V after the upgrade, that alone explains the 185 VAC. Set it correctly, then inspect K12 for pitting, scope the 24V ripple for anything above 200 mV, and torque the regenerative resistor connections. That sequence will kill this nuisance trip.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need your help. FX5-PLC379 at Binh Duong, Line 8, pick-and-place cell E — the inverter comm link threw error code 7602H three times in 20 minutes today, all around 14:22.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 7602H? That's a timeout where the sending from the inverter got aborted midway. What was the machine doing when it tripped?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Every time it happened during a high-speed positioning move of the pick-and-place arm. The inverter is a Mitsubishi FR-A800 series.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Also, the comm cable runs right near a servo drive that was recently added on Line 8. I'm thinking we should just swap the inverter out.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the inverter — that's likely unnecessary. The manual defines 7602H as sending aborted midway, so this is a communication timeout, not an inverter fault.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so what should I check first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That new servo drive on Line 8 emits high-frequency noise that couples into the inverter communication cable if the cable shield is grounded only at the PLC end.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: For FX5-PLC379, always check that the inverter communication cable shield is grounded at both the PLC and inverter ends, and that the cable is routed at least 30 cm away from servo drive power cables.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Ground both ends and keep 30 cm separation. Should I also check the timeout setting?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The PLC program uses a 100 ms timeout for inverter communication, right? If 7602H only occurs during high-speed moves, temporarily increase the communication timeout to 200 ms in the PLC parameters to confirm the issue is timing-related, not a hardware fault.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yes, 100 ms and baud rate is 19200 bps. So bump it to 200 ms just to test?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly — just to confirm it's timing-related. If the error stops at 200 ms, that points to noise or timing, not a dead inverter.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And what if it keeps happening even at 200 ms?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then go back to the shielding. Like I said about grounding the shield at both ends and keeping 30 cm from the servo power cables — that's where the noise is getting in.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I check anything else on the cable itself?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Back in 2024, a similar 7602H error on Line 8 was resolved by adding a ferrite core on the communication cable near the inverter, not by replacing the inverter.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: A ferrite core near the inverter. Okay, I can grab one from the spares cabinet.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Do that after you verify the shield grounding. Ferrite helps, but if the shield is only grounded at the PLC end, the noise still couples in.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. What about the retries — should I just restart the PLC and ignore the error for now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't ignore it and just restart the PLC. If you don't check the cable shielding, you'll get repeated 7602H errors, and if retries exceed the allowable number you could trip an inverter alarm stop.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right. So my order is: check shield grounding at both ends, check the 30 cm routing, then test the 200 ms timeout, then add the ferrite core if needed.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the right order. And remember, 7608H is a different one — that's a sending timeout when sending to the inverter isn't completed in the specified time. 7602H is the inverter aborting midway.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Good to know. I'll start with the shield grounding now and report back.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Sounds good. If the 200 ms test clears it, put the timeout back to 100 ms after you fix the shielding — don't leave it at 200 ms permanently.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we got a problem with FX5-PLC583 on Line 3. Operator tried FTP file transfer to the server at 10:15 and it timed out after 30 seconds, error 0x8005.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: What was running on the PLC at that time? Any backup/restore or programming connections?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, the backup/restore was running from 10:00 to 10:20 for routine maintenance. And MELSOFT connection was active on the network.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's your problem right there. The FTP instruction can't execute while backup/restore is running, and MELSOFT on UDP/IP at the same time will cause a timeout.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I swap the Ethernet cable or try a different switch port? Timeout usually means physical layer, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't touch the cable. On Line 3, MELSOFT connection uses UDP/IP, so switch to TCP/IP for programming during FTP transfers to avoid timeouts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. And what about restarting the PLC to clear the error?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't power cycle it. If transfer fails with timeout, wait for backup/restore to finish, then retry after 2 minutes. Restarting could interrupt the backup and corrupt data.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Anything I should check before we try again next time?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before any FTP transfer on FX5-PLC583, always check the CPU module's backup/restore status via the engineering tool's diagnostic buffer.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Is this a common thing here, or just bad luck today?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Historically, 80% of FTP transfer failures at Binh Duong plant were due to concurrent backup/restore or MELSOFT UDP traffic.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll check the diagnostic buffer and switch MELSOFT to TCP before we retry after the backup finishes.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. That's the standard procedure here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, i4L-R483 on Line 6 is oscillating bad during fast packaging. At 80% override I'm seeing visible vibration and 0.8 mm peak-to-peak on the Z-axis dial indicator. No alarm, but cell E keeps rejecting parts when the quill wobbles on downward placement.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: What changed on that robot recently? Anything swapped on the base?

turns.speaker: junior_01
