turns.text: Yeah, over the weekend someone replaced the original 20 mm steel base plate with a 12 mm aluminum one to save weight. I checked floor flatness too, 0.5 mm over 1 m, looks fine to me.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There's your problem. On i4L-R483, any mounting plate thinner than 18 mm or made of aluminum instead of steel has always produced Z-axis oscillation at speeds above 60%. Floor flatness isn't the issue here. But before you touch the robot, grab a torque wrench and check the four base bolts at 85 Nm, because loose bolts mimic a stiffness problem.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check the bolts. So what do we do about the plate itself?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: I keep a spare 20 mm steel plate with 25 μm surface finish in the Line 6 crib specifically for packaging cell E. Go get it. And here's a quick diagnostic first, command a 100 mm vertical move at 10% speed and feel for quill wobble by hand. If you feel wobble, the plate is too flexible.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Some guys were saying we should just replace the Z-axis quill or drop to 20% speed and keep running. That's not right, is it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. Don't swap the quill, the vibration isn't internal damage, it's the plate. And running slow just hides it, the oscillation won't get better with that aluminum plate in there. Put the 20 mm steel back on and torque those bolts to 85 Nm.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, i4L-R341 on Line 10 is dropping outputs 65 to 72 about twice a shift, always when the arm swings to the far right near the cable tray. I checked the IO Blox 1 switches myself and they're both OFF, so that part looks right.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Both OFF, yeah, that's the 65 to 72 block. Before you swap the whole IO Blox unit, did anyone put a meter on the cable shield? Last time this happened here the shield continuity was sitting above 2 ohms and that was enough to explain random dropouts on those exact outputs.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, I didn't check the shield. I was thinking maybe just replace the IO Blox 1 unit to be safe. Or could I move the outputs to 1 through 8 on XIO instead?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: XIO's a separate connector, your field wiring's already landed on IO Blox 1, so that's a bigger job than you want. I know the manual says the switches are fine, and they are. The wear point here is the cable itself.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That 3 meter IO Blox cable, part 04677-030, we put in last month? At Da Nang those things often go bad after about 6 months, because the robot's cable carrier bends them past a 50 mm radius. If you need production running tonight, flip IO Blox 1 to ON, OFF and rewire the outputs to 73 to 80 to bypass the damaged cable.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so shield check first, then the temporary rewire. By the way, are you on second shift next week? They're moving the spare-parts delivery to Thursday.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I'm on seconds. Let's get the meter on that shield before anything else, then if it's over 2 ohms we'll do the 73 to 80 bypass and order a fresh 04677-030.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand. i4L-R457 on Line 2, cell F, dropped out of Automatic into Manual mode twice on the night shift. Both times it stopped the cycle, first at step 40, then again at step 12.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Twice in one shift, that's not random. What did the front panel XFP mode selector show when it happened?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That's the weird part. The XFP switch still physically reads Automatic. Nobody touched the panel. Both dropouts were within 20 minutes of each other, right after a pallet change.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: After a re-pin, intermittent Manual-mode dropouts on i4L-R457 are almost always a loose crimp on pin 3 or pin 11 of the XFP connector. Did anything get re-terminated on that harness recently?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, the maintenance log shows the XFP connector was re-pinned last week during a cable repair.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then check those crimps before swapping the mode switch. The Hai Phong Line 2 XFP connector pins 3 and 11 were re-terminated last week, so that's your prime suspect.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Can we just swap the XFP mode selector? That's usually the fastest fix.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The switch is rarely the cause when the dropouts started right after a connector re-pin. Don't waste time on it yet.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: What about shorting pins 3 and 11 together to force Automatic, just until the end of shift?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Never tape or bypass the mode selector to keep Automatic. An open circuit on channel 1 or 2 is what selects Manual, so a bypass is also a safety risk.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so how do I actually confirm it's the crimp?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Wiggle-test the XFP harness at the controller end while watching the mode LEDs. A flicker on channel 1 points to the re-pinned wire.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Wiggle at the controller end, watch the LEDs, and if channel 1 flickers I re-crimp pins 3 and 11. No bypassing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. Fix the crimp properly and you'll stop those dropouts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on MR-JE-AX128 in packaging cell B. It tripped AL.98.1 right after a point-table move to 1250 mm, and it clears on power cycle but comes back every time we command that same step.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: What changed on Line 8 this morning before it started?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: They re-homed the conveyor earlier, and the operator said the forward stroke limit switch was replaced yesterday. No crash or obstruction, and it jogs fine at low speed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should we just swap the servo amplifier? I heard AL.98.1 means internal hardware failure.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the amplifier — AL.98.1 is a software-limit trip, not a hardware fault. Check Pr.PT15 through PT18 against the mechanical hard-limit first; back in 2023 we had three AL.98.1 trips on Line 8 from a 2 mm mismatch.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, and what about just disabling the software-limit function to clear it? The axis moves freely in JOG.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't disable the soft limits — that's how you crash it. After any re-homing on packaging cell B, verify point-table target 1250 mm is inside the software-limit window before running automatic mode.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And the limit switch they replaced yesterday — could that be related?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Very likely. That forward stroke limit switch replacement probably shifted the effective soft-limit origin by 1.5 mm, so re-teach the home position.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: If PT15 to PT18 look correct, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Like I said about checking PT15–PT18 first — if those are correct, temporarily drop JOG speed to 50 mm/s and step through the point table to isolate the offending step.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll check the parameters against the hard-limit, then re-teach home if needed, and step through at 50 mm/s if it's still tripping.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need a hand. MR-JE-AX154 on cell D threw AL. E3.4 at startup this morning, 06:40. Three short indexing moves in the same direction and it tripped.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: E3.4. Okay. Was the operator running point-table positioning mode?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, point-table mode, 0.75 second index cycle. And the log shows the amp already did two home position renewals in the previous 8 minutes.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Did we change anything on the motor or encoder cable lately? I don't want us pulling hardware if the log is clean.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Log's clean, no recent change to the servo motor, encoder cable, or the amplifier. Only thing is the line speed went up 12% last week.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. Last time this happened on Line 11, the speed bump was the culprit. Restore the previous 0.85 second index cycle before you replace anything, the 12% increase pushed the indexer above the E3.4 threshold.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I don't swap the motor? I already tried cycling power and E3.4 wouldn't clear.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the motor yet. E3.4 is excessive home position renewals in 10 minutes, not encoder failure. And power cycling alone won't help if you don't review CMX/CDV and the index cycle, it'll just come back next run.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First thing on Line 11, before touching any mechanical parts, verify Pr. PA06 CMX is 2000 and Pr. PA07 CDV is 1000. Check those two numbers first.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: If we have to keep CMX above 2000 for the resolution, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then cap the command speed at 3276.7 minus CMX times 0.1 r/min, and confirm it with a one-hour dry run. CMX has to be 15900 or less after reducing CMX/CDV anyway.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. And once I fix the cycle and the parameters, can I just do a home return right away?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. After any E3.4 correction, do the home position return again only after a full 10-minute power-off, that clears the EEP-ROM write counter.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good. Junior, log the parameter check and the cycle change, then dry run it before we restart the line.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on i4L-R329 in cell F. It's wall-mounted, and about twice a shift it makes a mechanical thud when the arm retracts toward the wall. It always happens after a product change that moves the pick position 30 mm closer to the wall.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that thud is the tool flange hitting the wall, not a servo fault. Before you even think about swapping a motor, check the flange for a scuff mark.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: There is a fresh scuff on the flange. But no collision alarm. I measured the wall angle at 87°, thought it was close enough to 90°.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That wall was shimmed back in 2019 and it's actually 88°. So I always add 2 mm to the calculated wall clearance on Line 7.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the manual just says wall-mounted robots need to be on a 90° vertical surface and to prevent collisions. I figured the angle was fine and the scuff was cosmetic.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't ignore it. On i4L-R329 I set a soft-limit exclusion zone 50 mm from the wall in the controller, because the standard retract path ignores wall proximity.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so should I just re-teach the pick position 30 mm away from the wall?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That alone won't fix it. Without that controller exclusion zone, the retract move can still collide even if you move the pick point.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. What's your check after a product change?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: After any product change, I jog the robot to the closest pick point at 5% speed and verify at least 25 mm gap to the wall.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And that 50 mm exclusion zone stays in the controller permanently?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, leave it in. It's your safety net when the retract path doesn't account for the wall.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll add the exclusion zone, recheck the gap at 5% speed, and keep an eye on the flange scuff.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember that 2 mm extra for the 88° wall on Line 7.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? The MR-JE-AX242 on Line 9, Inspection cell E is dead — no RS-422 comms with the controller at all.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Dead how? What's the controller showing?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Communication timeout after about 3 seconds every time it tries to link up. And the weird thing is we swapped the comm cable last week because it was flaky, but it's still doing it.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Before you two dive in — did the spare-parts delivery for Line 7 come in? I need to sign for it before lunch.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, it's by the tool crib. Anyway, I checked the station number on the amp, it's set to 1 and the master expects 1, so that's not it. I was about to just pull the amplifier and swap it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't swap the amp yet. On this cell the RS-422 cable routing passes right near a 7.5 kW motor drive, so first thing — check for induced noise by re-routing the cable away from the power lines.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I can move it. But honestly the cable's brand new, would noise really kill a fresh cable?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Happens all the time. And listen — historically, 80% of the RS-422 comm failures on Line 9 were loose terminal screws on the CN3 connector, not parameter errors. Go check those screws before anything else.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: I'm grabbing lunch at 12, you want me to bring you anything back?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Nah, I'm good. So CN3 screws first, then re-route. If it's still flaky after that, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If you need to keep the line running while you sort it, temporary workaround is to drop the baud rate to 9600 bps instead of 19200 — that tolerates longer cable runs until you do the permanent fix.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And if the re-route and the screws don't do it, is there anything else that bites us on these?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The root cause is often that the shield of the comm cable isn't grounded at both ends — that gives you common-mode noise. Check both ends of the shield while you're in there.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Perfect, I'll hit CN3, re-route away from the drive, and check the shield grounds. Thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on pick-and-place cell D, Line 7 — the arm just crawls at a constant slow speed no matter what speed the program commands. The servo amp MR-JE-AX201 shows no alarm, motor runs, but it's like 30% speed. Any idea?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch any parameters, check VC first. On this cell, the analog override potentiometer gets bumped during panel cleaning all the time — that's the usual culprit.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, a maintenance tech did adjust the analog override pot on the control panel just before this started. So I should just turn it back?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. But first wiggle-test the connector on the VC input terminal. We had a past incident on Line 7 where a loose connector there caused intermittent speed drop. Just give the wires a gentle wiggle while watching the speed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll do that. Oh, by the way, did you hear about the spare-parts delivery? The new servo motors are delayed again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I heard. Don't even think about replacing the servo amp yet — the manual says check VC and override settings first. A new amp won't fix a pot that's turned down.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I read the override value in MR Configurator2 — it's sitting at 30%. That matches the slow speed.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the override is set via network, verify the PLC override register matches the HMI display. A 10% mismatch is common because of scaling differences.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll check the PLC register. Also, should I just leave the pot at whatever it is now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. When you adjust the override, always return the potentiometer to the marked 100% position and lock it with the set screw. That way it won't drift again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Man, I'm starving — are we still on for lunch after this?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, after you finish. I heard the canteen has that chicken rice today. But first get that pot locked at 100%.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll wiggle the VC connector, check the PLC register versus HMI, then set the pot to 100% and lock it. Thanks!

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And next time you clean that panel, be careful around the override pot — it's sensitive.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Morning shift, 09:17 on 2026-01-12, pick-and-place cell A stopped mid-cycle. HMI shows inverter comm fault on channel 2. SM0 is ON and SD8067 reads H0002. It tripped three times in the last two hours, always right after we command the inverter to 45 Hz.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing: on this cell, H0002 inverter communication errors are almost always a loose shielded cable connector at the inverter end, not the PLC itself. So before you even think about swapping cards, go check that connector.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I just replace the PLC communication module to be safe? I have one in the spares cabinet.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, hold off on that. The manual says the operation error flag turns ON when the inverter communication instruction fails, and the hex code in SD8067 is what tells you it's that instruction. That points at the inverter side, not the PLC module.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I saw the cable looked fine at the PLC end. What else should I check while I'm in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Make sure the cable shield is grounded only at the PLC side. If it's grounded at both ends, you get intermittent communication faults just like this.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: How long do you need? The line's been down fifteen minutes already.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Give us ten. Junior, while you're at the inverter, check communication parameter 549, the station number. On this machine it should be set to 2, and it rarely needs changing, but confirm it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Parameter 549 is 2, and I reseated the connector at the inverter end. The shield drain wire was also tied to ground at the inverter, so I lifted that. Should I just reset the alarm from the HMI now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't use the HMI soft reset. Cycle power to the inverter after clearing the fault instead. A soft reset from the HMI often leaves the communication port locked.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, power-cycled the inverter. SM0 is OFF now and SD8067 cleared. I'll watch it through the next few cycles at 45 Hz.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. If it trips again, recheck that connector and the shield grounding before anything else. Those two cause most of the H0002 faults we see on FX5-PLC482.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Sounds like we're back up. Log the fix and keep an eye on it for the rest of the shift.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with the i4L-R127 on Line 11, Palletizing cell B. After a tool flange replacement last Monday, the robot places pallets with a consistent 2.8 mm offset in X.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Offset right after the swap, no alarms, motion smooth? That points to the flange seating, not the motion controller.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, no alarm codes at all. The tech said he used a standard L-key and tightened the setscrew very firmly by feel because the torque wrench wasn't available.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There's your problem. On i4L-R127, a 1.1 N-m setscrew torque error of more than 0.3 N-m typically produces a 2–3 mm X-offset at the palletizing tool center point.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the over-tightening pushed the flange off-center. Should we just replace the whole tool flange right away?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the whole tool flange yet—the manual states the setscrew torque is 1.1 N-m, and an over-tightened setscrew can be backed off and retorqued correctly.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, what about just re-running the robot calibration without touching the setscrew torque? Would that fix the offset?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that—re-running calibration without first correcting the setscrew torque will not fix the offset because the flange will still be off-center.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So first we need to get the torque right. Where's the torque wrench for this?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The plant's torque wrench for the tool flange setscrew is kept in the Line 11 maintenance cabinet, drawer 3, because the cell's own kit was lost in 2022.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Drawer 3, okay. Before I loosen anything, is there anything I should mark?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Before loosening any socket-head screws, mark the old tool flange orientation on the quill with a paint pen to preserve the calibrated position.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Paint pen on the quill, got it. Do we know if this has happened before on this unit?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The 2021 incident on i4L-R127 was traced to a stretched setscrew from over-tightening; the flange had to be replaced and the cell recalibrated.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if we're lucky, this setscrew isn't stretched and we can just back it off and retorque to 1.1 N-m with Loctite 243?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Clean the threads, apply Loctite 243 or equivalent, and torque to 1.1 N-m. And like I said about marking the orientation—that's what keeps you from losing the calibrated position.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And after retorquing, we should check the offset again before considering recalibration?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. If the flange goes back in the same position and the setscrew is at 1.1 N-m, the offset should clear. If it doesn't, then we look at the setscrew condition or recalibration.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll grab the wrench from drawer 3 and mark the quill first. Thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with MR-JE-AX868 at Dispensing cell E, Line 10. It tripped alarm 90 during a home position return after a tool change.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Alarm 90 means the home position return didn't complete normally. What did the operator see?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: They said it didn't decelerate to creep speed. The axis stopped abruptly about 5 mm past the normal home position.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That sounds like detail 90.2, the return speed never dropped to creep speed. Did anything change on the machine recently?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, the proximity dog was adjusted on 2026-05-10, moved 2 mm toward home to reduce cycle time.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There's your first suspect. On this cell, the proximity dog bracket bolts loosen after about 5000 cycles, letting the dog shift 1 to 2 mm and trigger alarm 90.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the dog moved on its own? Should I just replace the MR-JE-AX868 amplifier to rule it out?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the amplifier yet. The root cause is usually mechanical dog slippage, not a servo amplifier fault, so you verify the dog before touching the MR-JE-AX868.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. So what's the first thing I check?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Always check the dog bracket for looseness first. A 1 mm shift can change the dog-off point enough to skip creep speed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And the alarm only happens approaching home from the positive direction, three times in a row. From negative it's fine.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That fits a shifted dog. The dog turns off before the axis decelerates to creep speed, so the return never completes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The manual says to review dog position or home position return speed, creep speed, and travel distance after proximity dog. Should I just bump the return speed parameter?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, dog position is the first check for detail 90.2. Don't adjust the return speed parameter before you've checked the dog.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. If the dog position looks correct, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If the dog position is correct, temporarily increase the travel distance after proximity dog parameter by 10% to confirm the deceleration issue.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So that's just a test, not a permanent fix?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, it's only to confirm. If it clears, the problem is the dog geometry or timing, not the amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll check the bracket bolts and torque them first, then re-run home from positive.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. If the bolts were loose, that's your root cause. Retighten and verify the dog-off point before you change any parameters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. And if the dog is tight and in position, I'll try the 10% travel distance increase.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Only after the dog is verified do you consider anything on the MR-JE-AX868 itself.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got a problem on the i4L-R561 in cell D. After the E-stop got hit three times this morning and we reset it, the High Power button just does nothing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The High Power lamp stays dark, but Control Power is lit like normal. One of the guys already pulled the XFP jumper plug and left the connector empty while he was probing pins 6 and 14.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing — was the jumper plug put back in? On line 6 that jumper plug 10053-000 has to be fully seated during normal production.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, it's still out. He left it empty.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's your problem right there. Leaving that plug out disables the E-stop chain and locks out High Power. So put it back in, fully seated, before you do anything else.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. But he was saying maybe we should just jumper pins 6 and 14 to force it on and see if the panel is dead.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. Bypassing the High Power button is prohibited, it violates IEC 60204-1. Pins 6 and 14 are the High Power ON/OFF input, they're meant for a momentary push-button that only enables when all the safety circuits are satisfied.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so no jumpering. What about replacing the whole XFP front panel? He thinks the panel's gone bad.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's not the first fix. A dim or dark lamp like that with Control Power lit usually means the lamp load is below 10 mA and it needs a parallel resistor.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: A resistor across the lamp? What value?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 470-ohm, 2-watt, across the High Power lamp terminals. That's fixed this dim-lamp symptom on the i4L-R561 twice since 2022.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, so plug back in, resistor across the lamp. Before I go poking at pins 6 and 14 though, is there a check I should do first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes — always verify the E-stop channels are closed at the XFP connector first. Check channels 1 and 9, then 2 and 10.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Channels 1 and 9 first, then 2 and 10. And that's at the XFP connector itself?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, at the XFP connector, before you touch pins 6 and 14. If those channels aren't closed, High Power will never enable no matter what you do with the button.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so order is: seat the jumper plug, add the 470-ohm resistor, then verify channels 1 and 9 and 2 and 10 are closed.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And leave the XFP jumper plug in during normal production — don't leave it out like your technician did.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So the panel assembly is probably fine, it's just the lamp load and the missing jumper.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's usually it. The dim lamp and the enable failure are a lamp load and jumper-plug issue, not a panel failure. Don't order a new panel.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Great, I'll seat the plug, fit the resistor, check the channels, and try the button again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Sounds good. Call me if High Power still won't come up after that.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with FX5-PLC954 on Line 11, Machining cell A. The operator says the simple CPU communication to our new third-party MODBUS/TCP flow meter just stopped working at 09:15 this morning.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, what's SD10412 showing right now?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: CFB4H. And the Simple CPU communication error response code in SD10413 is 0000H. I don't get it, that code isn't even in the manual's common error table, so I was thinking maybe we swap out the CPU module.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on, don't touch the CPU. Did this start right after the device replacement?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, it's been faulting consistently since we swapped the flow meter last week. Before that it ran eight months with no errors. The device manual mentions ASCII mode, but our project is set up for binary.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. On the FX5-PLC954, the first thing you always check is the third-party device's response format setting, binary versus ASCII. A mismatch gives you exactly CFB4H with a non-error-code response value like your 0000H.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So it's just a wrong setting on the new meter?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Probably. We had the same thing in 2022, a CFB4H on Line 11. Turned out a MODBUS/TCP gateway had defaulted to ASCII after a firmware update.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I should go set the flow meter back to binary?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you change anything, open GX Works3 and monitor SD10412 and SD10413 together. If SD10413 reads 0000H, that tells you the device is sending an invalid response, not a communication timeout.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right, SD10413 is 0000H. So the meter is answering, just with garbage from our point of view.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. An abnormal response message, like an ASCII reply while you're communicating in binary, triggers CFB4H. And that's why the response code holds a non-error-code value instead of a real error number.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Do you want us to power-cycle the PLC to clear it first?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. Never power-cycle the FX5-PLC954 before you've captured a Wireshark trace on the engineering port. The error response code can clear on a restart, and then you've lost your evidence.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so Wireshark first, then fix the format setting. I was also going to reset all the simple CPU communication settings to default, is that a good idea?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. Defaulting everything would wipe the working binary format configuration we've had in there for months, and you'd likely just repeat the fault.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So capture on the engineering port, confirm SD10413 stays 0000H, then set the meter's response format to binary.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. Always verify the third-party device's response format setting on the FX5-PLC954 first, because that mismatch is the classic cause of CFB4H with a non-error-code value.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good, let's get the trace and get Line 11 back up.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And watch SD10412 and SD10413 together in GX Works3 while you test. SD10413 at 0000H means invalid response, so don't go chasing timeouts or the CPU.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a weird one on FX5-PLC139 in cell C — the read/write cycles to the line controller sometimes go past 40 ms and that's giving us 200 ms delays on pick-and-place moves.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Forty ms? And it started after you added those settings last week, right?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yep, 16 new simple CPU communication settings, all pointing at the same built-in Ethernet destination. No retry errors logged, it's just intermittent and worse when we're running fast.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First thing — don't go swapping the Ethernet cable or the switch. That delay looks like hardware but it isn't.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I was honestly about to grab a spare cable from stores, but okay. What about bumping up the scan time on the PLC to speed communication up?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, that won't help either — the manual says the execution interval depends on the number of settings, the number of communication points, and the scan time, and many settings to the same destination can stretch it up to about eight times.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Eight times? So that's why it got worse when we piled on all 16.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. On line 5 we cap simple CPU communication settings per destination at 8 to keep the interval below 25 ms.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So we're double the limit. Can we just cut some of them out?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If you need more than 8, split them across two different destination IP addresses on the same network. That keeps each destination under the cap.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Also, SD10350 gets toggled every 100 ms by the sequence program, and I've noticed SD10349 is sometimes off when the request goes out.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Always verify SD10349 is on before toggling SD10350, and put a 10 ms delay after Ready to avoid missed requests.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so check Ready first, then wait 10 ms, then toggle.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And this has happened before — last year a similar slowdown was caused by 32 settings to one destination, and reducing to 8 restored 15 ms cycles.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That's reassuring. I'll rework the settings this afternoon.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: By the way, did the spare-parts delivery for the other cell come in? The gripper seals were supposed to arrive Monday.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, still sitting on the loading dock I think. Also, are you on early shift tomorrow or the late one? I need to know who to hand off to.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Late shift, I'll be in around two. Are we still doing lunch at the canteen or the noodle place across the road?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Canteen probably — the noodle place got crowded last week. Anyway, back to FX5-PLC139, should I split the 16 into two groups of 8?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, two groups of 8, two different destination IPs on the same network. That keeps you under the cap per destination.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And the Ready check — I'll add the 10 ms delay after SD10349 goes on, then toggle SD10350.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Perfect. That should bring the cycles back down under 25 ms like we keep them on line 5.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Morning. MR-JE-AX505 on Line 10 tripped alarm 50.1 three times already this shift.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Three times? What's it doing when it trips?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: About 12 minutes into continuous running, cell at 80% speed. Load ratio on the monitor shows 135% right when it alarms.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And that power cable got swapped last week, right? I saw the work order.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, replaced due to wear. So my first thought was maybe the new cable's bad or the amp itself is going.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't jump to the amp. On Line 10, a 135% effective load ratio usually means the mechanical guide rails need lubrication, not a motor replacement.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Guide rails? Hm. So the servo's just working harder than it should.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Historical data shows 80% of alarm 50.1 cases on this cell got solved by re-lubricating the linear guides every 500 hours.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, that's an easy one to try first. Should I pull the encoder cable too while I'm in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you even touch the encoder cable, verify the U/V/W wiring torque is 1.5 N·m. Loose connections mimic overload.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 1.5 N·m, got it. I'll grab the torque wrench.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Also, the overload warning level on this drive is set to 120% instead of the factory default 110%. So it's extra sensitive.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: That explains why it's so twitchy. Were we supposed to change that back?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: It's intentional for this cell, leave it. Oh, did the spare-parts delivery come in? I ordered guide lube cartridges.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, truck's supposed to be here after lunch I think.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Fine. Anyway, some guys would just swap the servo amplifier right away. That's wrong, the manual sequence is power cable, then wiring, then brake release, then load ratio.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I check the cable first, then torque the U/V/W. And the brake release too.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And don't let anyone talk you into blaming the encoder and pulling the motor. Encoder checks only come after you've confirmed the effective load ratio is low.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. I'll start with the lube and the torque check.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Hey, you going to the shift-change meeting at two? They're moving the schedule around.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Probably, unless the cell keeps tripping. Cell B was making a weird noise earlier too.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Cell B's a different beast, don't mix them up. Focus on A.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. Lubricate the guides, torque the U/V/W to 1.5, check the brake, then watch the load ratio.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. If the ratio drops after lube, you know it was the rails.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Thanks. I'll report back before lunch break.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we got a problem with the FX5-PLC393 on line 2. The Ethernet module was replaced this morning after a power surge, and now the SCADA system keeps timing out every 5 to 10 minutes.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, what's the ERR LED doing on the new module?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It's blinking red. I checked GX Works3 and the error log shows C0F0 — communication data code mismatch.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you do anything else, check the error code in GX Works3 Ethernet diagnostics to confirm the fault is not a setting mismatch. That C0F0 already points to a data code problem.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So it's not a hardware failure? I was thinking maybe we should just replace the new Ethernet module again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace it again — that C0F0 is a data code mismatch, not a dead module. The manual says a mismatch in the communication data code setting prevents proper command decoding. We need to change the setting.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: What setting exactly? The old module worked fine before the surge.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The barcode scanner on line 2 is configured for ASCII data code, but the module's default is binary. So in GX Works3, set the module to ASCII.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll change that. Should I also reboot the scanner and the SCADA PC?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, after replacing the FX5-PLC393 Ethernet module, always power-cycle the barcode scanner and the SCADA PC to clear stale ARP entries. The scanner still has the old MAC address in its destination table.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll do that now. By the way, did you hear about the shift schedule change next week?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, they moved us to the early shift. Anyway, while you're at it, verify the ground wire is tight on the packaging cell F panel.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Ground wire? Why does that matter for Ethernet communication?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: A missing ground on that panel caused intermittent communication drops twice in 2023. If the module's ground terminal isn't grounded, noise can close the communication line and block communication.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll check the ground connection. Also, the spare-parts delivery for the other line is supposed to arrive this afternoon.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember, like I said about checking the error code first — always do that before replacing any Ethernet hardware. That way you know if it's a setting mismatch or a real fault.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So after I change the data code to ASCII, power-cycle the scanner and SCADA PC, and check the ground, we should be good?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That should clear it. If the timeouts continue, then we dig deeper. But nine times out of ten, it's those three things.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll get on it. Oh, did you grab lunch yet? The canteen closes at 1.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. I'll go after we finish this. Let me know once you've cycled the power on those devices.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. I'll start with the GX Works3 setting change first.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Perfect. And don't forget the ground wire — that one bit us before.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, something's off with i4L-R962 at Binh Duong, Line 8. After they upgraded the controller firmware to 2.6, the TIO outputs stopped responding. Toggling V+ signal 17 does nothing now, but it worked fine before.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I've seen this before. First thing, before you touch any logic — pull up the teach pendant and verify the controller firmware version. If it doesn't match what you think it is, that mismatch causes exactly this kind of silent output loss.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I checked, it's 2.6. So should we just swap out the TIO board? I figured maybe the output card crapped out during the upgrade.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go replacing the TIO board — the hardware is likely fine. The manual says firmware 2.6 remapped the signal numbers, so this is a mapping issue, not a dead card.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Remapped how? The TIO switch is still set to position 17–20, like the old wiring diagram shows.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the trap. On Binh Duong Line 8, any firmware change to 2.6 means you have to rewrite all the TIO output references in the V+ programs from 17–20 over to 33–36.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the physical wiring is still fine, just the numbers in the program are stale?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. The ejector solenoid is wired to TIO output 17 on that old terminal strip. After 2.6, you use V+ signal 33 for that same physical terminal. Same wire, new number.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Could we just move the ejector over to XIO output 1–8 instead? Might be simpler than rewriting everything.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that — XIO is a different connector per the manual, and you'd have to reroute the existing TIO wiring. Just fix the signal references, that's the clean fix.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So I go into the V+ program and change every TIO output reference from 17–20 to 33–36.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly, and do it for all of them, not just the ejector. Miss one and you'll be chasing ghosts later.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: By the way, did you hear about the shift schedule change next week? They're moving us to the early slot.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw that. Doesn't bother me much, I prefer early anyway. Lunch crowd is better too.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: True. Also the spare-parts delivery for Line 5 got delayed again, they said Thursday now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Of course it did. Anyway, back to this — like I said about verifying the firmware first, that check saves you from tearing into hardware you don't need to touch.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So firmware check first, then rewrite the references.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yep. And double-check the inputs while you're in there — 2.6 maps the TIO inputs to 1033 to 1037 now, so if anything on the input side looks weird, that's why.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Good to know. I'll update the wiring diagram notes too so the next guy isn't confused.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Smart. That old 17–20 label is what got us here in the first place.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll make the edits now and test the ejector. Fingers crossed the solenoid fires.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: It will. Just remember — no alarms on this one, it fails silent, so don't wait for a fault code to tell you something's wrong.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem at i4L-R524 in cell B. I got a tingle off the metal housing of that new vacuum gripper during a dry run.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: A tingle? You okay? That gripper was put in yesterday, right?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, contractor installed it. I checked with the multimeter between the gripper housing and the robot base ground point and I'm reading 48 VAC with the robot powered.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Forty-eight volts floating on the housing, that's a serious fault. Did the contractor run a separate ground wire?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Doesn't look like it. He said the robot's existing grounding should be enough. I was thinking maybe we just wrap the housing in insulating tape for now so nobody gets zapped.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that — insulating tape is not a valid fix. The manual requires a ground connection from the equipment to the robot base ground point. Tape just hides the fault.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so where do I actually land the ground wire? I was going to use the nearest cabinet frame.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, not the cabinet frame. At Da Nang Line 9, the grounding point on the i4L-R524 base is the M6 stud behind the J1 cover. That's the one you want.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Behind the J1 cover, got it. What gauge wire?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Use a 1.5 mm² green/yellow wire to that base stud. We had a 2020 incident on Line 9, same kind of tingle from an ungrounded gripper, and that was the fix.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. Why did the contractor skip it though? Seems like an obvious thing.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The contractor's ground wire is often omitted because the gripper's quick-disconnect plug has no ground pin. So you need a separate ring terminal on the housing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense now. Hey, did you see the spare-parts delivery came in? The new proximity sensors for Line 7 are finally here.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw the boxes by the crib. We'll deal with those after this. First thing, before anyone runs production, you verify zero voltage between the tooling housing and the base ground point with a calibrated meter.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Zero volts, calibrated meter. Should I just assume the robot's protective earth already covers the tool flange?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, that's wrong. The manual states the Joint 3 quill and tool flange are not grounded to protective earth. That's exactly why you need the separate wire.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So this gripper's listed as hazardous voltage equipment in the cell risk assessment anyway — 230 VAC pump with a 24 VDC control interface.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, and that's why grounding it isn't optional. Like I said about the base stud, land the ring terminal there and torque it down properly.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. What's the shift schedule looking like after this? Are we still on days next week?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Same rotation, days through Thursday. Anyway, once you've got the wire on, do the meter check again before you clear the cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. And if it still reads something after I ground it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then we've got a different fault and we dig deeper. But nine times out of ten it's just that missing wire to the base ground point.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Sounds good. I'll grab the wire and ring terminal from the crib. You want lunch after?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Sure, once this is signed off. Just don't let production start until that zero-voltage check passes, alright?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Copy that. I'll message you when it's done.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, i4L-R911 over at Plant Da Nang, Line 12, Inspection cell B threw error -1201 twice this morning. Power cycle clears it, but it comes back within half an hour.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Twice already, huh. Before you touch the controller — did you pull the FB.ERROR details? That's where the subcode lives, and the manual wouldn't push you there for nothing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Not yet, I just saw -1201 and cycled it. The fieldbus cable does run right past that new welding station they fired up last week, and no other robot on Line 12 is complaining.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that welding station is a red flag. Last time this happened in Da Nang, it was a loose M12 connector at the robot base — thermal cycling works those loose over time. So check that torque first, don't just yank the cable.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And read FB.ERROR properly. On this cell, subcode 3 means a cable shield break near the welding station. That tells you it's the fieldbus side, not the robot itself.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: To confirm it's electromagnetic interference, temporarily route that fieldbus cable 30 cm away from the welding transformer. If the errors stop, you've found it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: But only replace the fieldbus cable after you've checked the connector torque and shield continuity with a multimeter. New cable won't help if the connector's just loose.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it — FB.ERROR subcode, M12 torque, shield continuity, then the 30 cm reroute test. I'll report back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help. At 09:15 on Line 12, Inspection cell A, I tried to send a recipe file via FTP from FX5-PLC859 to the line server, and it failed with error code 4C44H. It happened twice in 10 minutes, HMI showed 'FTP client error', file didn't transfer.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 4C44H? That's the FTP client file transfer error. Did you notice anything about the PLC's backup/restore LED while you were trying?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, actually the backup/restore LED was blinking green during both failed attempts. So a backup was in progress. But I didn't change any FTP settings or cables recently.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, that blinking green is the clue. The root cause of 4C44H is typically a conflict between the FTP client and the CPU module's backup/restore process, not a network fault. So don't go restarting the FTP server.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so it's not the server. Should I just retry the FTP transfer right away?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, that'll just throw the same 4C44H again. The manual says retry only after the backup/restore function has finished. But better yet, before you trigger any FTP file transfer, always check the backup/restore completion flag SM6015.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: SM6015. Got it. So I should wait for that flag to be on before even trying.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And on Line 12, we schedule the FTP client transfer at 03:00 when no backup/restore or recipe update is running. That avoids the whole conflict.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 03:00, that makes sense. But why was a backup running at 09:15 anyway? Nobody told me about a scheduled backup.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Last month we had a similar mess. The backup/restore function on FX5-PLC859 was accidentally left running after a power dip. That caused repeated 4C44H errors for 2 hours until we caught it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Two hours? Wow. So someone forgot to stop the backup after the power came back.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yep. Power dip, then the backup started automatically or got triggered, and nobody checked SM6015. So we kept getting 4C44H. That's why I always check that flag first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check SM6015 from now on. By the way, did you see the spare-parts delivery for the inspection camera? It was supposed to arrive this morning.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, I haven't. I think it's coming after lunch. Speaking of lunch, are you on first shift tomorrow or second?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: First shift. But back to the FTP thing—so if I see SM6015 is off, I just wait, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. If SM6015 is off, the backup/restore is still active. Wait until it's on, then retry. Also, error codes are stored in SD10130 through SD10137 for connections 1 to 8, so you can check which connection had the issue.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: SD10130 to SD10137. I'll look at those next time. So the fix is just to wait for backup to finish, or schedule at 03:00.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And don't restart the FTP server or touch cables—4C44H is a CPU module backup/restore conflict, not a network fault. That's the key thing to remember.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I'll note that down. Also, the line 12 conveyor had a minor jam earlier, but it's cleared now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Oh, and remind me later—I need to check the spare-parts delivery for the other machine, the one on line 14. But anyway, you're clear on the FTP issue?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yes, clear. Check SM6015, wait for backup to finish, schedule at 03:00. Thanks!

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No problem. And if you see 4C44H again, just remember last month's two-hour mess. Always check that flag first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, i4L-R249 just stopped again with error -1021 on motor 2. That's the third time in the last hour, always after about 20 minutes of continuous 80% speed operation on the high-speed pick-and-place cycle.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: We bumped the throughput target from 600 to 750 cycles per hour recently. And it's 38°C near the robot base and climbing this afternoon. What's the plan?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First thing, check the regenerative dump resistor temperature. A hot resistor often tells you there have been repeated duty-cycle events.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check it. But should we just replace motor 2? It's the one that keeps faulting.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace it. The manual says the servo disabled power to protect the hardware, not that the motor failed. On Line 9, motor 2 of i4L-R249 historically overheats when ambient exceeds 35°C. Apply external fan cooling before you reduce speed.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So after we cool it down and re-enable High Power, do we just run it like before?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. Set acceleration for joint 2 to 65% and speed to 70% on the first shift after a duty-cycle alarm. Don't just restart High Power without reducing speed, or it'll recur and could damage hardware.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: We usually start it cold in the morning. Anything special for that?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Always perform a 5-minute warm-up at 20% speed if the robot has been idle overnight in Binh Duong's humid mornings.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So warm-up first, then run at the reduced joint 2 settings, and keep the external fan on motor 2 when it's hot.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And log the dump resistor temp each time. If it's hot again, we know the duty cycle is still too high.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: I'll adjust the throughput target for now so we're not pushing 750 cycles per hour in this heat. Let's get it cooled and restarted properly.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on the i4L-R765 in Inspection cell A. I pressed the built-in brake release button to hand-move Joint 3, and the quill just dropped on me.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: The quill dropped? Was the end-effector still on it?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, tool was still attached. Dropped maybe 8 mm in like a third of a second, flange hit the fixture before I could grab it. It was running fine earlier, no brake alarms. High Power was disabled, 24 volt control was on.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing — on the R765 you always pull the payload off and put a 50 mm wooden block under the Joint 3 quill before you ever press that release button. Every time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right. Should I be worried about the brake itself though? Like replace it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't go swapping it. That Joint 3 brake's held a 5 kg payload without slipping for 14 months now, and it still drops 3 to 4 mm if the quill isn't supported. That's just how it is. A 2 mm drop during release is normal on this machine — you only investigate if it goes past 5 mm under a 100 N downward load.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And if you want to do it remotely, use ACE to enable the remote brake release input — but only after you lock out the cell door and check nobody's under the quill. Oh, and did the spare gripper fingers show up yet? I'm still waiting on that delivery.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No sign of them. I'll grab the wooden block and pull the tool before we touch it again.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need your help on Line 7. Cell C stopped mid-cycle at 08:15 and the HMI on the FX5-PLC320 is showing error code C400H.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: C400H, that's the predefined protocol error on the SP.ECPRTCL instruction. Did the operator try to restart it?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, twice. Both times it came right back with C400H. The protocol setting data was last modified two days ago during a recipe change for the new tray size.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. On this cell, after any protocol setting data change, we always power-cycle the FX5-PLC320 before running SP.ECPRTCL. That forces SD10692 high.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So you're saying the ready flag SD10692 is still sitting at 0? The manual says C400H happens when SP.ECPRTCL runs while SD10692 is 0.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, and it can stay 0 for up to 3 seconds after a protocol data write. We wait for it in the ladder before enabling the instruction.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I just replace the CPU module? The manual lists that as one of the actions, and the operator's already impatient.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, hold off on that. Before replacing the CPU module, we check the SD10692 monitor and re-download the protocol setting data from the engineering tool.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. But would just cycling the power clear it without rewriting the protocol setting data?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not reliably. Historically, C400H on this machine was caused by a corrupted protocol file from an interrupted download, not a bad CPU.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the file from that recipe change two days ago might be bad? Nothing was touched on the Ethernet port, no cable changes.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Go into the engineering tool, re-download the protocol setting data, then power-cycle the FX5-PLC320 and check that SD10692 goes high before SP.ECPRTCL runs.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Re-download first, then power-cycle, then verify SD10692. I'll do that now and report back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Morning. At 06:40 start-up, MR-JE-AX356 on inspection cell A threw AL. 888 and the axis won't enable at all.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Operator cycled the 24 V three times in two minutes, but the alarm came right back every time. Nothing in the alarm history, and we haven't seen this on that amp in six months.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you condemn that MR-JE-AX356, reseat CN1 and CN3 and check the 24 V control supply for ripple. We had a loose CN3 encoder connector on this line once that gave a watchdog alarm, and it went away the moment the connector was reseated.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. And should I just order a new amplifier now, or is that too early?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Too early. A loose CN3 or CN1 can cause the same watchdog. If AL. 888 still repeats after you reseat the connectors, then pull the spare MR-JE from the Line 2 crib and swap it in, and keep the suspect unit for bench testing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And I won't keep cycling it like the operator did.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, don't power-cycle this amplifier more than twice in ten minutes. Repeated cycling can damage the servo amplifier and the servo motor. And don't go swapping the HG motor first, the manual points to the amp's internal parts for AL. 888.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on i4L-R910 down in cell F, Line 9. It threw error -606 three times this afternoon, between 13:40 and 14:10, right in the middle of peak pick cycle.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Overheated again? Alright, first thing you check on the i4L-R910 for repeated -606 is the cabinet fan filter. At the dust level in that plant it clogs up in about 90 days.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, that filter was last cleaned four months ago. And I checked the intake, ambient's reading 41 degrees. They also bumped the cycle rate from 55 to 68 picks per minute this week for the throughput trial.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. Cell F historically overheats once cycle rate goes past 60 picks per minute on the afternoon shift. Cap it at 58 until the filter's changed, that'll hold you over.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: And on the i4L-R910, put a 10-second dwell after every 500 picks. That keeps the processor board below its trip point during peak runs.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Someone was saying we should just swap out the embedded processor board, but that seemed like overkill.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Waste of a board. Back in the 2022 summer overheating incident on Line 9, that was traced to a blocked cabinet filter, not a failed fan. So check the airflow before you touch any electronics.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. I'll go pull that filter and set the rate cap. Oh, and did the spare-parts delivery for Line 7 come in this morning?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got a weird one on FX5-PLC362 over at Plant Dong Nai, Line 11, Palletizing cell C. The HMI keeps throwing timeout errors on the simple CPU communication link every 8 to 12 minutes during the morning shift. I was connected with my laptop doing a MELSOFT connection over UDP at the same time, and the timeouts started about 20 minutes after I opened that connection. Before that the link ran for 6 hours without a single timeout. Switch shows the Ethernet load around 65% during the timeout windows, and the PLC scan time jumps from 4 ms to 9 ms.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on, before you start swapping cards — did you open that MELSOFT session on UDP? On Line 11 palletizing, keep the MELSOFT laptop connection on TCP port 5007 instead of UDP, otherwise you starve the simple CPU communication receive buffer. That's exactly what bites you.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, it was UDP. But could the Ethernet module itself be going bad? I was thinking maybe we just replace it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace it yet. The manual is clear — this timeout is UDP reception not completing under heavy load, not a hardware failure. And listen, we had the same thing back in 2019 on this exact FX5-PLC362. Traced it to a UDP MELSOFT session the night shift left open. Not a faulty Ethernet module. Before you blame the PLC at all, go check the managed switch port counters for the CPU module — look for receive discards above 0.1% of packets.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll pull those counters. Also, should I switch the simple CPU communication itself over to UDP so it matches my MELSOFT connection?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, opposite. If other communications have to run during simple CPU communication, use TCP, that's what the manual recommends. Oh — and did the spare-parts delivery for Line 9 come in this morning? I need those rollers before lunch.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I think it's on the dock, I'll check after this. So just leave the simple CPU communication as is?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, and while you're in there, schedule the simple CPU communication execution interval at 200 ms minimum on cell C. The palletizing robot scan time peaks at 8 ms during layer changes, so anything faster than that just adds load for nothing.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need your help. MR-JE-AX730 on Line 3 threw alarm 91.1 at 14:30, right in the middle of continuous machining.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Overheat warning, huh. What's the temperature looking like around that amplifier?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I measured near the amplifier, it's 57 degrees. And the cabinet door's been shut for about 3 hours before it popped up.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 57 at the amplifier. But go measure at the top of the cabinet too, not just at the amp. Heat rises, so the top is usually the real number.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll grab a reading up top. Anything else I should be looking at while I'm in there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: How's it mounted? How much clearance on the sides?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: It's in with the other drives, only about 10 mm on each side.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 10 mm is tight. If the ambient is below 55, then you check the close mounting spacing against what the manual says is minimum. That's the first thing I'd verify.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So if it's under 55, the spacing could be the whole problem?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Last time this happened on another cell, everyone wanted to swap the amplifier out right away. Turned out it was just the spacing and airflow.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Someone did say we should just replace the servo amplifier, that the warning means internal failure.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't jump to that. And don't ignore it either — it's only a warning now, but let it ride and you'll be replacing more than an amp.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Fair. So what about the cabinet cooling itself?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: When was the cooling fan last touched? The filter on that fan needs cleaning every 3 months.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'd have to check the log. I think the fan was replaced a while back.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Check it — that fan was replaced 8 months ago, so the filter's way overdue if nobody's been on it every 3 months.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. What can I do right now so we don't lose the shift?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: For a quick fix, open the cabinet door and put a portable fan on it. That'll bring the temp down while you sort the real cause.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Just leave the door open then?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Only as a temporary measure, and you have to log it as temporary. Don't let it become the permanent setup.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So top-of-cabinet temp, then spacing check, then the fan filter.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. Get me the top reading and we'll go from there.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I'm stuck on FX5-PLC119 over in cell E — it's throwing a MODBUS serial fault. HMI shows SM8402 ON and error 7307H in SD8402 on channel 1. Started right after the integrator swapped the function code from 03H to 10H this morning.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, 7307H is an unsupported function code error at the slave. Before you touch anything in the protocol settings, go check the flow meter's vendor manual — that cell's meter only supports 03H and 04H. So 10H was never going to work.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Oh. So the integrator just picked the wrong code?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Looks like it. And listen — we saw this exact 7307H back in March 2023 on Line 8 after a firmware update reset SD9120 through SD9123 to defaults. Re-importing the saved protocol file fixed it right away.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Are we still on for lunch at eleven-thirty? The canteen's doing that noodle thing today.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll catch up after — I want to get this line running first.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There's a known-good protocol setting file on the maintenance laptop in the cell E cabinet. Just load that instead of rebuilding the settings by hand — saves you from typos in the registers.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Should I restart the PLC after loading it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Restarting the PLC won't hold — the error comes back in a couple minutes because the slave is still rejecting 10H. After you fix the master's function code back to 03H, power-cycle the slave device too. The slave caches the previous request format until you reset it.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: By the way, the spare-parts delivery for cell B got pushed to Thursday, so don't expect those proximity sensors tomorrow.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Noted. Junior, one more thing — don't go swapping the FX5 CPU. 7307H is a slave-side unsupported function code, not a CPU hardware failure. And don't just force the master to retry, the slave will keep rejecting it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right, I'll pull the saved file and load it now.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Also, the PM for the grinder on Line 9 is moved to next Tuesday — just so you both know.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Sounds good. Once you've loaded the file and power-cycled the meter, watch SD8402 for a few minutes — if 7307H stays clear, you're done.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, the remote brake release on i4L-R443 isn't working. The button on the operator panel won't release Joint 3 or Joint 4, but the built-in button on the outer link still works fine.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, does the XIO input 6.2 LED light up on the controller when you press that remote button?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, it stays dark. And we just added a new safety gate signal last week — the remote brake release was working before that.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: First thing: on the i4L at Hai Phong, the ACE Brake Release Input setting can revert to disabled after a controller firmware update. Check that setting before anything else.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Before you dig in, remember the line's running until 2 PM. Can you look at it during lunch?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, I can check it then. But I already looked at the ACE setting and it's enabled.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, then next: the remote brake release pushbutton on Line 1 Packaging cell E has a 24 VDC supply shared with the safety gate. A loose terminal there causes intermittent failures.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I should check the terminal block in the panel?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Measure 24 VDC at XIO connector pin 18 while pressing the remote pushbutton. If it's absent, trace back to the panel terminal block before you even think about replacing the XIO board.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Also, the spare parts delivery for the other line is coming at 3. Can someone sign for it?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I can do that after I check the voltage. But what if the voltage is there?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then you look at the XIO board. But since 2022, three i4L controllers at Hai Phong have had XIO input 6.2 fail after a nearby welding cable shorted. So inspect for cable damage before ordering parts.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Welding cable? There is a welding station on the other side of the wall, but that's pretty far.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Doesn't matter. Just check the cable runs near the robot for any sign of damage or shorting.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: I heard the packaging cell E had a similar issue last year. Did we ever find the root cause?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That was a loose terminal on the shared 24 V supply. Same thing could be happening here.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll check the ACE setting again, then the terminal block, then measure at pin 18. If all good, I'll look for cable damage.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And don't forget the warning label for the remote brake release — the z-axis can fall due to gravity if the brake is released.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Lunch is at 12:30 today, by the way. The cafeteria has pho.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Nice. I'll try to get this done before then. Thanks for the tips.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need a hand. At 14:20 today FX5-PLC339 on Line 4, pick-and-place cell C, just lost Ethernet. CPU stopped processing, whole network dropped.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Module diagnostics gave me error code 2160H, IP address duplication. Event log has the entry, but I can't read Un\G201, Un\G202 to Un\G204, or Un\G205 to Un\G207 at all.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's expected on this unit. The CPU firmware on FX5-PLC339 is version 1.050, so IP duplication causes a hard stop and those special devices just aren't supported.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I can't get the duplicate address from the PLC? Should I just swap the Ethernet module?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't swap the module. The manual says this is an IP conflict, not hardware failure. Always check the network switch MAC address table to find the duplicate IP without relying on the PLC special devices.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Anything new on the network side? We added a device to that subnet yesterday.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That fits. The most common duplicate IP source on Line 4 is a laptop with a static IP left in the 192.168.1.0/24 range by the vision system vendor.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, found it. Can I just clear the error from the HMI to get the line back up?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No. Clearing the error without changing the IP won't restore the network, the duplication is still there and the error will just come back.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So I change the duplicated IP to something unique first, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, make it unique. Then perform a full power cycle, not just a reset, to clear the held error and make sure the network stack reinitializes.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Power cycle, then reconnect the CPU module?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. The error info is held until a power cycle, reset, or error clear, so the full power cycle is what actually clears it properly. Reconnect and confirm the link.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good. Let me know once Line 4 is back and I'll log the vendor laptop.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a problem on Line 1 Inspection cell E. The MR-JE-AX554 is showing 'b##' and the HG motor won't move on a normal indexing command. No alarm, servo-on is there from the controller. Happened after a tech used MR Configurator2 on it last night for a test run.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, 'b##' after a test run on this cell? That's the test operation mode still enabled. First thing, don't touch the motor cable yet — verify the servo-on signal at CN1.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Servo-on at CN1 looks present. I checked it with the meter. So what next? Should I swap the drive or the motor?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace anything yet. Last time this happened, it was just the test mode left on. On this cell, you clear 'b##' by cycling [Pr. PC05] to 0000 and then power-cycling the amplifier. Not by replacing the drive.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so set PC05 to 0000 and power-cycle. But wait, the U/V/W cables were re-terminated last week during PM. Could that be causing the motor not to run?

turns.speaker: expert_01
