turns.text: Good point. Axis 554's U/V/W cable was re-pinned last week. Before you suspect the motor, check the U/V/W terminal torque at 1.2 N·m. If it's loose, that'll stop it from running.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it, I'll check torque. But why did the test mode stay on? The manual says check [Pr. PC05], but I don't see why it would be left at 0001.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There's a local parameter note on MR-JE-AX554 — [Pr. PC05] was left at 0001 after the last test run on 2024-06-10. That's why it's showing 'b##'. So cycle it back to 0000 and power-cycle.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll set PC05 to 0000 and power-cycle. But just to be sure, if the motor still doesn't move after that, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then you check the U/V/W wiring and torque at 1.2 N·m. But remember, when the display is 'b##', first verify the servo-on signal at CN1 before touching any motor cable. You already did that, so next is the parameter and power-cycle.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Understood. So order is: check CN1, then PC05 to 0000, power-cycle, then torque check. No drive or motor swap.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And don't let anyone talk you into replacing the HG motor or the MR-JE amplifier. The 'b##' points to the test mode parameter, not a hardware failure. Just clear PC05 and cycle power.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Thanks, I'll do that now and let you know.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with MR-JE-AX353 on Line 5, cell E. It's showing F6.6 cam control inactive every time we try to start the pick-and-place cam cycle, and it started right after we downloaded new cam data this morning.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Did you power-cycle the amplifier after that cam data download? On the MR-JE you always have to cycle power after any cam data write, even if the drive looks ready.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: No, we didn't cycle power. And the operator switched the cam control command on while the servo was already on, without doing a home return since the last power-down. Should I just swap the amplifier? F6 sounds like an internal cam control failure.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't replace anything yet. The F6.6 sequence on Line 5 has to be power cycle first, then home position return, then servo-on, then cam control command. That order matters.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so if we do the power cycle and home return properly, the alarm should clear? What if it comes back anyway?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If F6.6 persists after a correct power cycle and home return, check parameter PA05 home position offset before you replace any hardware. That offset being off will keep triggering it.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. One more thing, the operator said the drive also dropped servo-off during cam control a few times before this. Could that be related?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's the 24 volt control supply on cell E dipping below 21 volts when the adjacent welder fires. It's caused servo-off mid-cam three times since January, so get that supply checked too.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need a hand with MR-JE-AX426 on Line 6, cell B. It keeps tripping Alarm 30.1 about forty seconds into every downward indexing cycle, maybe five times a shift.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing — when did this start?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Same afternoon as the cabinet cleanup last Tuesday. The brake resistor got rewired to a new terminal block, and then it started tripping.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right, that fits. Have you looked at Pr. PA02 yet?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, it reads 0000. But the cabinet label says there's an external regenerative option.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There's your problem. At cell B the external regenerative option is mounted on the rear panel, so Pr. PA02 has to be set to 0001, not 0000.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I just change PA02 to 0001?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's part of it, but on this line always verify Pr. PA02 and the resistor connection before you go checking supply voltage, because the 2022 rewiring caused the same nuisance trips.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I measured 231 volts AC at the drive terminals during the fault, by the way.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's fine — below the manual's 264 volt threshold, so supply voltage isn't your issue. When the alarm repeats every cycle, first compare the cabinet label against Pr. PA02 instead of opening the motor cable.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: What are we looking at here? Do we need to swap the amplifier?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the servo amplifier. The manual shows 30.1 is usually a resistor setting or connection problem, and this drive was working before the rewiring.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Should I check the terminal block too?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. In 2023 a loose screw on the new terminal block caused intermittent 30.1 trips for three weeks until the torque was rechecked at 1.2 N·m.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I'll set PA02 to 0001, check the resistor connection, and torque that terminal block to 1.2 N·m.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. And remember, always verify Pr. PA02 and the resistor connection before checking supply voltage on this line.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good, let's get it done and log the fix.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. Thanks.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, we've got a problem on FX5-PLC873. SCADA's throwing error 7167H every time I try to write a recipe parameter to it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 7167H. Okay. When did this start, and what's the PLC doing right now?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Started today around 14:20. The PLC's been in RUN mode since the last maintenance on the fifth, and nothing's changed hardware-wise.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: But we did deploy a new SCADA recipe at 13:00. And reading from the PLC still works fine — only the write fails.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Reading's fine but writing isn't? That sounds like a comms module going bad to me. Those 7000-range codes usually mean hardware.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold on, don't swap anything yet. On the FX5, the RUN-mode write enable bit lives in D8120. A recipe download can reset D-registers and clear that bit by accident.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: So you're saying the recipe we pushed killed our write permission?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: It wouldn't be the first time. Back in March we had almost the same thing — turned out a corrupted recipe file had set D8120 to zero. Restoring the default value fixed it straight away.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I should just go in and write D8120 back to its default?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you touch any PLC mode or register, verify the machining cell is in a safe stop and no axis motion is commanded. That comes first, every time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, I'll check with the cell operator that everything's stopped. What if production needs this recipe written right now?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: If it's urgent you can temporarily switch the CPU to STOP, do the write, then put it back to RUN. But confirm with production first that stopping the line is acceptable.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Stopping the cell without warning could wreck the part in the fixture. We don't do that without asking.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. And that's exactly why we check the safe stop condition before changing modes — an unplanned stop mid-machining is what causes damage, not the mode change itself.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. So first safe stop, then look at D8120?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes. Check D8120 and see if it got zeroed. If it did, restore the default and try the write again while still in RUN.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if restoring D8120 doesn't fix it, then what?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then we go the STOP route. But we confirm with production first, do the write in STOP, then return to RUN.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: I'll radio the line lead now so we're covered either way.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I'll pull up D8120 on the monitor and check its current value.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember, in March the fix was just restoring that default value — no module replacement, nothing fancy.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: D8120 reads zero. That matches what you said.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: There it is. Restore the default, then retry the recipe write.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Write went through, no error. Recipe's in.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Next time a recipe download wipes D8120, you'll know where to look first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, need a hand with FX5-PLC987 over at Plant Binh Duong, Line 2, Palletizing cell B. Ethernet diagnostics for connection No. 1 is showing Latest Error Code C0H and TCP Status 'Closed'.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: PING to 192.168.1.50, the palletizing robot, fails with 100% packet loss, but PING to 192.168.1.1, the switch, works fine. The robot was replaced last week after a mechanical crash and configured with the same IP, and yesterday the cable to the robot was re-terminated because the old connector was loose.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Don't swap the PLC Ethernet module yet. On FX5-PLC987, connection No. 1 is configured as TCP Active to 192.168.1.50 port 5000, and a closed TCP status with error C0H usually means the remote device is not listening.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Two things to check first. After replacing a robot on this line, always power-cycle the robot controller before re-testing Ethernet communications, because the new controller may hold a stale ARP entry. And the palletizing robot's Ethernet port is sensitive to cable strain, so check that the RJ45 clip is fully seated and the cable is not pulled tight before you even think about replacing any PLC module.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so power-cycle the controller and reseat the RJ45. Should I also worry about the firewall on the new robot?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yes, that's exactly the kind of thing to look at. In 2023, a similar C0H error on Line 2 was caused by the robot's firewall blocking port 5000 after a firmware update, not by a faulty PLC.

turns.speaker: supervisor_01
turns.text: Good, so we're not pulling the PLC module. Junior, do the power-cycle and check that RJ45 seating, then confirm port 5000 isn't blocked. Report back before the end of shift.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Will do. And I'll run the PING from GX Works3 connected to the CPU module, not from my office laptop this time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, you got a minute? i4L-R436 up in cell D on line 9 threw a -1007 motor stalled fault on Mtr #2 twice this morning, 08:12 and 09:47.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Both times at the same spot?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Yeah, right after the gripper comes down near the pallet corner. Operator just re-enabled High Power and it ran fine for a few cycles, then did it again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We changed the pallet stack pattern yesterday, didn't we?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: New pattern, corner cases sit about 5 mm higher now.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, before you even think about pulling Mtr #2, that stall at the pallet corner on this machine usually means the case corner is catching the pallet lip. It's not a motor fault.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So don't swap the motor?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Not yet. First jog joint 2 slowly through that stall position with the gripper empty and feel for mechanical binding. Do that before you touch Mtr #2.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. And if it binds?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then you know it's mechanical. The new pattern on cell D puts those corner cases 5 mm high, so you need to lower the gripper by 5 mm in the approach step.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Five millimeters in the approach. Got it.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: We had a -1007 on cell D back in 2023, same corner, and that one was fixed by adjusting the case drop height, not by replacing the motor.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, that makes sense. Oh, by the way, did you hear about the spare parts delivery?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, what about it?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The gripper pads for line 9 are on backorder till Thursday. And the canteen's doing that noodle thing for lunch again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Figures. Anyway, don't just keep re-enabling High Power and repeating the motion like the operator did. The manual says check for obstacles and make sure the joint moves freely first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Right, so obstacle check, then free movement, then repeat.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. And swapping Mtr #2 right away is premature. The manual and our site history both point to an obstacle or path issue, so check that first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. Shift change is at 2, you gonna be around after?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I'll be here. Cell B's been making noise too, I gotta look at that later.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, I'll go jog joint 2 and check the corner.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Lower that gripper 5 mm in the approach step and let me know if the binding's gone.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, got a minute? MR-JE-AX635 on Line 6, Assembly cell C — we replaced the X-axis coupling during last night's shutdown, and now there's a low-frequency vibration on the load side.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Low frequency, huh. Does it show up right away or only at speed?

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Only when the axis moves above 400 mm/s and the load is over 60 percent of rated torque. No alarm, no warning on the drive.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: On this cell, a load-side vibration that only shows above 400 mm/s has twice been traced to coupling backlash, not gain settings. So before you go chasing parameters, think coupling.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: I was actually about to drop Pr. PA09 auto tuning response to calm it down. That's the quick fix, right?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Hold off on that. The manual points load-side vibration at advanced vibration suppression control II and a coupling backlash check first. Don't touch the response yet.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay. But could the motor itself be getting weak? Maybe we should just swap the servo motor.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't jump to replacing the motor. Load-side vibration like this is a machine-side thing — coupling backlash and adjustment. Motor swap is the last thing you'd try.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Before you even think about advanced vibration suppression control II, check the coupling clamp screws. They need to be torqued to 5 N·m, and in the order marked on the flange. Not just snug — 5 N·m, in that sequence.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Same spacer length went back in, but I didn't re-measure the load shaft runout after reassembly. Could that matter?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: It can. But first, pull up the status display and record the cumulative feedback pulse count for one full stroke. Watch it — it needs to advance smoothly before you adjust any filter.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Smooth as in no jumps or stalls in the count?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. If that count stutters, you've got a mechanical issue and no filter will fix it. Get that reading first.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. Hey, did you see the schedule change for next week? They've moved us to the early shift.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, I saw that. Early shift means we lose our morning coffee run, so plan around it. Anyway — back to the axis.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: One more thing — the spare-parts delivery for cell B is supposed to land Thursday. Should I chase it?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Chase it after lunch, not now. And don't forget the local parameter set for this axis uses a machine resonance suppression filter at 3.5 kHz — that's higher than the factory default, so don't assume it's stock.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: 3.5 kHz, noted. So what's the order — clamp screws first, then the pulse count, then suppression control?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Exactly. Torque the clamps to 5 N·m in the flange order, confirm the pulse count climbs smooth over a full stroke, and only then look at advanced vibration suppression control II.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And if all that checks out and it still vibrates?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Then go back and measure the load shaft runout properly. Last time on this cell we skipped that and wasted half a shift on gain tuning. It was the coupling the whole time.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright. I'll grab the torque wrench and start with the clamp screws.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. And remember the 3.5 kHz filter is already in there — don't let anyone tell you it's the default. Report back after the pulse count check.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I've got a weird one on the FX5-PLC480 at Plant Hai Phong, Line 2, Machining cell B. I changed the IP in the module parameter yesterday afternoon to 192.168.10.20, cycled power at 17:05, and it looked fine. But this morning at 06:40 shift start it came up as 192.168.10.55 again. Then after a 10-minute power-down for panel cleaning, the old address came back again.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Yeah, that's the storage area overriding your parameter. On Line 2 Machining cell B, the last technician wrote 192.168.10.55 into the IP storage area back in 2022, and the module parameter was never cleared afterward. So your parameter change is just sitting there ignored.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So the parameter setting isn't what's actually being used? I saw SM8498 ON and Un\G56 toggling briefly during the parameter download. No alarms on the CPU, but SCADA drops off after every power cycle.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Right. Before you touch parameters on the FX5-PLC480, check SM8498 and Un\G60 first to confirm whether the storage-area override is active. SM8498 being ON means the change function is enabled — it doesn't tell you which address is actually winning.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so Un\G60 is the one that shows if the storage area is holding the value. I was thinking of just re-downloading the module parameter a second time to make the new IP stick. Would that work?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, re-downloading won't help. The storage area still takes precedence until it's cleared, so the second download just gets overridden again. Don't waste a cycle on that.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. And someone suggested toggling SM8492 off and on quickly to force the write through. Is that safe?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't do that. The manual warns that the second write gets ignored and the first value stays. So you'd just end up with the same old address and no clear indication why.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Alright, so how do I actually get my 192.168.10.20 to take?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: To restore the parameter address on this PLC, you clear the storage area with SM8495, then power-cycle the CPU after the request drops to off. That's what removes the 2022 value that's been overriding everything.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: And after that, just power cycle and check the address?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Wait at least 30 seconds after Un\G58 returns to 0 before you pull 24 V from the FX5-PLC480 rack. If you cut power too early during the clear, the values may not get applied and you're back where you started.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So sequence is: check SM8498 and Un\G60, clear with SM8495, wait for Un\G58 to hit 0, hold 30 seconds, then power-cycle the rack.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's it. And remember the module parameter is what you want to stick, so once the storage area is cleared your 192.168.10.20 will hold across power cycles.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Hey, I need help with MR-JE-AX956 on Line 9. It tripped with AL. 51 during a carton jam on the index table, and it says Overload 2. I reset it twice but it came back within 30 seconds each time during the next indexing cycle.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Okay, first thing, stop resetting it. On Line 9 you always clear the carton jam completely and then rotate the index table by hand one full turn before you reset AL. 51. If you just keep resetting without clearing the jam, the overload repeats and you can damage the amplifier.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Got it. I did check the U/V/W power cable connectors and they look fully seated, no arcing or anything. Should I go ahead and swap the HG motor since it's an overload alarm?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: No, don't replace the motor yet. On the MR-JE-AX956, torque saturation after a jam is usually caused by the mechanical brake dragging, so check the brake release gap before you even think about replacing the motor. That's where I'd start.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: The brake release gap, okay. And what about the peak load ratio? The setup tool logged 285% during the failed cycles, that seems really high.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: 285% is high, that confirms it's saturating. But before you touch any parameters, remember this cell has history. Line 9 packaging cell E has had two prior AL. 51 events in 2024, and both of them traced back to a bent guide rail after carton pile-ups.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: So I should check the guide rail then. How do I know if it's straight enough?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Run a straight edge along it and look for any bend from the pile-ups. If the guide rail is verified straight and the jam is cleared, then you can temporarily set parameter PA08 to 120 percent peak load limit for this cell. Don't do that before the rail is checked.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Okay, so clear the jam, hand-turn the table one full turn, check the brake release gap, and verify the guide rail is straight. Then set PA08 to 120 percent if it's all good?

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: That's the order. And if the guide rail is bent, straighten or replace it first, because that's what caused the last two AL. 51 events in 2024 on this cell.

turns.speaker: junior_01
turns.text: Makes sense. I'll clear the jam and hand-turn the table now, then check the brake gap and the guide rail. Thanks, I'll let you know what I find.

turns.speaker: expert_01
turns.text: Good. Just remember, PA08 at 120 percent is only temporary and only after the jam is cleared and the guide rail is verified straight, not as a fix for a bent rail.
